bluetooth-fw/qemu: drop per-packet responsiveness log to DBG

`prv_set_connection_responsiveness` fires from PutBytes on every single
packet of an install (~12/sec).  At PBL_LOG_INFO each call pushes ~76
bytes into the 1200-byte advanced_logging ring buffer, which fills in
~16 packets and forces inline `handle_buffer_sync` flushes from
KernelMain via `write_buffer_locking`'s blocking retry loop.

SystemTask is simultaneously trying to take `s_flash_write_mutex` for
its scheduled async flash flush, so the two tasks ping-pong inside
flash-logging and PutBytes processing stalls.  The bound-the-drain fix
in 2a11deb2 keeps SystemTask from getting stuck forever in the loop,
but the underlying chatter still backs the install up.

CLAUDE.md is explicit: paths that fire repeatedly under normal use
must not log at INFO.  This one does.  Demote to DBG.

drivers/uart/qemu: fix RX IRQ storm during install

`uart_set_rx_interrupt_enabled(dev, false)` flipped the firmware
`rx_int_enabled` flag before clearing the hardware CTRL_RX_IE bit.
The QEMU pebble-simple-uart is level-sensitive on RX (per the qemu
repo's `Make RX interrupt level-sensitive` change), so as long as
CTRL_RX_IE is set and the device's rx_count is > 0 the IRQ keeps
firing.

During PutBytes install bursts the host pumps bytes into the UART
faster than KernelMain can drain them.  When KernelMain enters its
qemu_serial drain loop and calls `uart_set_rx_interrupt_enabled(false)`
to take the FIFO offline for processing, the window between line 123
(flag := false) and the eventual CTRL write is enough for the
level-sensitive IRQ to fire.  The ISR sees the flag false, skips the
drain, returns — and the IRQ immediately re-fires because the hardware
enable and rx_count are both still asserted.  KernelMain crawls forward
one Thumb instruction per IRQ entry/exit cycle and the install wedges
visibly; gdb attached to a frozen QEMU shows the CPU permanently inside
`uart_irq_handler` with the saved stack frame in
`uart_set_rx_interrupt_enabled`.

Fix by ordering the writes so the hardware enable is always cleared
before the flag is dropped (and on enable, the flag is set before the
hardware is armed).  After the change the ISR can't be re-entered with
a stale enabled flag.

event_loop: force-kill on phone-initiated app launch in SDK shell

`pebble install` over pypkjs sometimes stalls the install until the dev
manually toggles to the launcher.  Pypkjs sends a `SetUTC` right before
the install BlobCommand/AppRunStateStart, which fires
PEBBLE_SET_TIME_EVENT to the running watchface.  If the watchface is a
misbehaving third-party app that's busy in its set-time handler (or
otherwise not promptly dequeuing events) when the firmware tries to
deinit it for the install, the 3-second graceful close runs to
completion before the install can proceed.  Worse, that timeout exceeds
pebble-tool's expectation in some cases and the user perceives the
install as "stuck".

stall until manual toggle.  The bug is fundamentally in the watchface,
but devs iterating on a fresh install don't care about a graceful
close of the *previous* app revision - they want the new build running
now.

end-users) keeps the polite 3s graceful behavior.  For dev SDK shell,
when an AppRunStateStart from the phone causes a launch, force-kill
the current app immediately.

fw/system: defer "Ready for communication" log until app is responsive

pebble-tool's `--emulator` mode polls the QEMU pulse serial for one of
`"<Launcher>"`, `"<SDK Home>"`, or `"Ready for communication"`, then
starts the install immediately when any of them appears.  But
`notify_system_ready_for_communication` runs from
prv_launcher_main_loop_init right after `app_manager_start_first_app`,
which has only *created* the first app's task; main_func hasn't run
yet and the app hasn't pushed any windows.

later in the trace and pebble-tool will (also) wait on those.  For a
third-party watchface whose window name doesn't match either token,
"Ready for communication" is the only thing pebble-tool ever sees, so
the install begins ~ms after the firmware logs it — which is before
the watchface is event-loop-responsive.  The resulting AppRunStateStart
arrives at a watchface that's mid-init, the install pipeline stalls,
and only manual launcher-toggling unsticks it.  Repro:
  pebble install --emulator emery  (with a 3rd-party watchface default)

run main_func and push its initial window in the meantime.

it would lock up on the second install.

services/timeline/reminders: drive from RTC, not FreeRTOS ticks

Reminders armed a new_timer countdown of (timestamp - rtc_get_time()) ms.
new_timer runs off FreeRTOS ticks, which on Sifli drift relative to RTC,
so a countdown left to run for hours could fire minutes late vs the
intended wall-clock timestamp.

rtc_get_time() against the next reminder's absolute timestamp -- the
same pattern cron uses internally. An s_reminder_armed bool tracks
whether anything is pending, since timestamp 0 is a valid epoch value.

self-correct on the next tick.

blocks, so test_reminders was never being built. The test has been
rewritten to drive the new regular_timer callback via

fw/services/activity: close TOCTOU windows in workout handlers

Three handlers and pause_workout used the same pattern: call
workout_service_is_workout_ongoing() (which takes and releases the
mutex internally), then re-acquire the mutex and dereference
s_workout_data.current_workout. Between the two acquisitions another

turning the subsequent deref into a NULL crash.

access:

    lock.
  * activity event handler: drop the early-out; pause_workout handles
    the no-workout case itself.
  * pause_workout: a single locked block that checks current_workout,
    short-circuits if already in the requested state, then performs
    the transition.

No behavior change on the success path; the race-driven NULL deref is
gone.

fw/comm/ble/ancs: keep alive-check timer alive after failed recovery

The ANCS alive-check fires every 15 minutes; if iOS doesn't respond
within 5 seconds, prv_is_ancs_alive_response_timeout_launcher_task_cb
attempts to recover by re-subscribing to the ANCS characteristics. The
timer is only re-armed on the success path, via ancs_handle_subscribe()
when the Data characteristic's CCCD response arrives without error.

If anything in that recovery path fails -- characteristics already
invalidated, gatt_client_subscriptions_subscribe() returns non-OK
synchronously, or iOS never sends a CCCD response -- the alive-check
timer stays stopped permanently. The watch then appears connected
but silently drops every notification until reboot, which is the
symptom in this bug and the related FIRM-1692 / FIRM-951 reports.

Always re-schedule the next alive check at the end of the timeout
handler. On the happy path ancs_handle_subscribe() will cancel and
reschedule via prv_ancs_is_alive_start_tracking(); on the failure
paths we still tick again in 15 minutes and get another shot at
recovery instead of dying silently.

services/light: clear user-controlled flag on backlight setting toggle

If some path leaks s_user_controlled_state set to true (e.g. a voice
window that disappears before its exit handler resets the light), the
backlight ends up pinned in LIGHT_STATE_ON: button release skips the
auto-off timer transition because the flag is honored, and the only
ways out are light_enable(false), light_reset_user_controlled(), or a
reboot.

Users hit this by toggling the backlight setting off and back on, which
is exactly the workaround the FIRM-1874 reporter described. But
light_toggle_enabled() only drives the state machine
(LIGHT_STATE_OFF -> LIGHT_STATE_ON_TIMED) and never clears
s_user_controlled_state, so the flag survives the round-trip and the
next button release still skips the fade-out timer. The user thinks
they fixed it because the light went off, but the underlying state is
still wrong.

Clear s_user_controlled_state at the top of light_toggle_enabled() and
light_toggle_ambient_sensor_enabled() so the user's escape hatch
actually restores normal behavior. This is defense-in-depth: it does
not address whatever upstream path leaked the flag, but it guarantees
that the documented recovery procedure works.

fw/applib/voice: reset backlight on mic window disappear

prv_mic_window_appear() pins the backlight via
sys_light_enable_respect_settings(true) for the duration of the
dictation session. The light is released by prv_exit_and_send_result_event()
(back button, errors, success), the StateTransitionToText branch,
and voice_window_pop() (external pop / destroy). prv_mic_window_disappear()
itself, however, only calls prv_cancel_dictation() and leaves the
backlight held on, even though the window is no longer visible.

is harmless. The hole is that disappear can fire on its own when the
mic window is interrupted (modal preempt, voice_window_lose_focus,

voice_window_pop -- the light stays pinned until something else
clears s_user_controlled_state.

handler so the appear/disappear pair is symmetric. If a later
exit path also resets the light, that's a no-op; if no later path

fw/services/data_logging: chain flush to avoid KernelBG watchdog

The periodic flush iterated all sessions under s_list_mutex on
KernelBG. Each session's comm_session_send_buffer_begin_write can
stall up to 500 ms, so once DLS_MAX_NUM_SESSIONS slots fill up the
worst case is ~10 s -- well past the KernelBG watchdog threshold.

device in an unrecoverable boot loop until a factory reset clears
flash.

system task callback (mirroring prv_reopen_next_session_system_task_cb)
so KernelBG yields between sends and the watchdog gets fed.

fw/comm/ble/ancs: resubscribe when Notification Source goes silent

The ANCS alive-check fires a Control Point write every 15 minutes and
treats iOS' reply as proof the watch is still receiving notifications.
That probe only verifies the CP path. iOS can wedge in a state where it
keeps responding to CP requests but its Notification Source push has
been silently dropped (commonly after airplane-mode toggles and timezone
swings during travel), so the watch reports itself healthy while no
notifications arrive. Re-opening the iOS Pebble app is currently the
only way to recover, which is what the FIRM-1692 reporter had to do
after a 7-day silent outage.

Track how many consecutive alive-check intervals pass without any NS
traffic. After ANCS_NO_NS_TIMEOUT_HOURS (6 h, derived from the
alive-check interval so the two don't desync) we force a CCCD
re-subscribe to nudge iOS into pushing again, skip the CP probe that
round to avoid interleaving with the CCCD writes, and schedule the
next alive check as a backup in case the CCCD response never lands.
Any NS event (add/modify/remove) resets the counter, so users with
normal notification volume never see the refresh fire; users with
genuinely quiet phones absorb at most one harmless CCCD rewrite per
6 h window.

drivers/backlight: add backlight_refresh() to recover from silent chip resets

The AW2016 LED driver on Obelix can spontaneously reset (PUIS=1) when
VBAT briefly dips below 1.25V or its I2C watchdog trips on SCL held low
>130ms. After such a reset the chip comes up with CHIPEN=0 and all
registers cleared, but there's no INT line wired back to the MCU so the
firmware has no way to notice.

Today the AW2016 driver only writes GCR1 CHIPEN_EN + LCTR/LCFG on the
0->nonzero brightness transition. Once it's cached s_brightness>0,
subsequent writes only touch PWM registers, which silently do nothing
while CHIPEN=0.

Expose a new backlight_refresh() driver entry point that re-applies the
chip-enable, configures the LED registers, and re-emits the current
color. On AW2016 it's a real recovery path; on the PWM, AW9364E, QEMU,
and stub backends it's a harmless no-op since those drivers can't desync
from cached state in the same way.

services/light: refresh backlight on no-op wake transitions

The light-service state machine short-circuits in prv_change_state when
the target brightness matches the cached value, so a tap or wrist-flick
arriving while we're already in ON_TIMED never reaches the backlight
driver. That's normally fine, but on AW2016-equipped boards (Obelix) the
chip can silently reset on a VBAT dip or I2C watchdog with no signal
back to firmware, leaving the chip stuck off while we still believe the
light is on. The user then sees the backlight fail to respond to taps,
and each new tap just re-arms the fade-out timer -- extending the
outage from a single fade cycle (~3-5s) to multiple minutes if they
keep trying.

Call backlight_refresh() on the no-brightness-change branch when the
target state is ON or ON_TIMED. backlight_refresh() is a no-op on
drivers that can't desync, and on AW2016 it re-enables the chip and
re-applies the configured color, so user-initiated wake actions always
heal a previously-reset chip.

fw: stop runaway long-press when modal steals focus

When a modal (e.g. notification window) pushes over an app mid-hold,
the kernel masks BUTTON_UP events from the app task and routes them to
the modal's click manager instead. The app's recognizer is left with
is_button_down == true and any in-flight long-press / auto-repeat
keeps firing for the entire duration of the modal — in the Music app
this means volume_repeat_timer (registered from the long-click start
handler) spams MusicCommand{VolumeUp,VolumeDown} until the modal pops,
which is bad for music and worse for the user.

Two pieces:

  * fw/applib/app: reset the click manager on focus loss as well as
    focus regain, so the runaway is torn down the instant the modal
    appears rather than the instant it pops.
  * fw/applib/ui/click: when click_{manager,recognizer}_reset() catches
    a recognizer with is_button_down && hold_timer == NULL (long-click
    fired but never released), dispatch long_click.release_handler
    before clearing state. Mirrors the BUTTON_UP path so app-side
    cleanup hooked off the release handler (Music's volume timer
    cancel) still runs.

The message key header/C/JSON tasks set dep_vars to the message-keys
dict itself. waf expects dep_vars to be a list of env variable names and
hashes env[name] for each entry into the task signature. Iterating the
dict yields message-key names, none of which are env vars, so they all

fw/drivers/ambient: add event-gated continuous sampling API

Add two independent refcounted controls on the ambient light sensor:

- prime() / release(): "I will want ALS readings soon." While the
  prime refcount is positive, the chip integrates continuously in
  the background and reads collapse to a cache hit instead of paying
  a fresh integration time per call.
- suspend() / resume(): "the photodiode is being contaminated right
  now." Intended for callers that know the backlight LED is bleeding
  into the sensor.

Physical EN_ALS = (prime > 0) && (suspend == 0). Refcount bookkeeping
lives in ambient_light_common.c (cf. Zephyr's regulator API) so it
doesn't have to be re-implemented per chip; drivers receive only the
derived (active, sampling) booleans via ambient_light_driver_set_state.

On the W1160 specifically:

- Bump IT_SLOW from 16.83 ms to 99 ms (~6x integration, ~2.4x SNR
  improvement, and one full 50 Hz mains period for natural flicker
  averaging) and SAMPLE_TIME_SLOW to 200 ms.
- Maintain a software cache of the last good DATA_ALS read in the
  driver itself. Empirically the W1160 zeroes DATA_ALS whenever
  SAMPLING_EN=0, so a primed-but-suspended read can't just fetch
  the register: it has to serve the cache. Every read that's allowed
  to trust the chip (sampling active and at least one IT elapsed
  since the last 0->1 of EN) refreshes the cache; reads that can't
  (suspended, or just-resumed and still in the first-IT window)
  serve the cache instead. The cache is dropped when the active
  window closes so the next unprimed read is fresh.
- The unprimed path is still a classic one-shot enable/poll/read/
  disable cycle for callers that don't bother priming.

OPT3001 and the test/driver stubs get no-op implementations to keep
the driver API uniform across boards.

Hold the ambient light sensor in continuous-sampling mode across

continuous mode.

ambient_light_suspend()/resume() so the photodiode isn't latching
contaminated readings while the LED is illuminating it. The driver
composes these with the prime refcount, so they remain no-ops when
no one has primed.

third_party/nimble/transport/hci_sf32lb52: block on ACL pool exhaustion

The H4 RX task allocates an ACL mbuf from mpool_acl for every inbound
packet and forwards it to ble_hs_rx_q. The host event loop drains the
queue and frees the mbuf, but it can be parked for long stretches (e.g.
blocked in gatt_client_subscriptions_handle_server_notification()
waiting on a full per-client subscription buffer). While the host is
parked, ACL packets keep arriving via IPC and accumulate in ble_hs_rx_q,
each pinning one mbuf, so the pool can drain and the next alloc fail.

Handle this in the allocator: prv_alloc_acl_from_ll() blocks until a
buffer is returned to the pool instead of returning NULL, which the H4
state machine would treat as a fatal, unrecoverable framing error. A
binary semaphore signaled from the pool put callback wakes the RX task
as soon as the host frees a buffer; a 100ms timeout guards the
give-before-wait race and the shared from_hs pool. While the RX task is
blocked it stops draining the LCPU->HCPU IPC ring, which fills and
back-pressures the controller.

This keeps the upstream hci_h4_sm_rx() asserts intact, so no out-of-tree
mynewt-nimble patch is needed.

host task and blocks up to GATT_CLIENT_SUBSCRIPTIONS_WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS
waiting for space in the per-client subscription buffer, holding the
inbound ACL mbuf and stalling the ble_hs_rx_q drain. At 100ms this far
exceeds the sf32lb52 controller's HCI IPC write tolerance (~10ms), so a
slow notification consumer starves the transport ACL pool and can
desync the H4 stream.

Make the timeout and the per-client buffer depth Kconfig options
(BLE_GATT_NOTIF_WRITE_TIMEOUT_MS, BLE_GATT_SUBSCRIPTION_DEPTH) defaulting
to the legacy 100ms / depth 4 so other BT backends are unchanged, with a
SOC_SF32LB52-conditional default of 5ms / depth 8 for the sf32lb52
transport. The shorter timeout drops the notification at the recoverable
application layer instead of stalling the transport; the deeper buffer
absorbs bursts so the timeout rarely triggers. Unit tests that build the
source mock the values via test defines.

it returns false the instant the app's event queue is full. A subscribed
app that fails to drain its event queue fast enough therefore panicked

here would risk deadlock/watchdog. The expiring-subscription event now
only sets sent_expiration_event on success so it is retried rather than
lost.

test covering the full-queue drop path.

fw/services/clock: skip hourly chime on the first timer tick

The hourly chime added in 4808b8d4 runs from prv_watch_dst(), a per-second
regular-timer callback registered by clock_init(). That registration happens
before resource_init(), and the timer fires on the NewTimer task, so the
callback can run while the resource/vibe subsystem is still initializing.

On the first boot after an OTA the RTC is lost, so clock_init() snaps it to
MIN_VALID_BOOT_TIMESTAMP, which lands exactly on the hour. The top-of-hour
check then passes on the very first tick and calls
vibe_score_create_with_resource_system() against the half-initialized
resource subsystem, corrupting the heap and tripping the task watchdog.
resource_init() is also slower right after an OTA because it installs the
freshly received resource pack, widening the race window. The watch hangs on
the boot logo and only recovers on the next boot, once resources are installed
and the clock has moved past the hour.

resource-loading path is never reached until init has settled.

fw/kernel: pool TaskTimer allocations

TaskTimer creates churn very heavily on this device class (NimBLE
allocates one callout TaskTimer per ble_npl_callout — ~55 alive at
once just for the BLE stack — and total creates over a session can
exceed 16k). Each create/free was a kernel_malloc/kernel_free of
sizeof(TaskTimer) (40 B), which left 44 B holes scattered through
the heap. Coredump from a fragmented Asterix shows 28 free blocks
averaging 135 B; the dominant fragmentation source by count is the
TaskTimer churn.

Serve TaskTimers from a fixed 192-slot slab pool kept in
.kernel_bss instead. Create/delete now move slots on/off an
intrusive free list with O(1) cost and never touch the heap
allocator after init. The pool falls back to kernel_malloc on
exhaustion so worst-case behaviour matches the old code rather
than failing harder. 192 slots is ~1.7x observed peak (111) — the
2.4 KB of slab headroom above peak costs ~3 KB of kernel heap
(.kernel_bss takes the RAM back from .kernel_heap by linker
script) and trades it for eliminating per-TaskTimer fragmentation.

until the next 5-min flush tick. Sessions with under 8000 B of
accumulated data (activity_sessions tag 84 at 26 B/record is the
canonical case) get skipped on every non-empty tick, so they have to

send buffer is contended, the acquire times out, and the data sits

fw/services/settings: recreate file on bad magic, not just remove

When a settings file is opened with a corrupt magic, prv_open removed
the file but then returned E_INVALID_OPERATION instead of retrying.
Callers (e.g. timeline_item_storage_init) log the failure but proceed
with an uninitialized SettingsFile, and the next iteration call hits
fatal_logic_error -> PBL_CROAK, rebooting. Three crashes drop the watch
into PRF, the app re-pushes the same firmware, and the cycle repeats
forever.

Mirror the version-check path one block below: recurse into prv_open
after the remove, so the next open hits the uninitialized-header branch
and writes a fresh magic. Also check the pfs_close_and_remove return
value on both paths -- when the underlying PFS delete fails (seen in
the field as "Delete of N did not complete"), naive recursion would
trade an infinite reboot loop for a stack overflow. Return the error
to the caller instead.

The same fix delivered via OTA also self-heals devices already stuck
in the loop: when PRF accepts the updated firmware, the corrupt pindb
is recreated on first boot instead of crashing.

since the last feed), it triggers reset_due_to_software_failure()
directly from the high-priority tick ISR. The reboot reason set a few

have populated stuck_task_pc/lr via prv_log_failed_message() never got

on the real call site) only kicks in when stuck_task_pc or
stuck_task_lr is non-zero, so these coredumps fall through and end up
bucketed under "Software Watchdog at Unknown Location" — exactly the
crashes we most want to root-cause, since they fire when the system is
stuck above configMAX_SYSCALL_INTERRUPT_PRIORITY.

prv_log_failed_message and call it from the immediate-coredump branch.
The TCB reads (pebble_task_get_handle_for_task, ulTaskDebugGetStackedPC

third_party/memfault: split Unexpected Reset by hardware cause

When the device goes through a real hardware reset (brownout, hardware
watchdog, pin reset, power-on), the RTC backup register that holds the
firmware-level RebootReason gets cleared. reboot_reason_get() then
returns RebootReasonCode_Unknown, which prv_pbl_reboot_to_mflt_reboot
maps to kMfltRebootReason_Unknown — and Memfault buckets all of these
together under "Unexpected Reset at Unknown Location" with no usable
PC. This bucket is enormous in production (thousands of devices) and
gives us no signal at all about what's actually causing resets.

The MCU's hardware reset cause is already captured early in main.c via
watchdog_clear_reset_flag() but only used for one log line in
debug_reboot_reason_print. Cache the McuRebootReason so the Memfault
port can read it back, and when the firmware reboot reason is Unknown,
attribute the crash to the most specific hardware cause we can see
(brownout > watchdog > pin > deep-sleep > power-on > software).

This splits the single "Unexpected Reset at Unknown Location" bucket
into per-cause Memfault issues so we can actually investigate them.

fw: fall back to non-zero PC for HardFault reboot reasons

hard_fault_handler_c uses the stacked LR as reason.extra.value. When
the fault corrupts the stack (e.g. stack overflow into MPU guard, or
a fault during exception entry) the stacked LR slot reads zero and
Memfault's PC-override falls through, bucketing the crash as
"Hard Fault at Unknown Location". Same hazard in
attempt_handle_generic_fault and in hardware_fault_landing_zone (which
called prv_kill_user_process(0) unconditionally even though
s_current_app_crash_info holds the real address).

Fall back through stacked PC, BFAR, and MMFAR (whichever is non-zero
and valid) so Memfault always has a real address to fingerprint.

fw: capture caller LR for Assert/EventQueueFull, add Memfault fallbacks

Several reboot-reason call sites either passed an explicit 0 for the
LR or read the lr register from a helper function where the compiler
may already have clobbered it. When the resulting reason.*.value was
zero, the Memfault PC-override fell through and the crash bucketed as
"<Reason> at Unknown Location".

Specifically:

- passert.c:app_error_handler_bare passed 0 as the PC; replace with
  __builtin_return_address(0) so the nRF error handler points at the
  caller.

- services/system_task/service.c:handle_system_task_send_failure used
  `register uintptr_t lr __asm("lr")` from inside a helper, which only
  captures whatever happened to still be in lr at that point. Capture
  __builtin_return_address(0) at the public-API entry instead and
  thread it through.

- kernel/events.c:event_put/_isr/_from_process: same inline-asm-lr
  pattern. Switch to __builtin_return_address(0).

Also extend the Memfault PC-override fallback ladder for the cases

tools/font: fix bit polarity in pbf_extract/pbf_repack

The firmware renderer (text_render.c) draws a pixel where the source
bit is 1 — i.e. PBF format encodes glyph bits as 1 and background as
0, matching what fontgen.py emits from freetype.

pbf_extract.py and pbf_repack.py had the convention backwards in
both comments and code, so any glyph added by editing a PNG and
running pbf_repack was encoded with inverted polarity. The mistake
was self-cancelling on a pure extract→repack round-trip, which is
how it survived undetected.

Flip the polarity in both tools to match the firmware semantics:
black PNG pixel ↔ PBF bit 1 (glyph drawn as text_color).

bluetooth-fw/nimble: crash instead of abandoning a timed-out host start

bt_driver_start() scheduled a two-stage start then waited on s_host_started.
On timeout it abandoned the attempt via ble_hs_stop(), which no-ops when the
host is still OFF, leaving the queued start event behind. That orphaned event
later ran during the next start and tripped the ble_hs_event_start_stage2
assert (ble_hs_start() returns BLE_HS_EALREADY once the host is already
enabled).

Crash on the timeout instead of abandoning: we never return to schedule a
second start, so no stale start event can linger, and the reboot cold-recovers
the controller (waking the LCPU first on SF32LB52 so the coredump captures its
RAM). Raise the host start/stop timeout to 10s so a slow but recoverable
bring-up is not rebooted; a dead controller still self-recovers earlier via the
2s HCI command timeout.

A core dump read straight out of flash ends in 0xFF erased-flash
padding. The parser recognizes 0xFFFFFFFF as the terminator key, but the
following `size` field also reads back as 0xFFFFFFFF instead of the 0 the
firmware writes, so the payload union tried to read 4 GiB of nonexistent
data and aborted with:

fw/kernel/core_dump: dump LCPU RAM last and only when its domain is up

Capturing LCPU RAM (the SF32LB52 BLE coprocessor RAM in the LPSYS
domain at 0x20400000) was added as the second memory region, ahead of
the extra-register and thread chunks. On real crashes the dump
consistently aborted right after that region: reads into the LPSYS
domain hang/fault when it is powered down, and because the region sat
before the registers and threads, every dump lost the data needed to
symbolize the crash. readcore.py then produced a register-less ELF and
GDB reported "Couldn't find general-purpose registers in core file".

Move the LCPU RAM dump to the very end, after the thread walk, mirroring
the existing "threads last in case FreeRTOS structures are corrupt"
design so a faulting read can no longer cost us the RAM, registers, and
threads. Also gate it on the HPSYS AON ISSR LP_ACTIVE bit, which the HAL
already uses to decide whether LPSYS registers are reachable, so we skip
the region entirely when the domain is off instead of hanging on it.

The Memfault upload path is unaffected: it only caches addresses within
the main SRAM dump range, so the lcpu_ram extra region was already
dropped there regardless.

fw/services/analytics: actually pack the native heartbeat record

The packed attribute was placed before the struct keyword, where GCC
silently ignores it, so native_heartbeat_record was serialized with
natural alignment (e.g. timestamp at offset 8 instead of 1, plus padding
between every misaligned member). The DLS blob therefore did not match
the compact layout the source implies.

Because the BLE disconnect counters sit at the end of the record, they
absorbed all the upstream offset drift and decoded as garbage (the
ble_disconnect_conn_spvn_tmo_count field in particular). Blobs whose tail
fields happened to be zero still decoded plausibly, masking the issue.

Move the attribute between the struct keyword and the tag using the
PACKED macro so it is honored, yielding the intended compact layout. Add
a static assertion that the record size equals the sum of its members
(computed from analytics.def) to catch any future padding regression.

The record version is left unchanged: decoders resolve the per-build
layout from DWARF via the embedded build_id, so this is not an encoding
scheme change.

drivers/vibe: fix AW86225 F0 calibration math and trim writes

Three issues in the AW86225 F0 calibration made the result ineffective
or fragile:

- The calibration step used a numerator of 10000 instead of 100000. The
  rounding that follows assumes the step is pre-scaled by 10, so the
  applied trim came out ~10x too small and the LRA was left off
  resonance. Matches the AW862XX Software Design Guide and the vendor
  driver.
- TRIM_LRA was written with a full-register write, clearing the
  OSC_TRIM_SRC bit of TRIMCFG3. Use a read-modify-write of bits [5:0].
- F0 was measured with whatever trim was already applied. Reset TRIM_LRA
  to neutral before detection so a re-calibration is not biased.

bluetooth: advertise BR/EDR Not Supported on BLE-only watches

While LE-discoverable the watch advertised AD Flags = 0x02 (LE General
Discoverable only), never setting the "BR/EDR Not Supported" bit (0x04).
Combined with a Public advertising address, dual-mode hosts (e.g. BlueZ)
treat the watch as potentially classic-capable and issue a BR/EDR Create
Connection, which returns Page Timeout since these watches have no
connectable BR/EDR. The host does not fall back to LE, so the connection
fails unless classic is disabled host-side (btmgmt bredr off).

All watches supported by this firmware are BLE-only (NimBLE, no classic
transport), so advertise Flags = 0x06 (LE General Discoverable + BR/EDR
Not Supported) from both the discovery and HRM-reconnect advertising
paths. The General Discoverable bit is preserved.

bluetooth-fw/nimble: report persistent bond state in pairing service

The Pebble Pairing Service connectivity status reported ble_is_bonded
from desc.sec_state.bonded, which NimBLE only sets once encryption has
been restored on the current link, not when a bond record exists. If the
gateway reads the connectivity characteristic after connecting but before
re-encrypting the link, the watch reports itself as unpaired even though a
valid bond is present (the peer address was resolved via the stored IRK).

On Android this drives a reconnect storm: the app sees paired=false,
calls createBond(), which the OS rejects because a bond already exists,
the link is torn down (reason 0x213) and the cycle repeats until the user
manually forgets the device.

Derive ble_is_bonded from the NimBLE security store keyed on the peer
identity address, and populate has_bonded_gateway from the stored bond
count, matching the field semantics documented in the connectivity status
struct. Existing bondings are restored into the store before the link is
brought up, so the record is present even before re-encryption.

Fixes FIRM-2212

fw/coredump: wake LCPU during dump so BLE crashes capture its RAM

The LCPU (BLE controller) RAM lives in the LPSYS domain and is only
reachable while that domain is powered. NimBLE host asserts (e.g.
ble_hs.c start_stage2) crash through the generic assert path, which
leaves the LCPU asleep, so their coredumps dropped the 24 KB LCPU
region entirely.

Wake the LCPU from prv_dump_lcpu_ram() so the controller RAM is captured
for every crash type. If the LCPU is fully powered down the wake blocks
until the watchdog reboots us, costing only this dump. The two
special-case wake calls in the NimBLE init path are now redundant and
removed, along with the wrapper.

fw/drivers/speaker/nrf5: apply volume across codec power states

audio_set_volume() returned early whenever the codec wasn't running, and
prv_codec_prepare() then reset DAC_R_GAIN to 0 dB on every cold start. Since
the speaker service sets volume before audio_start(), every volume request
was silently dropped and playback always ran at fixed 0 dB gain on asterix —
speaker_play_tone() volume, speaker_set_volume() and the system volume
setting all had no effect, and a pre-start mute (volume 0) was undone by the
unconditional soft-mute clear in prepare.

Cache the requested volume in AudioDeviceState (default 100) and apply it
both immediately when the codec is powered and from prv_codec_prepare() on
cold start. Codec writes from audio_set_volume() take the audio mutex so
they can't race the deferred idle shutdown's power-down.

Also fix the gain mapping: DAC_R_GAIN is a 0.75 dB-per-step register with
0 dB at 0x6F, but the old code scaled the register code linearly across
0x01..0x7F, so volume 100 amplified +11 dB into clipping while volume 10 sat
near -74 dB. Map volume 100 to 0 dB and attenuate linearly in dB over a
48 dB range below it.

Fixes FIRM-2464

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

bluetooth-fw/nimble: hand ATT errors back as raw spec codes

NimBLE reports ATT-layer failures as BLE_HS_ERR_ATT_BASE (0x100) plus the
ATT error code, and the GATT read/write callbacks forwarded that value
offset by BTErrnoInternalErrorBegin. GATT clients compare responses against
spec-level BLEGATTError codes, so the encoding broke any client that matches
a specific ATT error.

ANCS is the victim: it expects ATT Invalid Parameter (0xA2) from iOS both as
the reply to its periodic alive-check probe and when fetching attributes for
a notification that was already retracted. Receiving 9418 instead of 0xA2
misclassified these expected replies as hard BT errors, flushing the entire
pending notification queue and forcing an ANCS re-subscribe every 15-minute
alive-check cycle, and dropping whole bursts of notifications whenever one
UID in the queue had been retracted (which apps like Gmail do constantly).

Translate ATT-range errors back to the raw ATT code in the driver; all other
NimBLE error ranges keep the internal-error offset. No other GATT client
matches specific error values, so this only restores the semantics the FW
side was written against.

Fixes FIRM-2191

fw/syscall: run unprivileged tasks' syscalls on a dedicated stack

App and worker syscalls execute privileged on the calling task's own
small, unprivileged stack, so a task near its stack limit overflows
mid-syscall in privileged mode -- which the kernel cannot unwind, so the
whole system reboots (the original Muninn-on-launch crash).

Give the App and Worker tasks a dedicated 2 KiB privileged syscall stack
in KERNEL_RAM and relocate their syscalls onto it via the CM33 port's
xApplicationGetSyscallStack() hook. prv_drop_privilege switches PSP and
PSPLIM back to the task stack -- while still privileged, since the
privileged-only syscall stack is unreadable once unprivileged -- before
returning. A task that exhausts its own stack now faults unprivileged
(recoverable: only that process is killed); a syscall-stack overflow
remains a rare reboot indicating a genuine kernel-side over-budget.

Gated by SYSCALL_PRIVILEGED_STACK, enabled by default on ARMv8-M (the
relocation needs PSPLIM); ARMv7-M keeps today's behaviour. Moddable apps
use mcu_call_unprivileged() and are intentionally left on their own stack.

Add PBL_LOG_MODULE_DEFINE/PBL_LOG_MODULE_DECLARE macros that bind a compilation

  module = MYMODULE

  source "src/fw/Kconfig.template.log_level"

other units of a cross-unit module):

  PBL_LOG_MODULE_DEFINE(mymodule, CONFIG_MYMODULE_LOG_LEVEL);

apply to QEMU builds; as on hashed builds, logs above the compile-time

tests/wscript: add -fno-common to host test CFLAGS

A bare tentative definition (e.g. `enum { X } Name;` at file scope in a
header included by multiple TUs) is silently merged by macOS ld64 but
rejected by GNU ld. That asymmetry means a duplicate-symbol bug can
pass on macOS CI and only surface on Linux, or vice versa.

-fno-common makes both toolchains reject the collision at link time, so
the bug is caught on whichever host runs the tests first.

GCC has defaulted to -fno-common since GCC 10 (released 2020), so this
flag is a no-op on any current Linux host. It only changes behaviour on
macOS, where Clang still accepts tentative definitions unless told not to.

The flag is placed in the 'local' env CFLAGS block (wscript lines
237-251) which applies to every host unit test; it has no effect on
firmware builds, which use a separate cross-compilation environment.

Signed-off-by: Joseph Mearman <joseph@mearman.co.uk>
Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

declarations.

<pblibc_private.h> include in floor.c, matching the safe pattern
already used by pow.c, scalbn.c, and sqrt.c (system headers first,

hosts.

build/arm-gcc: add reproducibility flags to firmware toolchain

Add -ffile-prefix-map and -fdebug-prefix-map to the firmware CFLAGS and
ASFLAGS, mapping the absolute source root to '.'.  This removes
machine-specific paths from debug info and __FILE__ strings, making
firmware binaries byte-reproducible across different checkout paths.

-ffile-prefix-map is the preferred flag (covers both debug info and
macros); -fdebug-prefix-map is included as well for compatibility with
older toolchain versions that pre-date -ffile-prefix-map.

Also set ARFLAGS to 'rcsD' (deterministic mode) for the firmware ar
step.  Without the 'D' modifier, gcc-ar embeds timestamps and UIDs in
.a files, producing non-reproducible archives even when object files
are identical.  'D' suppresses those fields.

Both flags apply to the firmware env only; host-test compilation is
unaffected.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

tests/wscript: add floating-point determinism flags to host test CFLAGS

Add -ffp-contract=off and -fexcess-precision=standard to the host
unit-test CFLAGS (alongside -fno-common in the local test env).

-ffp-contract=off stops the compiler contracting multiply-add pairs
into FMA instructions, which macOS clang does by default but Linux
clang typically does not. This contraction changes intermediate
precision and is the classic source of last-ULP float differences
between platforms, so floating-point test results are now reproducible
across hosts without changing any test assertions.

-fexcess-precision=standard is a no-op on SSE-only x86-64 (where
the compiler already uses 64-bit SSE registers), but it future-proofs
any 32-bit or x87 host path where the compiler might otherwise keep
80-bit intermediates in registers between operations.

Neither flag affects firmware builds; they are applied only to the
host test environment configured in the 'local' waf conf block.

Signed-off-by: Joseph Mearman <joseph@mearman.co.uk>
Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

libc/math: replace pow test host-libm oracle with reference table

test_pow compared pblibc_pow against the host libm at runtime: it
defined pow_theirs() before the pblibc_private.h rename so it called the
host pow, then compared pblibc_pow within 1 ulp. glibc and Apple's libm
disagree in the last ulp, so the expected values were host-specific.

Precompute correctly-rounded reference values off-host instead.
gen_pow_reference.py evaluates pow(2, v) as exp(v * ln 2) in the stdlib
decimal module at 80 significant digits and rounds to the nearest double
(round-half-to-even), for v = i * 0.001, i in [0, 10000), matching the
inputs the test exercises. It emits input and expected IEEE-754 bit
patterns into pow_reference.h so no decimal round-trip loss occurs. The
table is identical on every host and the script is checked in so it is
regenerable.

The test now compares pblibc_pow against the table within 1 ulp.
pow.c (newlib) documents its result as "nearly rounded"; measured
against the correctly-rounded reference it is within 1 ulp, so 1 ulp is
the justified tolerance, not an invented one. The host libm is no longer
called.

fw/applib: add per-glyph font fallback

A codepoint missing from a loaded font's offset table previously yielded
no glyph data at all (prv_get_glyph_table_offset returns 0 on a miss,
prv_get_glyph_data_offset bails on offset <= 0), so notification strings
mixing scripts the primary font lacks rendered only the covered glyphs.

On a primary miss prv_get_glyph now retries the same codepoint once
against the system fallback font (the wider internal coverage font)
before falling through to the primary wildcard/space. The retry goes
through prv_get_glyph_in_font, which does not itself consult the
fallback, so at most one extra font is ever looked up: no recursion and
no cycle. A guard skips the second lookup when the primary already is
the fallback font.

The fallback is a process global, not per-font state, so it is read in
the renderer rather than stored on FontInfo. FontInfo is an applib-malloc
managed type with a frozen size budget (applib_malloc.json size_2x 40,
size_3x 56) for app-heap ABI compatibility; adding a pointer to it trips
the generated _Static_assert in applib_malloc and breaks the firmware
build on every board. The fallback font is fetched with the
sys_font_get_system_font(NULL) syscall directly, the same one
fonts_get_fallback_font wraps, so text_resources stays independent of
the fonts.c config layer and links in every test that already stubs the
syscall. When no fallback font is configured the lookup returns NULL and
behaviour is byte-for-byte identical to before.

Refs #967

Rewrite the LSM6DSO driver from scratch using direct register access
over I2C, modeled on the LIS2DW12 driver, and drop the STMicro
hal_lsm6dso HAL dependency.

The driver implements the LIS2DW12 feature set: WHO_AM_I check and soft
reset, ultra-low-power mode (XL_ULP_EN), ODR over the [12.5, 208] Hz
range, continuous-stream FIFO (up to the full 512-sample depth) with a
watermark and an INT1 re-arm watchdog, wake-up based shake detection,
single-shot peek and shake sensitivity control. The gyroscope and the
previous diagnostics/health/recovery machinery are removed. Double-tap
detection is left as a TODO, matching the LIS2DW12 driver.

Configuration follows the LIS2DW12 pattern: a board-provided
LSM6DSOConfig (I2C slave port, INT1 EXTI, axis map and direction)
replaces the bare I2C_LSM6D export and the BOARD_CONFIG_ACCEL axis
lookup. board_nrf5.h pulls in the I2C definitions before the board
definitions so the config struct can embed the slave port by value, as
board_sf32lb52.h already does. New Kconfig options (scale, wake
thresholds, FIFO threshold) mirror the LIS2DW12 ones and are set in the
asterix defconfig. The hal_lsm6dso build wiring is removed (the submodule
is left in place).

fw: limit the 4 KiB app stack to emery and gabbro

APP_STACK_NORMAL_SIZE to 4 KiB for every platform and bumped each
app_segment by 2 KiB to compensate. On flint that takes the App RAM
region to 68K + 30K = 98 KiB (0x18800), which the ARMv7-M MPU cannot
express: a region must be n*2^k bytes with n <= 8 subregions, and
98 KiB = 2^11 * 49. Since db56c6c4 the subregion math runs at runtime
instead of via tools/mpu_calc.py at build time, so the illegal size no
longer fails the build and instead trips PBL_CROAK while booting asterix:

  base=0x20027800 size=0x18800

Only emery and gabbro (ARMv8-M, which programs the MPU limit register
directly) need the larger stack and can afford it. Restore the historical
app_segment sizes for the other platforms, keep emery/gabbro bumped, and
hand out the 4 KiB stack only to 4x/System apps on those two platforms.
Legacy 2x/3x apps keep the 2 KiB stack matching their unchanged segments,
and flint's App RAM returns to a clean 96 KiB (0x18000) that maps to
6 x 16 KiB MPU subregions.

soc/sf32lb: add sleep level block/release API

Introduce an SF32LB-specific, refcounted API to limit how deep the
system may sleep. The levels, from shallowest to deepest, are active,
WFI, deep WFI and deep sleep. A caller blocks a level and every deeper
level (e.g. blocking deep WFI also forbids deep sleep), so the deepest
permitted level is one step shallower than the shallowest outstanding
block; with no blocks the system may reach deep sleep. SOC_SF32LB_ACTIVE
cannot be blocked.

The idle path computes this ceiling, folds in the generic stop-mode and
minimum-idle-window constraints, and selects the matching sleep routine
via a single switch.

The implementation only builds for SF32LB52, keeping the symbols
SoC-local; the header lives in the shared pbl include tree.

No callers are migrated yet, so behavior is unchanged.

comm/ancs: recover from a wedged notification queue

When a Control Point request is sent, the queue head stays in flight until
its Data Source response arrives. There was no timeout on that wait, so a
lost DS response — common during the GATT churn of a reconnect — left the
head stuck forever. With the 16-entry queue cap, every later notification
then hit "queue full" and was dropped, so notifications went silent until
the user forced a BLE reconnect or rebooted. The 15-minute alive check that
should recover this only ran when the state machine was Idle, so a wedged
head also blocked the recovery path.

Add three layers of defense:

- An in-flight op watchdog (10s). If a GetNotificationAttributes /
  GetAppAttributes / PerformAction response never lands, drop the stuck
  head and advance so the queue keeps draining. Inbound DS chunks refresh
  the window so slow multi-part reassembly isn't killed mid-stream.

- Evict the oldest pending request instead of dropping the newest when the
  queue is full, so fresh notifications still get through during a backlog.
  The in-flight head and user-initiated actions are never evicted.

- Escalate in the alive check: if the client stays busy across two
  consecutive checks (the watchdog somehow missed it), force a flush +
  resubscribe rather than stay silent until reboot.

Add unit tests covering wedged-head recovery, eviction-when-full, and the
alive-check escalation.

Fixes FIRM-2581

applib/text_layout: pre-load glyph bitmaps in RTL rendering path

The BiDi (RTL) rendering path in walk_line() calls render_glyph()
without first pre-loading glyph bitmaps into the font cache.  Unlike
the standard LTR path — which calls text_resources_get_glyph() before
the visitor callback so that render_glyph() hits a warm cache — the
RTL path lets render_glyph() trigger the full flash I/O call chain
(text_resources_get_glyph → prv_load_glyph_bitmap →
sys_resource_load_range) from deep in the stack.

Combined with the 256 bytes of RTL shaping/reversal buffers already on
the stack, this makes the RTL rendering path significantly more
stack-hungry than the LTR path and contributes to KernelMain stack
overflows during notification text rendering (FIRM-2575 crash family).

Add text_resources_get_glyph() pre-load calls before every
render_glyph() in the BiDi rendering block — for RTL segments, LTR
segments within mixed text, and the trailing suffix glyph — matching
the pattern the standard path already uses.

drivers/i2c/nrf5: write register address and data in one transfer

Register writes used a two-buffer TWIM transfer (NRFX_TWIM_XFER_TXTX)
that sets up its data phase mid-transfer, between starting the
register-address byte and its completion. When issued from a
preemptible/offloaded task context that data phase could be silently
dropped: the device ACKs an address-only write and ignores it, so the
write never lands while the call still reports success.

This surfaced on asterix as the LSM6DSO FIFO never being flushed (its
bypass re-arm is written from the accelerometer's offloaded watchdog
context), leaving INT1 stuck high and no FIFO interrupts delivered.
Reads (TXRX) and writes from the init/app context were unaffected,
which masked the problem.

Build the register address and data into a single contiguous buffer and
issue one TX, mirroring the Zephyr nRF TWIM driver which never uses
TXTX. The buffer is per TWIM instance (transfers are serialized by the
bus mutex); an oversized payload fails the transfer rather than
silently falling back to the broken path.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Gerard Marull-Paretas <gerard@teslabs.com>

drivers/backlight: don't assert on AW2016 I2C failures

A transient I2C NACK/bus error to the AW2016 LED controller, or a wedged
chip on boot, would trip PBL_ASSERTN and crash the OS. On boot this is
especially harmful: backlight_init() asserts on the chip-ID read, so a
stuck chip/bus bricks the watch into a recovery/factory-reset loop that
reinstalling firmware does not clear.

Degrade gracefully instead: log an error and continue at each I2C call
site. A dark or stale backlight is preferable to a reboot, and boot now
survives an unresponsive chip. On a failed write we return early so we
don't act on or cache state the chip never accepted, while the cached
brightness still lets backlight_refresh() re-apply it once the bus
recovers.

The backlight settings row could show a nonsensical "On - 204%" when
dynamic intensity was enabled. The intensity preference is a logical
0-100% value (the light service scales it to the HW maximum), and the

drivers/imu/lsm6dso: read all INT1 registers before processing

The INT1 work handler runs in thread context on the timer task and is a
chain of individually-blocking I2C transactions. Previously the FIFO
sample conversion/dispatch (accel_cb_new_samples()) ran inline between
the FIFO data read and the ALL_INT_SRC read, so a preemption in that
window stretched the gap between those two transactions.

Read FIFO_STATUS, the FIFO data and ALL_INT_SRC back-to-back, then run
the conversion and shake handling afterwards. The processing has no
dependency on the register reads, so this keeps the I2C critical section
contiguous and moves the variable-latency work to the tail.

Split prv_lsm6dso_read_samples() into the FIFO read (now in the handler)
and prv_lsm6dso_process_samples() which is free of device I/O.

services/activity: batch a full epoch per accel callback on LSM6DSO

The activity algorithm processes accel data in 5s epochs (125 samples
at 25Hz), but only requested 25 samples per callback. This woke
KernelBG once per second just to buffer samples, doing real work only
on every 5th wakeup.

Add CONFIG_SERVICE_ACCEL_MANAGER_BATCH_SAMPLES to the accel manager
(which owns the shared buffer) to control the batch size, defaulting to
a full epoch (125) on LSM6DSO so the FIFO watermark fires once every 5s
instead of every second, cutting activity-driven wakeups ~5x. LIS2DW12
stays at 25 as its FIFO is limited to 32 samples. The accel manager
dimensions its shared buffer from this value, and
CONFIG_SERVICE_ACTIVITY_BATCH_SAMPLES defaults to it. Keeping the config
in the accel manager avoids the layering violation that broke the PRF
build, where the activity service is not compiled in.

Raise the LSM6DSO FIFO watermark to 128 (the chip FIFO is 512 deep; the
previous 32 was an artificial cap).

applib: reorder bidi boundary spaces and measure Arabic ligatures

Two bidi line-layout fixes in text_layout.c that share the same
segment-collection loop, so they ship together:

- Boundary spaces: a space between an RTL and an LTR run is direction-
  neutral. Kept inside a run it was reversed with that run, and the
  segment reorder then carried it to the run's far edge, collapsing the
  gap between the two runs. Peel trailing spaces into their own neutral
  segment so they stay put. Adds rtl_segment_content_end() and raises
  MAX_BIDI_SEGMENTS to 16.

- Ligature width: width was measured per codepoint, so a Lam-Alef pair
  counted as two glyphs while the renderer draws one. Measure with
  arabic_shape_pair() (skipping the consumed Alef) on every path that
  measures width -- word_init, RTL segment fit, and the line-width /
  truncation pass (update_dimensions) -- so layout matches what is
  drawn. Non-Arabic text is unaffected.

apps/prf/mfg_test_aging: derive charge-complete from PMIC state

Decide "fully charged" from the PMIC charge state instead of requiring the
SoC to touch a hard 100%, mirroring the discharge test:

- plugged && charging              -> keep cycling/waiting
- plugged && !charging && %<99     -> transient, keep waiting (may restart)
- plugged && !charging && %>=99    -> complete; latch and disable charging

Completion is read from a genuine !is_charging before charging is disabled,
then the latch stops re-deriving it, so the now-false is_charging is harmless.

CHARGE_COMPLETE_MIN_PERCENT (99) and drop the post-charge "dropped below 99%"
fail: with completion now at 99% and charging disabled for the rest of the
phase, normal cycling-load sag would falsely fail healthy units, and charge
retention is already validated by the idle phase. The 90-min charge timeout

services/vibe_pattern: scope app-cleanup clear to app-owned vibes

The vibe pattern engine is a global singleton with no notion of who started
the active pattern. prv_app_cleanup() calls sys_vibe_pattern_clear() on every
app exit, which unconditionally stops whatever is playing.

The alarm popup is a modal and starts its (Reveille) vibe from KernelMain.
When the foreground app relaunches/transitions during an alarm, app cleanup
clears the alarm's in-progress vibe. The alarm popup's repeat timer restarts
it one cycle later (~17s for Reveille), so the user sees the vibration stop
within seconds and sometimes resume on its own. The fingerprint in the
captured logs is "App PP receiver already closed" immediately followed by
"vibe_pattern: clear (was_in_progress=1)".

Track a VibePatternOwner for the active pattern, recorded when a fresh queue
is started (app vibes default to VibePatternOwner_App). Add
vibe_pattern_clear_for_owner(), which clears only when the active pattern is
owned by the given source. app cleanup now clears VibePatternOwner_App, so an
app exiting no longer kills a kernel/modal vibe, while still clearing vibes
the app itself started. Mirrors the existing
speaker_service_stop_for_task(PebbleTask_App) call in the same path.

fw/alarms: don't cancel in-flight smart alarm on benign clock change

alarm_handle_clock_change() unconditionally cleared the smart-alarm
snooze timer and reset s_smart_snooze_counter whenever a clock change
arrived while an alarm was active, even when it did not force-trigger.
The in-flight smart-alarm snooze loop is driven by s_snooze_timer_id and
counts toward the guaranteed fallback fire, so cancelling it means the
smart alarm never goes off. Phones push periodic time syncs (delta

applib: treat Arabic diacritics as transparent for cursive joining

Arabic combining marks (harakat) sit on a base letter and must not break
the cursive connection between the letters around them. Both the shaping
(render) path and the layout measurement paths used each codepoint's
immediate neighbours as joining context, so a mark between two letters
shaped them as if disconnected: a shadda before a Lam-Alef left the
ligature isolated instead of joined, and a fatha between Lam and Alef
stopped them ligating at all. Vocalized words fragmented, and measured
width disagreed with what was drawn (wrong wrap/truncation).

Add arabic_is_transparent() and skip transparent marks (U+0610-061A,
U+064B-065F, U+0670, U+06D6-06ED) when choosing the previous/next letter
-- in arabic_shape_text() and in the three text_layout measurement sites
(word width, RTL segment fit, line/truncation). Marks keep their own
width; an Alef consumed into a Lam-Alef across a mark is skipped once.

fw/services/light: add under-display ALS screen-luminance compensation

On obelix/getafix the ambient light sensor sits under the display, so
the pixels in front of it modulate how much ambient light reaches the
photodiode (black blocks it, white passes it). The same ambient level
reads differently depending on screen content, polluting every
ALS-driven decision.

Correct the raw reading by the luminance of the framebuffer region in
front of the sensor: gain(L) = 256 / lum, the inverse of the front-pixel
luminance, clamped to [1.0x, black_scale]. Measured transmittance tracks
luminance, so this fits far better than a gain linear in luminance.

The correction is applied once at the light-service ingest point
(prv_get_als_level), before the 1s cache, so every consumer sees a
screen-corrected value. The driver stays graphics-free; the framebuffer
read lives in the service via compositor_get_framebuffer_as_bitmap().

Gated by CONFIG_ALS_SCREEN_COMPENSATION (depends on AMBIENT_LIGHT and
SCREEN_COLOR_DEPTH_BITS_8), enabled for obelix/getafix. The sensor
region and black-scale clamp are Kconfig parameters (ALS_SENSOR_{X,Y,W,H}
and ALS_BLACK_SCALE_Q8); per-board values are set in defconfig as they
are measured.

fw/kernel/fault_handling: kill process on app/worker-heap OOM

Moddable apps run their whole event loop inside the privileged
moddable_createMachine syscall, so an app-heap OOM hit the privileged
branch of trigger_oom_fault and rebooted the whole OS, crash-looping
the device into recovery and a forced re-pair.

own app/worker heap kills just that process via sys_app_fault; only a
kernel-heap OOM (or an OOM on a kernel task) still reboots. Gate the
kill path on a safe context (not in an ISR, scheduler running).

syscall: gate Moddable FFI re-entry SVC per-task instead of by section

mcu_call_unprivileged() drops privilege to run an app-supplied native
callback, then re-elevates via an inner `svc 2` once the callback
returns.
That SVC previously lived in .syscall_text so the SVC gate would accept
it,
which meant any code reachable in .syscall_text could re-elevate through
the
same callsite.

Move the re-entry SVC out of .syscall_text and accept it only while a
mcu_call_unprivileged() call is active for the current task:

  - Capture per-task continuation state (callee-saved r4-r11, caller LR,
    entry SP, outer syscall TLS LR/SP) in mcu_call_unprivileged_enter()
    before dropping privilege; privilege is now dropped inline so the C
    helper can't clobber the restored app registers.
  - xApplicationIsAllowedToRaisePrivilege() consults
    mcu_call_unprivileged_reentry_is_allowed(), which only matches the
    exact
    return PC of the labeled callsite and only when a call is active for
    the
    current task.
  - vSetupSyscallRegisters() calls
    mcu_call_unprivileged_reentry_setup(),
    which rechecks the stacked return PC, consumes the saved state,
    restores
    the outer syscall TLS slots, and redirects the exception frame into
    the
    fixed mcu_call_unprivileged_resume() continuation rather than back
    into
    the callback's stack. A udf #0 after the SVC fails closed if it is
    ever
    denied.

This replaces the old syscall_set_outer_lr()/.syscall_text scheme.

fw/apps/prf: rewrite mfg touch test as follow-the-line

Replace the tap-every-cell touch test with a guided line test that
also validates coordinate accuracy, not just touch detection.

A gray guide line must be followed in a single stroke within 30 s:
a full-screen 5x5 boustrophedon (snake) grid on rectangular
displays, and two concentric rings joined by a radial connector on
round displays, which are easy to follow on a circular panel. The
round display splits into equal-width ring lanes around a central
hub holding the status text, with each guide circle centered in
its lane. Reported touch samples are drawn as a black trace and
dots turn green as they are reached. Maze-style wall lines are
drawn on the lane boundaries, with gaps where the path crosses,
and the elapsed time / result is shown on a small overlay in the
center. Rendering is kept cheap (no antialiasing, redraws only on
visible changes) so touch events cannot back up the app queue.

The stroke must start at the marked dot and stay within a corridor
that extends exactly to the walls (half the lane separation).
Samples outside of it (finger slip or distorted coordinates) or a
liftoff reset the stroke, so a panel with offset, scaling or
nonlinearity errors cannot complete the path and fails at timeout.
The previous trace stays on screen until a new stroke starts. A
small forward lookahead along the path keeps fast drags with
sparse samples from stalling, while staying well below the lane
separation so a stroke cannot tunnel between lanes. The best
progress reached is reported as the test result data.

Verified under QEMU (emery and gabbro, PRF) by injecting absolute
pointer events: an exact drag passes on both shapes and a drag
with a constant 25 px offset never progresses and fails.

bluetooth-fw/nimble: fix bt_lock/ble_hs_mutex deadlock in store glue

NimBLE invokes the ble_store callbacks with ble_hs_mutex held
(ble_store.c wraps store_read/write/delete_cb in ble_hs_lock()), and
the store glue took bt_lock inside them. Meanwhile firmware code
routinely calls NimBLE APIs that acquire ble_hs_mutex while holding
bt_lock, e.g. gatt_client_discovery_discover_all ->
conn_mgr_set_ble_conn_response_time ->
bt_driver_le_connection_parameter_update -> ble_gap_conn_find_by_addr.

On reconnection to a bonded peer both happen concurrently: NimbleHost
restores the LTK/CCCDs via the store callbacks (ble_hs_mutex ->
bt_lock) while KernelMain starts service discovery (bt_lock ->
ble_hs_mutex). Both tasks block forever, the task watchdog reboots the
watch, and in the field the subsequent reset often wedges, leaving the
watch dark, draining the battery, and unresponsive until a long-press
hardware reset. Confirmed from a customer coredump: NimbleHost holds
ble_hs_mutex blocked on bt_lock, KernelMain holds bt_lock (taken in
gatt_client_discovery_discover_all) blocked on ble_hs_mutex.

Fix by never acquiring bt_lock, directly or transitively, from the
store callbacks:

- Guard the in-memory sec/CCCD lists with a dedicated mutex instead of
  bt_lock.
- Defer the IRK-updated and bonding-changed notifications to
  KernelMain, as their handlers take bt_lock.
- Call bt_persistent_storage_* without the store lock held: deleting a
  pairing calls back into bt_driver_handle_host_removed_bonding/_cccd
  (which take the store lock) while holding the settings-file lock, so
  holding the store lock across bt_persistent_storage_* calls would
  invert lock order against the settings-file lock.

fw/drivers/ambient: add per-board raw-count to lux conversion

Add lux conversion coefficients to BoardConfig
(lux = (level - dark_offset) * num / den) and an
ambient_light_level_to_lux() helper. Boards without coefficients
(den == 0) return the level unchanged, so consumers can route every
reading through the conversion unconditionally: calibrated boards get
lux, uncalibrated boards keep their raw-count domain and thresholds.

Coefficients were fitted from a lightbox session (8 levels, 860-5745
lux measured at the watch plane, white screen, backlight off, raw
"als curve" readings):

- obelix: 3 production units, least-squares through origin pooled over
  all levels gives 4.834 counts/lux -> lux = counts * 100 / 483.
  Per-unit slopes 4.805/4.868/4.829 (1.3% spread), so a fixed board
  constant needs no per-device trim. One reading (unit 1 at 2765 lux,
  -13.8%) excluded as an outlier.
- getafix: 1 DVT2 unit, fitted over the 4500-5745 lux levels where the
  response is stable at 10.345 counts/lux -> lux = counts * 50 / 517.
  Readings below ~4000 lux deviated (-12% to +31%) in a pattern common
  to all screen fills; needs a re-measure before the low-lux mapping is
  trusted.

Dark-box readings were <20 counts (<4 lux equivalent) on all units, so
dark_offset stays 0. Drop the unused W1160_ADC2LUX_COEF define,
superseded by the per-board coefficients.

services/vibe_pattern: scope app-cleanup clear to app-owned vibes

The vibe pattern engine is a global singleton with no notion of who started
the active pattern. prv_app_cleanup() calls sys_vibe_pattern_clear() on every
app exit, which unconditionally stops whatever is playing.

The alarm popup is a modal and starts its (Reveille) vibe from KernelMain.
When the foreground app relaunches/transitions during an alarm, app cleanup
clears the alarm's in-progress vibe. The alarm popup's repeat timer restarts
it one cycle later (~17s for Reveille), so the user sees the vibration stop
within seconds and sometimes resume on its own. The fingerprint in the
captured logs is "App PP receiver already closed" immediately followed by
"vibe_pattern: clear (was_in_progress=1)".

Track a VibePatternOwner for the active pattern, recorded when a fresh queue
is started (app vibes default to VibePatternOwner_App). Add
vibe_pattern_clear_for_owner(), which clears only when the active pattern is
owned by the given source. app cleanup now clears VibePatternOwner_App, so an
app exiting no longer kills a kernel/modal vibe, while still clearing vibes
the app itself started. Mirrors the existing
speaker_service_stop_for_task(PebbleTask_App) call in the same path.

Fixes FIRM-2617

fw/alarms: don't cancel in-flight smart alarm on benign clock change

alarm_handle_clock_change() unconditionally cleared the smart-alarm
snooze timer and reset s_smart_snooze_counter whenever a clock change
arrived while an alarm was active, even when it did not force-trigger.
The in-flight smart-alarm snooze loop is driven by s_snooze_timer_id and
counts toward the guaranteed fallback fire, so cancelling it means the
smart alarm never goes off. Phones push periodic time syncs (delta
> 15s) that land inside the 30-minute smart window, so smart alarms
silently failed to fire while basic alarms (which fire directly from
cron) kept working.

Only tear down the snooze loop when the alarm is actually
force-triggered; otherwise leave it running so it reaches its fallback.

applib: treat Arabic diacritics as transparent for cursive joining

Arabic combining marks (harakat) sit on a base letter and must not break
the cursive connection between the letters around them. Both the shaping
(render) path and the layout measurement paths used each codepoint's
immediate neighbours as joining context, so a mark between two letters
shaped them as if disconnected: a shadda before a Lam-Alef left the
ligature isolated instead of joined, and a fatha between Lam and Alef
stopped them ligating at all. Vocalized words fragmented, and measured
width disagreed with what was drawn (wrong wrap/truncation).

Add arabic_is_transparent() and skip transparent marks (U+0610-061A,
U+064B-065F, U+0670, U+06D6-06ED) when choosing the previous/next letter
-- in arabic_shape_text() and in the three text_layout measurement sites
(word width, RTL segment fit, line/truncation). Marks keep their own
width; an Alef consumed into a Lam-Alef across a mark is skipped once.

fw/services/light: add under-display ALS screen-luminance compensation

On obelix/getafix the ambient light sensor sits under the display, so
the pixels in front of it modulate how much ambient light reaches the
photodiode (black blocks it, white passes it). The same ambient level
reads differently depending on screen content, polluting every
ALS-driven decision.

Correct the raw reading by the luminance of the framebuffer region in
front of the sensor: gain(L) = 256 / lum, the inverse of the front-pixel
luminance, clamped to [1.0x, black_scale]. Measured transmittance tracks
luminance, so this fits far better than a gain linear in luminance.

The correction is applied once at the light-service ingest point
(prv_get_als_level), before the 1s cache, so every consumer sees a
screen-corrected value. The driver stays graphics-free; the framebuffer
read lives in the service via compositor_get_framebuffer_as_bitmap().

Gated by CONFIG_ALS_SCREEN_COMPENSATION (depends on AMBIENT_LIGHT and
SCREEN_COLOR_DEPTH_BITS_8), enabled for obelix/getafix. The sensor
region and black-scale clamp are Kconfig parameters (ALS_SENSOR_{X,Y,W,H}
and ALS_BLACK_SCALE_Q8); per-board values are set in defconfig as they
are measured.

larger scale, raising getafix's dark threshold from 150 to 2000. An

fw/kernel/fault_handling: kill process on app/worker-heap OOM

Moddable apps run their whole event loop inside the privileged
moddable_createMachine syscall, so an app-heap OOM hit the privileged
branch of trigger_oom_fault and rebooted the whole OS, crash-looping
the device into recovery and a forced re-pair.

Route by which heap ran out instead of privilege: an OOM on a process's
own app/worker heap kills just that process via sys_app_fault; only a
kernel-heap OOM (or an OOM on a kernel task) still reboots. Gate the
kill path on a safe context (not in an ISR, scheduler running).

syscall: gate Moddable FFI re-entry SVC per-task instead of by section

mcu_call_unprivileged() drops privilege to run an app-supplied native
callback, then re-elevates via an inner `svc 2` once the callback
returns.
That SVC previously lived in .syscall_text so the SVC gate would accept
it,
which meant any code reachable in .syscall_text could re-elevate through
the
same callsite.

Move the re-entry SVC out of .syscall_text and accept it only while a
mcu_call_unprivileged() call is active for the current task:

  - Capture per-task continuation state (callee-saved r4-r11, caller LR,
    entry SP, outer syscall TLS LR/SP) in mcu_call_unprivileged_enter()
    before dropping privilege; privilege is now dropped inline so the C
    helper can't clobber the restored app registers.
  - xApplicationIsAllowedToRaisePrivilege() consults
    mcu_call_unprivileged_reentry_is_allowed(), which only matches the
    exact
    return PC of the labeled callsite and only when a call is active for
    the
    current task.
  - vSetupSyscallRegisters() calls
    mcu_call_unprivileged_reentry_setup(),
    which rechecks the stacked return PC, consumes the saved state,
    restores
    the outer syscall TLS slots, and redirects the exception frame into
    the
    fixed mcu_call_unprivileged_resume() continuation rather than back
    into
    the callback's stack. A udf #0 after the SVC fails closed if it is
    ever
    denied.

This replaces the old syscall_set_outer_lr()/.syscall_text scheme.

fw/apps/prf: rewrite mfg touch test as follow-the-line

Replace the tap-every-cell touch test with a guided line test that
also validates coordinate accuracy, not just touch detection.

A gray guide line must be followed in a single stroke within 30 s:
a full-screen 5x5 boustrophedon (snake) grid on rectangular
displays, and two concentric rings joined by a radial connector on
round displays, which are easy to follow on a circular panel. The
round display splits into equal-width ring lanes around a central
hub holding the status text, with each guide circle centered in
its lane. Reported touch samples are drawn as a black trace and
dots turn green as they are reached. Maze-style wall lines are
drawn on the lane boundaries, with gaps where the path crosses,
and the elapsed time / result is shown on a small overlay in the
center. Rendering is kept cheap (no antialiasing, redraws only on
visible changes) so touch events cannot back up the app queue.

The stroke must start at the marked dot and stay within a corridor
that extends exactly to the walls (half the lane separation).
Samples outside of it (finger slip or distorted coordinates) or a
liftoff reset the stroke, so a panel with offset, scaling or
nonlinearity errors cannot complete the path and fails at timeout.
The previous trace stays on screen until a new stroke starts. A
small forward lookahead along the path keeps fast drags with
sparse samples from stalling, while staying well below the lane
separation so a stroke cannot tunnel between lanes. The best
progress reached is reported as the test result data.

Verified under QEMU (emery and gabbro, PRF) by injecting absolute
pointer events: an exact drag passes on both shapes and a drag
with a constant 25 px offset never progresses and fails.

bluetooth-fw/nimble: fix bt_lock/ble_hs_mutex deadlock in store glue

NimBLE invokes the ble_store callbacks with ble_hs_mutex held
(ble_store.c wraps store_read/write/delete_cb in ble_hs_lock()), and
the store glue took bt_lock inside them. Meanwhile firmware code
routinely calls NimBLE APIs that acquire ble_hs_mutex while holding
bt_lock, e.g. gatt_client_discovery_discover_all ->
conn_mgr_set_ble_conn_response_time ->
bt_driver_le_connection_parameter_update -> ble_gap_conn_find_by_addr.

On reconnection to a bonded peer both happen concurrently: NimbleHost
restores the LTK/CCCDs via the store callbacks (ble_hs_mutex ->
bt_lock) while KernelMain starts service discovery (bt_lock ->
ble_hs_mutex). Both tasks block forever, the task watchdog reboots the
watch, and in the field the subsequent reset often wedges, leaving the
watch dark, draining the battery, and unresponsive until a long-press
hardware reset. Confirmed from a customer coredump: NimbleHost holds
ble_hs_mutex blocked on bt_lock, KernelMain holds bt_lock (taken in
gatt_client_discovery_discover_all) blocked on ble_hs_mutex.

Fix by never acquiring bt_lock, directly or transitively, from the
store callbacks:

- Guard the in-memory sec/CCCD lists with a dedicated mutex instead of
  bt_lock.
- Defer the IRK-updated and bonding-changed notifications to
  KernelMain, as their handlers take bt_lock.
- Call bt_persistent_storage_* without the store lock held: deleting a
  pairing calls back into bt_driver_handle_host_removed_bonding/_cccd
  (which take the store lock) while holding the settings-file lock, so
  holding the store lock across bt_persistent_storage_* calls would
  invert lock order against the settings-file lock.

Fixes FIRM-3155
Fixes FIRM-3177
Fixes FIRM-3181

fw/drivers/ambient: add per-board raw-count to lux conversion

Add lux conversion coefficients to BoardConfig
(lux = (level - dark_offset) * num / den) and an
ambient_light_level_to_lux() helper. Boards without coefficients
(den == 0) return the level unchanged, so consumers can route every
reading through the conversion unconditionally: calibrated boards get
lux, uncalibrated boards keep their raw-count domain and thresholds.

Coefficients were fitted from a lightbox session (8 levels, 860-5745
lux measured at the watch plane, white screen, backlight off, raw
"als curve" readings):

- obelix: 3 production units, least-squares through origin pooled over
  all levels gives 4.834 counts/lux -> lux = counts * 100 / 483.
  Per-unit slopes 4.805/4.868/4.829 (1.3% spread), so a fixed board
  constant needs no per-device trim. One reading (unit 1 at 2765 lux,
  -13.8%) excluded as an outlier.
- getafix: 1 DVT2 unit, fitted over the 4500-5745 lux levels where the
  response is stable at 10.345 counts/lux -> lux = counts * 50 / 517.
  Readings below ~4000 lux deviated (-12% to +31%) in a pattern common
  to all screen fills; needs a re-measure before the low-lux mapping is
  trusted.

Dark-box readings were <20 counts (<4 lux equivalent) on all units, so
dark_offset stays 0. Drop the unused W1160_ADC2LUX_COEF define,
superseded by the per-board coefficients.

build: encode boot priority in pblboot firmware header

The pblboot bootloader picks between the two firmware slots by an
unsigned 64-bit compare of the header timestamp field, which was
stamped with the build wall-clock time. Now that releases are cut from
branches, a maintenance release (e.g. v4.19.2) can be built after a
newer version (e.g. v4.22.0), so the newer version would never boot
when promoted.

Reinterpret the field as a banded boot priority, selected by the top
byte:

- Release builds (exact vX[.Y[.Z]][-betaN|-rcN] tag): band 0x01, with
  major/minor/patch in the next three bytes and the tag commit
  timestamp in the low 32 bits, so a higher version always wins
  regardless of build order and the commit timestamp breaks ties
  within a version (e.g. beta vs final).
- Dev builds (anything else, including dirty trees): band 0x80 plus
  the build wall-clock time, outranking all releases so a freshly
  flashed dev image always boots; among dev builds the most recently
  built one wins.

Legacy images carry a plain unix timestamp (< 2^32), below both bands,
so the first release using this scheme upgrades cleanly over any
already-deployed firmware. Bands 0x02-0x7f and 0x81-0xff are reserved
for future encodings and overrides.

Known limitation: a device running a dev image will not boot an
OTA-installed release until the dev slot is invalidated (PRF entry,
which invalidates both slots, or a flash erase).

fw/services/process_management: check app load size arithmetic

The app header stores the image size (load_size) and the relocation entry
count. The load size helper added those with unchecked arithmetic
(load_size + num_reloc_entries * 4), so a crafted relocation count could
wrap before the loader compared the result against the destination
segment.

parameter, which makes the error path explicit and lets the loader bail
out on overflow.

fw/services/process_management: validate sdk app relocation data

The SDK app loader runs privileged and applies relocation fixups taken
directly from an untrusted app binary:

  addr_to_change = prv_offset_to_address(destination, reloc_array[i]);
  *addr_to_change = ...;

reloc_array[i] was used as a write offset with no bounds checking, so a
malicious app could craft a relocation entry with an arbitrary offset and
turn the privileged loader into an arbitrary write primitive
(*(segment->start + attacker_offset) = ...), escaping the app sandbox.

Validate the header, image/virtual sizes, entry point, SDK jump table
slot, relocation table alignment, relocation targets, and relocated
pointer values before turning any of them into pointers. Relocation
targets must be word-aligned, past the header, and within the loaded
image; relocated values must stay within the app image (a value equal to
virtual_size is allowed as a one-past-the-end sentinel, which is never
dereferenced by the loader).

Also confirm the header loaded into RAM still matches the header used for
validation (closes a theoretical TOCTOU), tie the header to the trusted
process metadata, and apply relocations before writing the SDK jump table
pointer so app relocation data cannot overwrite it.
