bluetooth: add reversed PPoG transport

Add reversed PPoG, so that the phone can subscribe to the watch's PPoG
service instead of the other way around.

Reasoning:
- This is simpler and will fix a class of bugs we see in the field where
  the watch either can't find the phone's ppog service, or doesn't
  realize that it needs to resubscribe on iOS because the link never
  dropped (kept alive by ANCS). Also may fix some bugs on weird Android
  devices.
- In the future it would enable us to use AccessorySetupKit on iOS
  (which is currently a pre-requisite to the new Accessory Notifications
  framework), which will not work while running a GATT server on the
  phone.

Changes:
- Add the reversed PPoG GATT service (NimBLE): notify-only data
  characteristic for outbound packets, write-without-response
  characteristic for inbound ones.
- Driver callbacks dispatch all work to KernelMain, where forward-mode
  RX (kernel_le_client GATT events) and comm session send_next jobs
  already run, keeping the whole PPoG state machine on one task. The
  NimBLE host task itself is ruled out because the state machine
  (bt_lock acquisition plus re-entrant NimBLE calls) does not fit on its
  stack. KernelBG is ruled out because its callbacks may block for
  seconds on Pebble Protocol send progress (e.g. the BT log dump blocks
  up to 4 s per line in comm_session_send_buffer_begin_write()); inbound
  ACKs would sit unprocessed behind them until the system task queue
  overflows and forces a reset (RebootReasonCode_EventQueueFull).
- Sends that fail with BTErrnoNotEnoughResources (mbuf exhaustion, e.g.
  the put_bytes inbound flood during a firmware update) are retried via
  a per-client one-shot timer after PPOGATT_SEND_RETRY_DELAY_MS (20 ms,
  about one connection event). NimBLE has no buffers-freed event to wait
  for: its NOTIFY_TX GAP event fires synchronously per send attempt with
  the attempt's own status, so a failed attempt never produces a
  follow-up event and waiting on one would stall the transport
  permanently. The timer callback bounces to KernelMain (NimBLE calls
  must not run on the timer task) and pumps prv_send_next_packets()
  directly rather than via comm_session_send_next(), because the session
  does not exist yet if a Reset Complete send fails during the
  handshake. Stalls log a warning on the first failed attempt and, on
  recovery, how many retries it took.
- The service self-registers a GAP event listener
  (ble_gap_event_listener_register) for subscribe events, the same
  pattern upstream service-grade modules (ble_eatt, ble_audio) use, so
  no central dispatcher changes are needed. Registration tolerates
  BLE_HS_EALREADY because bt_driver_start can run multiple times while
  the listener list is only reset by nimble_port_init.
- The service requires an encrypted link. The data-write characteristic
  carries WRITE_ENC and the data-notify characteristic READ_ENC, which
  the CCCD now inherits (needs the bundled mynewt-nimble fix), so both
  writing PPoG data and subscribing get an ATT insufficient-encryption
  error on an unencrypted link - triggering pairing on well-behaved
  phones. The kernel additionally refuses to start a client on an
  unencrypted connection as a backstop. This matters because, unlike
  forward PPoG (where the watch only talks to its bonded gateway), any
  central can connect to the advertising watch.
- The phone subscribes to this service if it exists, otherwise it opens
  a GATT server with the "normal" (forward) ppog service.
- The watch ignores the phone's ppog service if the phone subscribes to
  the reversed service, i.e. reversed has priority and is intended to be
  the primary connection path going forward.
- The phone is expected to send the initial ResetRequest after
  subscribing. This makes it clear that the phone initiates the
  connection and never needs to wait for the watch, which is what caused
  a lot of problems previously.

Remaining issues:
- Both iOS and Android cache the watch's GATT services and return a
  stale list to the mobile app until the device is re-paired, so the
  phone app will not see this new service initially (users are expected
  to pair in PRF, which does not have it). This is OK for now - the
  existing ppog mechanism continues to work. We should follow up by
  potentially implementing the 0x2B2A database hash characteristic,
  which NimBLE doesn't support yet (both phone OSs should trigger a full
  discovery refresh when it changes).

Testing:
- Tested on iOS and Android; works in both normal and reversed mode,
  depending on whether the app can see the new reversed service or not.
  Tried pairing in PRF -> update to FW with this service (continues to
  use normal ppog, unless the GATT cache is force-refreshed on Android,
  in which case it uses the new reversed service). Tried pairing to a
  device running this service: works using the new reversed mode.
- Firmware-update stress tested on iOS during the MOB-9394
  investigation: 16/16 consecutive update loops completed with the
  paired libpebble3 fixes (the remaining stall was an iOS bluetoothd
  GATT-pipeline issue, worked around phone-side).

bluetooth: serialize GATT client procedures with an op queue

NimBLE runs GATT client procedures concurrently and dispatches
incoming ATT responses to the first pending procedure that consumes
that response opcode (see ble_gattc_rx_read_type_elem_entries). Two
concurrent procedures consuming the same opcode get their responses
cross-delivered, corrupting both. This was observed as the GAP device
name read (read-by-UUID) racing characteristic discovery, which both
consume ATT Read By Type responses: the "device name" ended up
containing raw characteristic declaration bytes (rendered as a blank
name on the PRF getting-started screen) while discovery/PPoGATT
received the other half of the cross-delivery (meta protocol errors,
session failures, phone reconnect loops).

Add a driver-level FIFO of GATT client operations so only one
procedure ever runs at a time: an op starts when the previous op's
terminal callback fires. Ops are started from KernelBG, which makes
pushing safe from any context, including with bt_lock held (calling
NimBLE APIs under bt_lock deadlocks against the NimBLE host task, see
commit 3d5009dd0). Service discovery, the GAP device name read and
the pairing-confirmation name read in advert.c all go through the
queue now.

While at it:

- The device name read callback resolves the connection by device
  address under bt_lock instead of trusting a raw GAPLEConnection
  pointer that can go stale, and copies the name with
  ble_hs_mbuf_to_flat() so chained mbufs don't truncate it.
- Discovery start errors are reported through
  bt_driver_cb_gatt_client_discovery_complete, since the actual start
  is now asynchronous.
- Fix a discovery context leak when ble_gattc_disc_all_svcs fails.

comm/ble: fix gateway intent registration racing IRK update

After pairing completes, the driver persists our and the peer's keys
through two separate launcher-task callbacks. The first one creates
the bonding, whose DidAdd handler re-registers the kernel gateway
intent; the second one delivers the peer IRK to the connection. When
the intent was registered, prv_register_intent() looked the live
connection up by IRK only (the by-address fallback was gated on the
bonding having no IRK), so the lookup missed, the intent was
registered as not connected, and the ConnectedAndEncrypted event that
kicks off the kernel LE clients (PPoGATT, service discovery) was
never emitted. The second key store is treated as a re-pair
(DidChange), which the kernel client ignores, so pairing a different
phone got stuck after pairing completion until the phone reconnected.

The connection address is already updated to the identity address by
the time the bonding change handlers run (the identity resolved event
is delivered synchronously from the host task), so fall back to
matching by address whenever the IRK lookup misses.

services/filesystem/pfs: unlink stale corrupt file copies during scan

A start page whose header no longer passes its CRC check but still
carries a matching file name (e.g. left behind by an interrupted
rewrite or delete) was skipped by every flash scan with a 'CRC corrupt
for page N' warning, forever: nothing ever reclaimed it, so it leaked
its pages and spammed the log on each lookup of that file.

When the scan finds a valid copy of the file, unlink the corrupt match
so it stops shadowing scans and its pages become reclaimable. If no
valid copy exists the corrupt page is left untouched, since the failed
check may be a transient read glitch and a later scan can still succeed.
The unlink walk is bounded by the per-page next_page CRC8, so a corrupt
chain cannot mark unrelated pages.

fw/drivers/imu/lis2dw12: track FIFO reads for the INT1 stall watchdog

burst reads instead, which is the signal the watchdog actually guards.

with a 1 s floor so small FIFO batches do not trip recovery on normal

fw/drivers/imu/lis2dw12: quiesce INT1 routing during stream recovery

The previous recovery only rewrote FIFO_CTRL and read ALL_INT_SRC.
Field logs (FIRM-2490) show it firing repeatedly without reviving the
stream: when the INT1 pad is left latched HIGH after a FIFO overrun
(known quirk, see implementation notes), rewriting FIFO_CTRL does not
release the pad, so the rising-edge EXTI never fires again.

Add a shared recovery helper, used by both the stall watchdog and the
FIFO overrun path, that disables INT1/INT2 routing first (forcing the
pad low so re-enabling produces a fresh edge), salvages queued samples
instead of discarding them, clears latched function INT sources while
quiesced (so a shake landing mid-recovery is not silently consumed),
and then re-asserts the full dynamic configuration (ODR, FIFO mode,
INT routing).

fw/drivers/imu/lis2dw12: re-check INT1 pad level after servicing

INT1 aggregates level-based (FIFO threshold) and latched (wake-up)
sources on a rising-edge EXTI, so a source asserting while the pad is
already high produces no new edge. Example: the FIFO crosses its
threshold between the sample drain and the ALL_INT_SRC read of the same
servicing pass, keeping the pad high through the wake-up clear; no edge
ever follows and the stream stays dead until the stall watchdog fires,
losing seconds of samples.

Close the race deterministically: after each servicing pass, read the
INT1 pad level back. If it is still high after FIFO progress, service
again (the pending event will produce no edge). If it is high with
nothing serviced, the pad is stuck (post-overrun latch-up quirk) and
only an INT routing reset produces edges again, so run the recovery.
The stall watchdog remains as a backstop; with this change its
recovery counter should stay at zero in normal operation.

Two constraints shape the requeue rule. WU_IA stays set while the
wake-up condition persists (LIR does not clear on source read), so
shake is dispatched only on WU assertion, tracked across passes and
reset on a fresh edge (which proves the pad went low); dispatching per
pass would flood shake events at I2C pass rate during continuous
motion. For the same reason only FIFO progress requeues the handler: a
pad held high by a persistent wake-up condition resumes producing
edges once the condition deasserts, and a FIFO threshold crossing
during the hold is covered by the stall watchdog, whose recovery
drains (rather than discards) the queued samples.

that does not release the pad, so the rising-edge EXTI never fires

FIFO overrun path, that disables INT1 routing first (forcing the pad
low so re-enabling produces a fresh edge), salvages queued samples
instead of discarding them, clears latched function INT sources while

fw/drivers/imu/lsm6dso: re-check INT1 pad level after servicing

INT1 mixes level (FIFO threshold) and latched (wake-up) sources on a
rising-edge EXTI, so a source asserting while the pad is already high
produces no new edge and the stream stays dead until the stall watchdog
fires, losing seconds of samples.

Close the race deterministically: after each servicing pass, read the
INT1 pad level back. If it is still high after FIFO progress, service
again (the pending event will produce no edge). If it is high with
nothing serviced, the pad is stuck (post-overrun latch-up quirk) and
only an INT routing reset produces edges again, so run the recovery.
The stall watchdog remains as a backstop.

WU_IA stays set while the wake-up condition persists (LIR does not
clear on source read), so shake is dispatched only on WU assertion,
tracked across passes and reset on a fresh edge (which proves the pad
went low); dispatching per pass would flood shake events during
continuous motion. For the same reason only FIFO progress requeues the
handler: a pad held high by a persistent wake-up condition resumes
producing edges once the condition deasserts, and a FIFO threshold
crossing during the hold is covered by the stall watchdog, whose
recovery drains (rather than discards) the queued samples.

Same change as the lis2dw12 driver (see #1701).

fw/services/speaker: drain audio pipeline before stopping

The service stopped the audio driver as soon as the active source had no
more samples to generate. The drivers queue up to 64 ms of audio ahead of
the DAC (double-buffered DMA/I2S pipe primed with silence plus a circular
buffer), so playback was cut off up to 64 ms early. Sounds shorter than
the pipeline depth were never heard at all: on sf32lb52, whose audio_stop
halts the DMA and cuts amplifier power immediately, a 25 ms
speaker_play_tone() produced only the amplifier pop.

Once the source is exhausted, keep feeding silence until the pipeline has
drained, then stop. Playback transitions through SpeakerStateDraining so
clients can observe it. While only padding silence remains, allow
same-priority playback to start instead of rejecting it, so rapid
re-triggers (e.g. a metronome app) are not dropped.

On nrf5/da7212 the change is behavior-neutral: its warm-pause audio_stop
keeps the I2S stream draining anyway, so the warm pause merely starts
~80 ms later. Adds a host test suite with a fake audio driver covering
the drain and preemption behavior.

fw/drivers/imu/lsm6dso: return fresh data from accel_peek while sampling

While sampling is active, accel_peek() returned the sample cached at
the last FIFO drain. The FIFO watermark is set by the most demanding
subscriber; with only the activity tracker subscribed (25 Hz x 125
samples) that sample can be up to 5 seconds old. Apps that poll
accel_service_peek() for tilt input (Gyro Maze, Mr. Runner Up, Fluid
Sim, ...) therefore saw multi-second input lag, while apps subscribing
with a small batch size were unaffected. Classic-era drivers (bmi160)
read the current output registers on every peek, which is why these
apps worked on older watches.

Read the output registers on peek instead: they update at ODR
independently of the FIFO on this part. The cached sample is now
unused, so drop it.

ci: rebase PR branches onto target branch before running

Check out the PR head SHA and rebase it onto the current tip of the
target branch before any CI job runs, following the approach used by
Zephyr. If the rebase does not apply cleanly, the job fails immediately
with an error asking the author to rebase locally.

This replaces building GitHub's ephemeral merge commit, which only
reflects the target branch at event time, so stale branches were tested
against an outdated base.

The rebase logic lives in a reusable composite action
(.github/actions/rebase) with a checkout-style 'submodules' input
(default false) to re-sync submodules after the rebase so gitlinks
match the rebased tree. Compliance diff ranges now use
origin/$GITHUB_BASE_REF instead of the event base SHA, which would
include unrelated upstream commits after the rebase.

ci: resolve rebase action from the merge ref

Workflows checked out the PR head SHA before resolving the local
rebase action, so PR branches created before the action existed were
missing it from the workspace and every job failed at action
resolution.

Check out the default merge ref instead, which always contains the
current merged copy of the action, and let the action itself switch to
the PR head before rebasing. The head SHA is always fetchable since it
is a parent of the merge commit and the checkout is full depth. If the
PR conflicts with its base, the merge ref does not exist and checkout
fails, which surfaces the same rebase-locally error one step earlier.

fw/services/process_management: allow unaligned relocation table offsets

The SDK app relocation-data validation added in 68b30e60 rejects any
app whose image size (load_size) is not word-aligned, since the
relocation table starts right at that offset and was read as a
uint32_t array.

Legacy SDK apps routinely have non-word-aligned image sizes: the store
build of Timer (c64aae42-b822-4d6d-995b-bc7c38e843f4) ships load_size
values of 17370/18110/18182 (all 2 mod 4) with 11 relocation entries,
so v4.24.0 rejects it at launch on every platform with "Invalid app
relocation table offset alignment" and bounces back to the launcher.

Drop the alignment requirement on the table start and read the entries
bytewise instead. All security-relevant validation is unchanged:
relocation targets must still be word-aligned, in-bounds, and past the
header, and relocated values must stay within the app image.

Verified on qemu_emery: the store Timer PBW is rejected at launch
before this change and launches and runs correctly after it.

fw/drivers/imu/lsm6dso: retry INT1 servicing before stream recovery

The stuck-pad heuristic recovers the stream when a servicing pass takes
no action and the INT1 pad still reads high. A wake-up or FIFO threshold
source asserting between the status register reads and the pad re-check
is indistinguishable from a stuck pad, so the heuristic recovers a
healthy stream and discards the event that raced it (recovery clears
ALL_INT_SRC without dispatching).

Field logs show this clustering during sustained motion, up to 7
recoveries in 23 minutes, each one dropping a wake-up event.

Retry the servicing pass once before recovering: a racing source is
latched (wake-up) or level (FIFO threshold), so it is visible on
re-read and gets serviced normally. Only recover when a second
consecutive pass finds nothing with the pad still high, which is then a
genuinely stuck pad.

fw/put_bytes: scope BLE slowdown to the raw storage erase

pb_storage_raw_init() requested ResponseTimeMiddle with
max_period_secs=0 (added in 6d679bc73 to reduce NimbleHost stack
pressure during blocking flash operations). This had two problems:

- 0 does not mean run forever (that is MAX_PERIOD_RUN_FOREVER), it
  creates an already-expired request: the bt_conn_mgr watchdog deleted
  it ~1s later and, with no requests left, dropped the connection to
  ResponseTimeMax (45ms interval, slave latency 3).
- It shares BtConsumerPpPutBytes with the ResponseTimeMin request held
  during chunk streaming, so it cancelled the fast interval at every
  raw object boundary.

As a result, during a firmware update each object init (firmware, then
system resources) bounced the connection Min -> Middle -> Max -> Min,
and the multi-second slot erase plus its init ACK ran at up to 180ms
effective interval, adding ~5-10s per object.

Request Middle only for the duration of the erase, with a bounded
timeout as a safety net, and restore Min right after so the init ACK
goes out at the fast interval and the streaming request is never
cancelled. The NimbleHost stack overflow remains covered by the stack
size increase from 6d679bc73.

drivers/speaker: map SF32LB volume to attenuation-only DAC gain

The DAC-path volume was converted from the 0-100 UI scale as
(vol - 36) * 2 half-dB, i.e. -36..+64 dB. Any volume above 36 applied
positive digital gain, which hard-clips full-scale content: alarm tones
(volume 60, +24 dB) played as a digital-full-scale square wave, at
maximum loudness regardless of the speaker volume preference, and
overdriving the speaker well past the level the factory test validates.
Volumes above 90 exceeded the HAL's +54 dB limit, so
HAL_AUDCODEC_Config_DACPath_Volume failed without writing the gain
registers and the error was ignored, leaving the 0 dB baseline and
making the volume curve non-monotonic (90 was louder than 100).

The mapping had been dead code until 0e2afbddb started re-applying the
volume after DAC path setup (v4.20.0), which is when alarms became
loud and distorted in the field.

Map 1..100 linearly to -36..0 dB instead (0 still mutes), and log a
warning if the HAL rejects the value.

comm/ble: request connection parameter update sooner after connect

iOS creates connections with a 720ms supervision timeout and only
relaxes it once the peripheral requests new parameters. We waited the
full TGAP(conn_pause_peripheral) = 5s before sending the request, so
any RF fade during that window killed the link. Logs from a getafix
unit showed reconnect storms where most connections died of supervision
timeout (0x208) within 1-6s of connecting, i.e. before the update could
be requested, while connections that reached the 6s supervision timeout
stayed up for hours.

Shorten the initial pause to 1s. The 5s pause is a spec recommendation
("should", not "shall"), and Apple has confirmed relaxed handling of
TGAP timings (see the pre-existing note about the 30s Tgap timeout).

Related to FIRM-3330.

Co-authored-by: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Gerard Marull-Paretas <gerard@teslabs.com>

comm/ble: back off reconnect advertising during connection churn

When the link repeatedly drops right after connecting (e.g. supervision
timeouts in bad RF conditions), every disconnection restarted reconnect
advertising with a 30s short-interval (20ms) burst. A getafix unit
hitting a reconnect storm went through ~130 connect/disconnect cycles
in 70 minutes, each paying the full burst.

Track how often plain reconnect advertising is (re)started: after 3
starts within a 60s window, schedule only the long-interval (~1s) term.
One attempt per window still gets the short-interval burst, so
reconnection latency recovers as soon as the churn stops. BLE HRM
reconnection advertising is user-initiated and time-bounded, so it is
not backed off.

Related to FIRM-3330.

services/notifications: fix leak and deleted-entry handling in rewrite

notification_storage_rewrite() never freed the TimelineItem buffer that

buffer per notification on each rewrite (e.g. timezone migration).

the previous item's stale payload. Skip deleted entries entirely,

drivers/speaker: throttle sf32lb52 DMA refill callbacks

The AUDCODEC DMA half/full-complete ISRs enqueued a prv_audio_trans_bg
refill callback on every interrupt with no in-flight tracking. When
KernelBG is starved (e.g. an app blocking on a slow flash resource read
while holding the pfs mutexes), the system task queue fills up and the
watch hard-reboots with Event Queue Full, cutting alarm tones off a few
seconds into playback.

Mirror the nrf5/da7212 driver: track a callback_pending flag so at most
one refill callback is in flight, clearing it again if the enqueue
fails. The flag is also reset in audec_start() so a stale value cannot
block refills on a new session.

services/ecompass: relax calibration gates for weak geomagnetic fields

The sphere-fit solver only accepts a four-point sample set when the
points are spread further apart than an absolute distance threshold:
point-to-point, point-to-line and point-to-plane all had to exceed
370 (37 uT), with a single fallback to 220 that was only armed after
two 300-sample windows in which the point-to-point gate had passed.

All samples lie on a sphere whose radius R is the local geomagnetic
field strength. In weak-field regions such as the South Atlantic
Anomaly (~22 uT, R ~= 228) those gates are unsatisfiable:
point-to-point > 370 needs ~108 degrees of orientation change, more
than the calibration UI coaches, and point-to-line > 370 is
geometrically impossible since its maximum is
R + sqrt(R^2 - (370/2)^2) < 370 for R < ~231. Because the fallback
was gated on the point-to-point pass that weak fields cannot produce,
the threshold never dropped and calibration never completed (bug
report logs show zero solutions over a 7 minute session).

Replace the strike-based fallback with deterministic progressive
relaxation: every 300-sample window that ends without a complete
point set lowers the threshold by 70, down to a floor of 90 (9 uT).
The floor keeps all three gates satisfiable at ~20 uT with realistic
<= 90 degree orientation coverage. Normal-field behavior is
preserved: the strict 370 threshold is still tried first and only
relaxes after demonstrated failure to fit, and the existing
requirement of three consecutive consistent fits within 50 counts
still rejects noisy solutions.

Also reset the threshold and the fit-consistency history in
ecomp_corr_reset() so each calibration session starts from the
strict gates instead of inheriting relaxed state.

Unit tests cover weak-field convergence (radius-228 sphere with a
hard-iron offset, 50-degree cap coverage, sensor noise: the old
gates provably never fire, the new code locks within ~80 simulated
seconds and recovers the offset within 2 counts), normal-field
regression (radius 470, locks within the first strict window), and
rejection of degenerate stationary and coplanar inputs.

services/alarms: fix user snooze delay on smart alarms

User snoozes and the smart alarm's internal sleep poll share the same
snooze timer, and its expiry always funneled back into the smart-alarm
sleep gate. Snoozing a firing smart alarm therefore turned "Snooze for
N minutes" into an open-ended 1-minute sleep-poll loop that only
re-fired the alarm once sleep exit was detected or the poll cap was hit.

Track whether the pending snooze timer was armed by an explicit user
snooze and bypass the sleep gate in that case, so the alarm re-fires
after exactly the configured snooze delay. The flag is cleared on every
snooze-timer teardown (dismiss, disable, delete, new alarm, clock-change
force trigger).

Add a regression test: a firing smart alarm that is user-snoozed while
the user still looks asleep (RestfulSleep, VMC 0) must put the alarm
event when the snooze timer fires instead of re-entering the sleep poll.

fw/services/activity: fire sleep summary notification once per sleep window

The "Good morning" sleep summary re-fired hours after the real morning
notification whenever the day's sleep bounds changed. Two paths re-armed
it: a pin update for an extended sleep exit cleared the notified flag,
and any shift of sleep_enter_utc was treated as a new day and reset the
whole pin state. A falsely detected evening sleep session (sedentary
awake time misclassified by the algorithm, tracked separately) was
enough to trigger either path, buzzing the user with last night's
summary in the evening or in the middle of the night.

Key the pin state to the sleep-day window (the 9pm local cutoff used by
activity_sessions_prv_get_sleep_bounds_utc, now exposed as
activity_sessions_prv_get_sleep_window_start_utc) instead of comparing
exact enter timestamps. Within one window the notification fires at
most once: pin updates no longer clear the notified flag, and only a
new window resets the state. Additionally, only notify when the sleep
exit lands at a plausible local wake-up time ([4am, 6pm)); skipping
outside that window does not consume the once-per-window notification,
so a mid-night false exit stays silent and the real morning wake-up
still notifies. The timeline pin keeps updating silently in all cases.

The persisted SleepPinState grows by a trailing window_utc field. Older
persisted blobs fail the settings read cleanly (E_RANGE zeroes the
output), and a zero window is re-seeded at init as already-notified so
the state layout change cannot re-fire a summary the user already saw;
the cost is at most one missed summary right after the update.

resources: fix '#' floating above the baseline in GOTHIC_36

The U+0023 glyph header in GOTHIC_36.pbf carries top_offset_px = 6,
leaving its bottom edge 14px above the baseline, while every other size
in the family raises '#' by only 2..6px:

  GOTHIC_14       h 6  top  5  bottom 11  (+3 above baseline)
  GOTHIC_18       h 8  top  7  bottom 15  (+3)
  GOTHIC_24       h 9  top 10  bottom 19  (+5)
  GOTHIC_28       h12  top 10  bottom 22  (+6)
  GOTHIC_36       h16  top  6  bottom 22  (+14)  <- broken
  GOTHIC_36_BOLD  h16  top 14  bottom 30  (+6)

The defect is visible at the largest notification text size on boards
whose display maps it to GOTHIC_36: '#' hangs well above the line the
surrounding text sits on. It came in with the original font asset
import; no generated source for the legacy Gothic bitmap fonts exists
in tree, so patch the metric in place.

Set top_offset_px to 14, matching GOTHIC_36_BOLD's '#', which has the
identical glyph height. Exactly one byte changes (offset 3637,
0x06 -> 0x0e); the bitmap data, all other glyphs, and the offset
tables are untouched. The glyph data is not shared with any other
codepoint. Verified by re-parsing the font: '#' now sits at bottom 30
(+6 above the baseline), in line with the rest of the family.

fw/graphics: align substituted glyphs on the primary font baseline

render_glyph() places a glyph at cursor.origin.y + top_offset_px, but
top_offset_px is baked relative to the baseline of the font the glyph was
taken from (== that font's base resource max_height for PBF). When a glyph
is served by another font — the system emoji font, or the 14px system
fallback font — that baseline sits higher than the primary font's, so the
glyph is drawn too high. With a 36px body font a fallback glyph landed
~22px above the baseline, which is what made emoji look tiny and shifted
up in notifications at text size "Large".

Report the FontInfo that owns the resolved resource and hand the caller a
draw-time correction of MAX(0, primary base max_height - owner base
max_height). Keying it on the owning font rather than on the concrete
resource is what keeps an extension from moving: an extension belongs to
the same font and its offsets are already baked against that font's base
baseline (resource_generator_font.py passes fontgen baseline =
the nominal name_height), while the PBF header records
max_height = pixelHeight, which may be far smaller — the shipped ar_SA
pack uses pixelHeight 12/14/17/20/20 against base fonts of 14/18/24/28/36.
Measuring the resource would therefore have shoved Arabic glyphs 2..16px
too far down, and, since FontInfo.max_height is MAX(ext, base), a taller
extension would have shifted the base font's latin glyphs instead. The
adjust is consequently exactly 0 whenever the glyph came from the font we
were asked to draw with, base or extension. The clamp at 0 keeps a taller
substitute from bleeding into the previous line. For the same reason the
emoji font is now sized against the base resource height, the very
baseline its glyphs get aligned to.

The correction is applied to the glyph rect in render_glyph() before the
target and clipping rects are derived from it, so the source row maths
stays consistent; nothing is baked into the cached glyph metadata, which
is keyed by source resource and shared across primary fonts. Layout and
line heights are untouched, and horizontal advance still comes from the
substituting font as before.

text_resources: pre-load glyph bitmaps during layout to prevent stack overflow

During text rendering, walk_line() calls get_horiz_advance() immediately
before render_glyph() for each character. Previously, get_horiz_advance()
only loaded glyph metadata (need_bitmap=false), so render_glyph() had to
load the bitmap from flash via a deep call chain (pfs_read -> flash_read
-> qspi_flash_read_blocking). On the app task's tight 2 KB stack, this
38+ frame deep chain overflows when rendering non-Latin text (e.g.
Cyrillic) through action menus.

By passing need_bitmap=true in get_horiz_advance(), the bitmap is loaded
into glyph_buffer during the advance call. The immediately following
render_glyph() then finds it cached, avoiding the deep flash I/O path
entirely.

fw/coredump: add memfault_exported flag to flash region header

Add a memfault_exported byte to CoreDumpFlashRegionHeader to track
whether a coredump has been exported to Memfault. The field starts as
0xFF (erased flash) and is cleared to 0x00 via a NOR flash bit-clear
(no sector erase needed) after Memfault chunks have been fully read.

This allows the Memfault coredump reconstruction to skip already-
exported coredumps on subsequent reboots, while keeping the unread
flag independent so the phone can still fetch the original PebbleOS
coredump via Bluetooth.

third_party/memfault: add coredump reconstruction from PebbleOS flash coredump

On SF32LB52, HAL_PMU_Reboot() power-cycles the SoC so RAM does not
survive across reboots, and calling Memfault SDK functions from
NMI/ISR context is not possible (mutexes, flash reads). Instead of
capturing the coredump during the crash, reconstruct it after reboot
from the PebbleOS flash-based coredump.

The reconstruction reads the PebbleOS coredump from SPI flash, extracts
crash registers, FreeRTOS kernel state (task lists, pxCurrentTCB), per-
thread TCBs, and stack memory from pxTopOfStack for each thread. This
data is serialized into a Memfault-format coredump in dynamically
allocated RAM storage, which is freed after the chunk collector has
read all data.

New files:
- memfault_pebble_coredump.c/h: Core reconstruction logic. Parses the
  PebbleOS coredump chunks, builds CachedMemory regions for thread
  stacks and TCBs, and calls memfault_coredump_save(). Uses the
  memfault_exported flag to avoid re-exporting the same coredump.
- memfault_platform_coredump_storage.c: Dynamically allocated RAM-backed
  coredump storage with platform hooks (read/write/erase/clear).

Modified files:
- memfault_platform_port.c: Call reconstruction at boot, remove old
  crash-time coredump region collection code that could not work from
  NMI context.

Fixes FIRM-1331

bluetooth-fw/nimble: fix infinite loop in NimBLE store delete

When deleting a bonding via ble_store_util_delete_peer(),
NimBLE's ble_store_util_delete_all() loops calling our
store_delete callback until it returns BLE_HS_ENOENT.

prv_nimble_store_delete_sec() returned 0 (success) but relied on
a side-effect chain to remove the entry from the in-memory list:
bt_persistent_storage_delete_ble_pairing_by_addr() would call
prv_remove_ble_bonding_from_bt_driver(), which reads the identity
from SPRF, then calls bt_driver_handle_host_removed_bonding() to
remove the in-memory entry.

On the first iteration, this worked and also erased SPRF. On
subsequent iterations, SPRF was already erased, so
shared_prf_storage_get_ble_pairing_data() returned false,
prv_remove_ble_bonding_from_bt_driver() returned early without
removing the in-memory entry, and the callback returned 0 again,
creating an infinite loop that starved all lower-priority tasks
and triggered the task watchdog.

This was triggered in PRF by a repeat pairing scenario (pair
phone A, pair phone B, then phone A reconnects after removing
its pairing).

Fix by removing the entry directly from the in-memory list in
prv_nimble_store_delete_sec() before calling into persistent
storage. bt_driver_handle_host_removed_bonding() already handles
the entry being absent (null check), so no double-free risk.

Fixes FIRM-1522

analyze_coredump: handle GDB errors without aborting script

GDB --batch mode aborts the entire sourced command file on the first
error. When analyzing corrupted coredumps, commands like
'thread apply all info frame' can fail with inaccessible memory,
which silently prevents all subsequent commands (pbl heap, pbl
lockstats, pbl metadata) from ever running.

Wrap each GDB command in a python try/except so errors are printed
but execution continues. Also add a backtrace limit to prevent
infinite frame chasing on corrupted stacks, and a 5 minute timeout
as a safety net.

fw/comm/ppogatt: reset disconnect counter on destroy

The global s_disconnect_counter was not reset when ppogatt_destroy() was
called during a BLE disconnection. This meant the counter persisted
across BLE connections, and after enough disconnect cycles (triggered by
supervision timeouts during RF interference), the PPoGATT client would
enter a permanent "stalled" state with no automatic recovery path,
requiring the user to manually toggle Bluetooth.

Reset the counter in ppogatt_destroy(), since tearing down all clients
means we are starting from a clean slate and each new BLE connection
should get a full set of recovery attempts.

fw/apps/system/music: fix divide-by-zero in track progress

Guard against track_length being zero before computing the progress
percentage. A TOCTOU race exists between music_get_pos() (which copies
track_length into local app data) and music_is_progress_reporting_supported()
(which re-reads track_length from the music service). If track_length
transitions from 0 to non-zero between those two calls, the else branch
is taken with a local track_length of 0, causing an integer divide-by-zero
UsageFault that crashes the system.

fw/services/common/accel_manager: implement accel_manager_enable

accel_manager_enable() was a no-op stub, meaning the accelerometer
was never disabled when the runlevel dropped to BareMinimum (e.g.
during factory reset). This caused an event storm as the driver kept

third_party/nimble: fix H4 stream desync on transport OOM

When hci_h4_sm_rx returns -1 (OOM), the transport was breaking out of
the processing loop, dropping unprocessed bytes still in the read
buffer. Since ipc_queue_read is destructive, those bytes are
permanently lost, causing the H4 state machine to desync. Eventually
the parser interprets a data byte as a packet type, leading to asserts
like the one at hci_h4.c:122 (CMD packet received from controller).

Instead of dropping bytes, yield with vTaskDelay(1) and retry, giving
other tasks a chance to free buffers. This turns a transient OOM into a
brief stall rather than a fatal desync.

fw/services/common/battery: fix false critical shutdown after charger removal

The s_low_on_first_run flag in battery_monitor was a one-way latch (||=)
that could get permanently stuck. If the first battery event after boot had
is_charging=false (e.g. charge complete) and a transiently low fuel gauge
reading, the flag latched true and never cleared. Any subsequent unplug,
even at 100%, triggered critical mode and immediate shutdown.

Fix by:
- Only setting s_low_on_first_run when booting unplugged with a low battery

fw/drivers/vibe: fix vibration strength having no effect on AW86225

vibe_set_strength() only wrote to CONTCFG7 (phase 2 amplitude), while
phase 1 amplitude in CONTCFG6[6:0] was left at the chip's power-on
default. Since vibe_ctl() sets both phase durations to max, the motor
spent all its time in phase 1 at a fixed amplitude, making the strength
setting imperceptible.

Fix by:
- Writing the scaled amplitude to both CONTCFG6[6:0] and CONTCFG7
- Initializing CONTCFG6 with full-scale drv1_lvl during vibe_init()
- Applying a blended linear/quadratic curve for wider perceptual spread
- Scaling drive durations (CONTCFG8/CONTCFG9) with strength

Fixes FIRM-1023

tests/fakes/fake_spi_flash: cover obelix filesystem without huge alloc

Tests historically pass (0, 0x1000000) to fake_spi_flash_init — sized
for snowy's flash layout, where the filesystem region sits inside the
first 16 MB of flash. On platforms whose filesystem region lives at a
higher absolute address (obelix's filesystem starts at 0x12AB0000),
every flash_read_bytes call from PFS trips the
start_addr <= s_state.offset + s_state.length assertion.

A naive expansion of length to FLASH_REGION_FILESYSTEM_END would
allocate ~319 MB per test on obelix (0x13F40000 - 0), which blows
DUMA's protect-free heap and manifests as test_put_bytes_obelix
failing on CI around install_message_while_not_idle.

Translate offset 0 to FLASH_REGION_BASE_ADDRESS on platforms with a
non-zero base, then expand length to FLASH_REGION_FILESYSTEM_END.
The obelix window now spans 0x12000000 → 0x13F40000 (~32 MB) instead
of 0 → 0x13F40000 (~319 MB). Snowy and silk are unaffected (their
base is 0, so they already cover their filesystem region).

Guarded with #ifdef so the shared_prf_storage_v3 tests, which
substitute their own minimal flash_region.h, continue to compile.

fw/drivers/mic/sf32lb52: statically allocate PDM buffers

The PDM circular buffer (20 KB) and DMA rx buffer (1152 B) were being
kernel_malloc'd on every mic_start. On obelix the ~93 KB kernel heap is
prone to fragmentation, and the 20 KB contiguous allocation started
failing reliably in the field once commit 486b2860 bumped the circular
buffer from 128 ms to 320 ms. Every voice session then aborted at
pdm.c:97 ("Failed to allocate circular buffer storage") before any
audio was captured.

Both buffers are fixed-size, exist once per device, and are only used
while the mic is running. Move them to .bss, drop the alloc/free
helpers, and remove the now-dead NULL guards. This also takes ~21 KB of
pressure off the kernel heap for everything else.

Fixes FIRM-1662

fw/services/normal: instrument storage mutex and settings compaction

Add temporary timing instrumentation to help diagnose multi-second
KernelMain UI stalls reported in FIRM-1649. Two known triggers (a
QuickView event arriving from the phone, saving an Alarm) both reduce
to "something wrote a settings/BlobDB file while a flash-heavy
operation was running", and the suspected root cause is
settings_file_compact() running under TimelineItemStorage->mutex while
ftl_erase_sector_blocking() ties up the flash bus for several seconds.
flash_erase_sector_blocking() feeds the task watchdog internally, which
explains why the user sees a recoverable freeze rather than a reboot.

This patch wires up two pieces of telemetry to confirm or kill the
hypothesis:

- timeline_item_storage.c: wrap every mutex_lock/unlock pair with
  prv_storage_lock/prv_storage_unlock helpers that measure both the
  wait-for-lock time and the hold time, and PBL_LOG_WARNING when
  either crosses 100 ms. The log line includes __func__ and the
  storage name so we know which operation stalled and on which
  database (pin_db, reminder_db, ...).

- settings_file.c: log entry and exit of settings_file_rewrite_filtered
  with elapsed ms and final status. This covers both the auto-trigger
  via settings_file_compact() from settings_file_set() and the
  explicit rewrite path used by timeline_item_storage_flush().

If the hypothesis is right we expect to see triples like:

  FIRM-1649: settings_file_rewrite_filtered start file=pin_db
  FIRM-1649: settings_file_rewrite_filtered end file=pin_db
  elapsed=4823ms status=0
  FIRM-1649: timeline_item_storage_read waited 4810ms for pin_db mutex

To revert once we land the real fix:
git grep FIRM-1649 src/fw/services/normal

Refs FIRM-1649

fw/comm/ble/ppogatt: fix infinite disconnect/reconnect loop

ppogatt_destroy() was unconditionally resetting s_disconnect_counter on
every BLE disconnect. This meant the stall protection (which should kick
in after PPOGATT_DISCONNECT_COUNT_MAX consecutive failed resets) never
triggered, causing an infinite disconnect/reconnect loop when the phone
doesn't respond to ResetRequest.

Only reset the counter when the disconnect was external (e.g. RF
interference, phone out of range). When we initiated the disconnect
ourselves due to max resets (disconnect_requested), preserve the counter
so the stall state can be reached after repeated failures.

This partially reverts 5b55ae808 ("fw/comm/ppogatt: reset disconnect
counter on destroy"), which fixed the opposite problem (FIRM-1419:
premature stalling after legitimate disconnects). The new approach
handles both cases by checking disconnect_requested to distinguish
self-initiated from external disconnects.

third_party: scope per-library cflags to their targets

Several third_party wscripts modified the shared bld.env.CFLAGS via
append_unique to add library-specific warning suppressions. Because
bld.env is global and targets capture it at definition time, those
flags leaked into every subsequently-defined target (hal_sifli,
fw drivers, nimble, ...). This hid the fact that some of those
downstream targets had genuine sign-compare/type-limits/unused-*
warnings, and flagged them only on boards where the upstream leak
path wasn't taken (e.g. getafix_dvt, which doesn't build gh3x2x and
so did not inherit -Wno-sign-compare from nonfree).

Move each suppression to the cflags= keyword of the specific target
that needs it:

- qr_code_generator: -Wno-type-limits on qrcodegen.c
- nonfree/gh3x2x: -Wno-sign-compare on the gh3x2x objects
- hal_sifli: existing -Wno-unused-* plus -Wno-sign-compare and
  -Wno-type-limits on the hal_sifli stlib

With the prior commits cleaning up the warnings in our own code
that were previously masked by the leak, both obelix_dvt and
getafix_dvt now build cleanly without relying on flag leakage.

shell/battery_ui_fsm: skip first warning when next one is imminent

If the battery crosses a warning threshold already close to the next
one (e.g. from a fast drop or a fuel-gauge correction), we can show a
gray "Powered 'til tomorrow" and then immediately a red "Powered 'til
tonight" — individually correct, but contradictory to the user because
the daypart message is computed from different reference times.

Require a minimum of 3h of headroom above the next warning threshold
before firing the current warning. If the headroom isn't there, skip
the earlier warning and let the next one fire normally with an accurate
daypart message.

fw/kernel: fix task_cpu_app_pct overflow when apps come and go

The App and Worker task slots are dynamic: tasks are created on launch
and destroyed on exit, so their FreeRTOS ulRunTimeCounter does not
persist across an app restart. Diffing the current counter against a
stale previous value underflowed uint32 and pushed the reported
percentage to ~4 billion cycles per delta_total, surfacing as spikes
around 116k on the task_cpu_app_pct chart.

Capture each dying task's final ulRunTimeCounter into a per-slot
sticky accumulator from pebble_task_unregister(), and report cumulative
slot cycles (sticky + currently-alive counter) in the heartbeat. This
keeps cycles attributed to the App/Worker slots even when several apps
launch and exit within a single (~1 hour) heartbeat period.

The unregister clears the task handle before crediting the cycles, and
the collector snapshots sticky cycles before walking the live task
list. Together these orderings ensure cycles consumed by a task that
dies mid-collection are never double-counted; in the worst case they
are reported one heartbeat late.

fw/apps/prf/mfg_test_aging: rework test flow

Restructure the aging test to better stress the system and validate
battery health:

  1. Charge while cycling components for 4 hours, charge must complete
     within 90 min. Always display the live charge status.
  2. Wait for operator to unplug, fully charged.
  3. Idle for 10 hours; fail if battery drops more than 6%.
  4. Discharge to a safe shipping level (65%) using the backlight.

The previous drop-during-cycling check is replaced by a charge-complete
check (must reach 100% within 90 min and stay there). Charging is no
longer disabled at 100% so the battery remains topped off until the
operator unplugs at the end of the combined phase.

When a factory reset is triggered via the phone protocol, the watch
becomes a zombie for ~47s while filesystem_regions_erase_all() runs:

running, so the user can navigate menus and interact with apps with

this also closes the PFS-write race window during the erase.

skips the progress bar and just shows the dialog.

fw/drivers/vibe/aw86225: check init register writes

The CONTCFG6, two PLAYCFG3 modify_reg calls (BRK_ENABLE,
PLAY_MODE_CONT),
and the SYSCTRL1 modify_reg call at the tail of vibe_init() did not feed
into ret. prv_modify_reg also returned void, swallowing both read and
write I2C failures.

If any of these silently failed during the boot I2C transaction storm,
init "succeeded" with s_initialized=true and the chip responsive enough
to pass the CONTCFG2 readback in vibe_ctl(), but PLAY_MODE_CONT was
never
written, so PLAYCFG4 GO did not drive the LRA. Reboot would re-run the
writes and fix it. Matches user reports of brand-new watches that never
vibrated until a reset (MOB-6609, FIRM-1718).

Have prv_modify_reg return its read+write success and fold every init
write into ret. Tighten logging while we are here: log chip ID on read,
log "init complete" on success, and surface the previously-silent
re-init in vibe_ctl() with a distinct message for I2C failure vs.
register-value mismatch.

Fixes MOB-6609

settings_file_open pre-allocates the PFS file at ~120% of
max_used_space, so a large per-app cap forces every persist file to
claim that much flash up front, even when most apps only use a few
hundred bytes. To make raising the cap cheap, decouple the enforcement
cap from the physical allocation.

Add an alloc_used_space field to SettingsFile that tracks the physical
allocation budget separately from max_used_space. A new
settings_file_open_growable() API sets alloc_used_space to a small
initial value. When a write needs more physical space but fits within
the enforcement cap, the file is automatically grown via rewrite with
doubling allocation (e.g. 4K -> 8K -> 16K -> ... up to max_used_space).

To prevent grown files from holding flash hostage indefinitely after
the data is no longer needed, settings_file_compact picks the smallest
doubling step that leaves ~2x headroom over live data and lowers
alloc_used_space toward the floor before rewriting. The new
min_alloc_used_space field tracks the per-file floor (the
initial_alloc_size requested at open) so files never shrink below the
caller's stated minimum. Existing callers of settings_file_open() are
unchanged: alloc_used_space and min_alloc_used_space both equal
max_used_space, preserving the old pre-allocation behavior with no
shrink.

The persist service now uses settings_file_open_growable() with a
4 KiB initial allocation (~5 KiB physical), close to the existing
6 KiB cap.

fw/services/settings: speed up file rewrite, pause watchdog

settings_file_rewrite_filtered runs under a held mutex while issuing
flash erases and writes that, on a 1 MiB persist file, can take many
seconds. Once the per-app cap was raised the rewrite started tripping
the 5-second task watchdog and triggering App Throttling. FIRM-1649
flagged this; it didn't matter at the old 6 KiB cap.

Three changes:

- Pause the task watchdog for the duration of the rewrite (60 s
  budget, comfortably covers a worst-case 1 MiB rewrite). Same pattern
  already used during boot in main.c.
- Add settings_raw_iter_read_key_val / write_key_val helpers that
  read or write the key and value as a single contiguous PFS call.
  Drops per-record I/O from 6 PFS round-trips (separate header, key,
  val) to 4, which on a file with thousands of records saves a few
  hundred ms of seek/read state-machine overhead.
- Allocate one reusable buffer outside the rewrite loop instead of
  two kernel_malloc/kernel_free pairs per record.

Flash erase and program time still dominate, so this doesn't make
small rewrites feel different, but the watchdog pause keeps big
rewrites from triggering throttle/recovery storms in the logs.

fw/services/notifications: only persist migrated vibe scores at boot

alerts_preferences_init() unconditionally rewrote all three vibe score
keys to the settings file on every boot. With settings sync now using
settings_file timestamps for conflict resolution, that fresh-timestamp
rewrite let the watch win every conflict against the phone and made the
phone's INSERT_WITH_TIMESTAMP for the user's chosen value look stale.
The watch's writeback then got DATA_STALE from the phone, sync.c marked
the item synced anyway with no retry, and the user's setting could no
longer propagate.

Capture each vibe score after RESTORE_PREF and only re-persist a key
when migration or validation actually changed its value. Steady-state
boots no longer touch the file, so on-disk timestamps reflect real user
intent rather than the most recent boot.

Refs: FIRM-1760

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Joshua Jun <lets@throw.rocks>

fw/services/blob_db: canonicalise notif-pref key length

The phone-side BlobDB protocol writes notif-pref keys with a trailing
null terminator (key_len = strlen+1), while alerts_preferences locally
uses strlen() (no null) for both reads and writes. settings_file matches
records on exact key_len, so a phone-pushed value landed in a record
that alerts_preferences_init's RESTORE_PREF could not find on the next
boot, leaving the in-memory state at the platform default
(VibeScoreId_NudgeNudge on obelix). The user-visible symptom was the
notification vibe pattern resetting to "Nudge Nudge" after every reboot.

Strip a trailing null at every settings_blob_db notif-pref entry point
so on-disk records converge on the canonical strlen() length, and probe
both lengths in RESTORE_PREF so legacy records written before this
change still resolve.

Fixes: FIRM-1760

fw/services/compositor: render request for App-to-App transition

When `compositor_transition()` reached the "App to App" else branch
(also taken when a Modal-to-App transition was cancelled mid-animation
and a new transition kicked off while no modal exists), it set the
state to `AppTransitionPending` without calling
`prv_send_app_render_request()`. This left the compositor waiting on a
`PEBBLE_RENDER_READY_EVENT` that the app never sent, freezing the
display until an external event triggered another transition.

This was reproducible by dismissing a notification and immediately
receiving and dismissing a second one, leaving the screen frozen
until a third notification arrived.

Mirror the Modal-to-App branch and request an app render before
moving to `AppTransitionPending`.

Fixes FIRM-1713.

applib/graphics: measure Arabic words using shaped widths

word_init() and the renderer's segment-collection pass measured
each Arabic letter using its basic codepoint (U+0621-U+064A), but
the renderer shapes letters to their contextual presentation forms
(initial/medial/final/isolated) before drawing. Isolated forms are
typically wider than the connected forms that actually render, so
the layout over-estimated word widths and wrapped them to the next
line even when they fit, and the segment-collection pass dropped
trailing letters once its (unshaped) running width hit the line's
(shaped) budget, leaving a visible gap at the line edge.

Extract the per-letter shaping decision from arabic_shape_text()
into arabic_shape_codepoint(prev, curr, next) and use it for width
measurement in both places so layout, segment collection, and the
draw pass agree on every glyph's advance. Non-Arabic codepoints
short-circuit and pass through unchanged, so other scripts are
unaffected.

services/speaker: anti-alias square wave with PolyBLEP

Naive square-wave generation produced clean output only at
frequencies whose half-period was an integer number of output
samples, i.e. f = 8000/n at our 16 kHz output rate. For every
other frequency, including essentially all MIDI notes, the
half-cycles drifted in length and the unbandlimited harmonics
aliased into the audible band, producing the harsh distortion
users reported.

Apply PolyBLEP at the rising and falling edges of the square wave
to suppress aliasing without changing the fundamental. Sine,
triangle, and sawtooth are unchanged; only the square branch picks
up the correction.

Verified at 16 kHz output: zero-crossings now match the requested
fundamental exactly for 100, 261.6 (C4), 440 (A4), 1000, 2000 and
4000 Hz. The amplitude tapers near Nyquist as the band-limited
square converges to a sine, which is the expected behavior.

Fixes SDK-99 / #1215

bluetooth-fw/nimble: roll back host state on failed start

When bt_driver_start() fails after ble_hs_sched_start() has already run
(host_started semaphore timeout, or ble_hs_util_ensure_addr failure),
NimBLE has already transitioned ble_hs_enabled_state to ON. Returning
false to the caller leaves a state mismatch: bluetooth_ctl believes the
stack is stopped (s_comm_is_running = false), but NimBLE thinks the
host is on. The next bt_driver_start() call schedules another start,
ble_hs_start() returns BLE_HS_EALREADY, and the bare assert(rc == 0)
in ble_hs_event_start_stage2 reboots the watch.

Fix it from both ends:

- Add an idempotency guard at the top of bt_driver_start(): if the
  host is already enabled, treat the call as a successful no-op so
  the bluetooth_ctl state machine can converge.
- On the failure paths inside bt_driver_start(), call ble_hs_stop()
  and wait for it to drive the state back to OFF before returning.

Fixes FIRM-1837.

fw/drivers/nrf5/audio: keep codec + I2S warm across pause

Spamming play/pause distorted audio on Asterix as a sweeping phaser
that only a hard power cycle would clear. Each audio_stop power-cycled
the DA7212; over many cycles, residual DC bias from mid-ramp DAC
shutdowns latched onto the LINE-out coupling cap and drove the speaker
amp into self-oscillation, beating against new audio.

Stop power-cycling on every pause. audio_stop now just clears
is_running / trans_cb — the codec stays SYSTEM_ACTIVE=1 with its DAI
master running, the nRF I2S keeps clocking, and the ISR's
prv_fill_i2s_buffer auto-zero-fills as soon as the circular buffer
drains, so the codec sees uninterrupted clocks and a continuous (silent)
data stream throughout a spam sequence. Within
AUDIO_IDLE_SHUTDOWN_MS, audio_start just flips is_running back on and
the next refill lands real audio — no PLL re-lock, no I2S re-init, zero
transitions on the analog domain. A new_timer fires the real shutdown
only after the device has actually been idle.

Add a PebbleMutex around the cold/warm/active transitions so
audio_start, audio_stop, and prv_idle_shutdown can't race across
threads.

fw/comm/ble/ancs: bound notification queue and fail-soft on OOM

Users with many chatty ANCS apps (e.g. Tapo, Apple Home, Nanit,
Outlook, Mail, Slack, Twitter, Flipboard) hit a watch reboot whenever
the post-reconnect notification storm drove the kernel heap to
exhaustion. prv_notif_queue_push_attr_request used kernel_malloc_check
for a 20-byte allocation; a single failure called PBL_CROAK_OOM and
took the system down — losing BlobDB sync state and forcing the user
back through pairing.

Cap the pending-attribute queue at 16 entries, bounding worst-case
heap exposure to ~320 B regardless of how many UIDs the iPhone pushes
in a burst. Action ops aren't capped — they're user-initiated and
rare.

Switch both push paths to kernel_malloc and drop the request with a
WRN if the allocation fails. Missing one ANCS get-attributes round
trip is recoverable (iOS will resend on the next state change); a
reboot is not.

flake.nix: pin make SHELL to /bin/sh on Darwin

Moddable's build/makefiles/mac/tools.mk generates launcher scripts for
mcconfig, mcrun, etc. via `echo '#!/bin/bash\n...'` and relies on the
shell's `echo` builtin expanding `\n` into a real newline. macOS
/bin/sh (bash 3.2, XSI-compliant in POSIX mode) does this; Nix's bash
5.x — which `make` finds first as `sh` via PATH inside the devshell —
does not. The result is a single-line script with a malformed shebang,
so `mcconfig` fails to launch and `./waf configure` aborts with
"Failed to build Moddable tools".

Export `MAKEFLAGS=SHELL=/bin/sh` from the Darwin shellHook so make
runs recipes under the expected shell regardless of PATH ordering.

fw/drivers/mic/sf32lb52: switch to mono capture

Obelix and Getafix were configured for stereo PDM capture even though
Speex compresses to mono and there is no current consumer of the second
channel (it is reserved for future environmental noise cancellation but
unused today). The PDM circular buffer was hard-coded for two channels
and asked the kernel heap for a 20 KB contiguous block on every voice
session, which frequently fails once the heap fragments.

Drop the hard-coded PDM_CH_COUNT macro and size the circular buffer
from MicDevice.channels at allocation time, so the board file controls
the footprint. Flip both Obelix and Getafix to mono, halving the
contiguous block we ask the heap for (10 KB requested / 4 KB floor).

fw/services/voice: keep Speex encoder alive across sessions

voice_speex_init() allocated the Speex encoder state, frame buffer, and
encoded buffer on every dictation session; voice_cancel_dictation()
armed a 100 ms timer to call voice_speex_deinit() on every cancellation.
When the phone fires a retry storm (e.g. sessions 14 through 25 within
a second on the same connection) the watch runs that alloc/free cycle a
dozen times in quick succession, which is the textbook way to fragment
a coalescing heap. Once fragmented, even the fallback 4 KB PDM circular
allocation can fail.

Stop tearing the encoder down between sessions. voice_speex_init()
already short-circuits when initialized, so the first dictation pays
the alloc cost and every subsequent session reuses the buffers.

This also removes the delayed-cleanup machinery whose only reason for
existing was to dodge a race between cancel and the audio endpoint
shutdown -- with no cleanup happening the race vanishes. The three
divergent branches in voice_cancel_dictation collapse to a single
inline teardown.

Cost: the Speex state (~6 KB after the mono switch) and its frame /
encoded buffers stay resident in the kernel heap once voice has been
used at least once. Boot footprint is unchanged.

fw/kernel: report largest free heap block and log on OOM

The kernel heap analytics reported only memory_pct_max (peak usage),
which hides fragmentation: an allocation can fail because no single
free block is large enough long before the heap as a whole is full.
That is exactly the failure mode we have been seeing on the voice
path, but it has been invisible in Memfault.

heap_calc_totals(), and have croak_oom() log used / free / max_free
alongside the bytes requested and the LR. The OOM log now distinguishes

MALLOC_INSTRUMENTATION enabled, so future field failures are

third_party/memfault: fingerprint crashes on the real call site

The reconstructed Memfault coredump's PC came from the PebbleOS coredump's
running/ISR thread, which is unconditionally set to NMI_Handler in
core_dump.c. That made every assert/OOM/watchdog/EventQueueFull issue group
under titles like "Assert at NMI_Handler" or "Out Of Memory at __DSB" /
"... at core_dump_reset" depending on how far Memfault's symbolicator
unwound past the handler frame.

The kernel already stashes the real crash-site address in RebootReason
before pending the NMI (the LR captured via __builtin_return_address, or
the specialized fields for OOM/watchdog/EventQueueFull). Use that to
override s_core_regs.pc so Memfault fingerprints on the function that
actually faulted instead of the crash handler.

The deeper stack trace still won't unwind cleanly through NMI_Handler
since SP points into ISR context — that's a separate problem.

fw/services/bluetooth: replace any existing BLE pairing on new pair

The firmware nominally supports only a single BLE pairing at a time,
but the bonding DB had no enforcement: re-pairing with a different
phone left the previous bonding behind. The user could end up with
two entries (especially after pairing in PRF on top of an existing
normal-FW pairing) and could not connect until they manually forgot
the stale one.

When storing a new BLE pairing, drop any other BLE bonding so the new
one replaces the old. Also prune at boot in case the DB was already in
a multi-bonding state (legacy data, or a PRF pairing layered on top of
an existing one): keep the most recently modified BLE bonding (by the
settings file last_modified timestamp) and delete the rest.

The pruning path must not erase the shared PRF pairing slot, so factor
the delete out into an internal helper that does not touch shared PRF
storage; the existing public delete keeps its current behavior of
erasing it.

Also adjust the test fake's bt_driver_handle_host_removed_bonding to
match the qemu/stub driver behavior (no-op when the bonding was never
registered) instead of asserting, since the new prune path issues
removes for entries the driver may never have been told about.

bluetooth-fw/nimble: track driver state to prevent stage2 assert

ble_hs_event_start_stage2 asserts if ble_hs_enabled_state isn't OFF when
it runs. The existing ble_hs_is_enabled() guard at the top of
bt_driver_start only catches the ON case, so a leaked STOPPING state
(error-path ble_hs_stop whose s_host_stopped wait times out before the
vendor's completion callback fires) slips past the guard and trips the
stage2 assert on the next start attempt, rebooting the watch.

Track our own driver state (Stopped / Starting / Started / Stopping) and
gate bt_driver_start on it:

- On entry, if state is Stopping, retry the s_host_stopped wait so a
  late vendor completion (the vendor's own 2 s timeout always fires
  ble_hs_stop_done eventually) can transition us back to Stopped before
  we schedule a new start.
- On a successful start, advance to Started; on the err: path, mark
  Stopping before invoking ble_hs_stop and roll back to Stopped only
  once the stop completion is observed (or vendor reports EALREADY).
- Drain stale host_started / host_stopped signals before each wait so a
  semaphore left over from a prior cycle can't satisfy this cycle's
  wait.
- bt_driver_stop mirrors the same transitions; keeps the existing
  PBL_ASSERT on stop timeout.

If the retry wait still times out, probe the vendor with
ble_hs_stop(NULL, NULL, NULL) to recover from a lost completion signal:

- BLE_HS_EALREADY -> vendor state is OFF; the completion signal was
  lost, but it's safe to mark Stopped and proceed with the start.
- 0 -> vendor is still STOPPING; refuse, as before.

The probe is side-effect-free in OFF (no work done) and STOPPING (no
listener registered since we pass NULL). It would otherwise initiate
a stop from ON, which can't happen on this path: we only enter
Stopping by calling ble_hs_stop ourselves, and the only vendor
transition out of STOPPING is to OFF.

Writes to s_driver_state happen only on the lifecycle thread (callers
serialize via bluetooth_ctl's state mutex); the stop completion callback
still only signals the semaphore.

Refs FIRM-1837.

fw/services/activity: gate sleep tracking on HRM off-wrist

The kraepelin sleep detector already treats charging as a definite
not-worn signal, but its accel-only off-wrist heuristic takes 30+
minutes to fire and is easily defeated by ambient vibration. Users
report multi-hour false sleep sessions when the watch sits on a desk.

Cache the worn-status from each HRM BPM event in the activity service
and OR a recent HRMQuality_OffWrist reading into the not-worn signal
passed to kalg_activities_update. The logged AlgMinuteDLSSample.plugged_in
field keeps its original "is charging" meaning; only kraepelin's
internal definite-not-worn decision sees the combined signal.

The cached reading goes stale after 15 minutes, which comfortably
covers the default HRMonitoringInterval_10Min (~11-min) cycle. At the
30/60-min intervals the cache will expire between bursts and sleep
detection falls back to the existing accel heuristic, rather than
leaning on a possibly-stale on-wrist reading.

fw/syscall/event: reject unsafe event types from unprivileged callers

sys_send_pebble_event_to_kernel forwarded any PebbleEvent posted by an
app/worker straight onto the kernel queue without inspecting its type.
The kernel then dispatched it under privilege, so an app could post a
PEBBLE_CALLBACK_EVENT carrying its own function pointer and have the
kernel main loop call into app-supplied code with full kernel rights.

Whitelist the small set of event types apps and workers legitimately
post (process kill, render ready, dictation, health, plugin) and call
syscall_failed() for anything else. Events forwarded from privileged
code (e.g. the app outbox service finishing a syscall) are unaffected
since the check is gated on PRIVILEGE_WAS_ELEVATED.

fw/syscall/event: validate handler list nodes on (un)subscribe

sys_event_service_client_(un)subscribe accepted an EventServiceInfo
from app memory but only asserted the struct itself was in userspace.
The embedded ListNode prev/next pointers were trusted, so an app could
craft a handler whose list_node.{prev,next} aimed at kernel memory and
call unsubscribe to make list_remove() run

  node->next->prev = node->prev;
  node->prev->next = node->next;

which is a 4-byte arbitrary write primitive (`*a = b; *b = a`). The
user-supplied list head also let list_find traverse from app memory
into kernel memory.

Validate the handler's prev/next pointers against the caller's task
RAM before list_remove runs, and re-derive the list head in-kernel
from the authoritative per-process state instead of trusting the
caller's `state` argument.

fw/services/accel_manager: validate user-supplied state pointers

Every syscall in this file (data_unsubscribe, set_sampling_rate,
set_sample_buffer, get_num_samples, consume_samples) took an
AccelManagerState* straight from the app. The kernel then read and
wrote fields on it (timestamp_ms, raw_buffer, num_samples, list_node)
without checking the pointer was one we had handed out. An app could
fabricate a struct that overlaid a target kernel address and use
get_num_samples in particular as an arbitrary 8-byte read/write
primitive on kernel memory:

  // read
  void *state = (void *)(addr - offsetof(AccelManagerState, timestamp_ms));
  get_num_samples(state, &value);
  // write
  AccelManagerState fake = { .timestamp_ms = value };
  get_num_samples(&fake, (uint64_t *)addr);

Walk the kernel-side s_data_subscribers list to confirm the pointer
really is one we allocated, and reject the call via syscall_failed()
otherwise. Also validate the timestamp_ms out-parameter is in the
caller's userspace.

sys_activity_get_minute_history validated minute_data with
`syscall_assert_userspace_buffer(minute_data, *num_records *
sizeof(HealthMinuteData))`. Two problems:

  * `*num_records * sizeof(HealthMinuteData)` is a uint32_t multiply
    that wraps for `*num_records > UINT32_MAX/12`. A huge num_records
    can wrap to a tiny size, pass validation, then have KernelBG write
    far past the validated buffer.

    can change *num_records after we validated it but before the
    callback reads it — classic TOCTOU.

syscall_failed() when `requested * sizeof(HealthMinuteData)` would
overflow size_t, and pass kernel-stack copies of num_records and
utc_start down to activity_get_minute_history so the worker thread
operates on memory the app can no longer race. Copy the updated values

sys_pbl_log accepted a LogBinaryMessage* straight from the caller and
handed it to kernel_pbl_log() without any range check. An app could
aim it at any kernel address: log_level steers whether the message is
forwarded, message_length sizes the trailing data, and the flash log

kernel-memory exfiltration primitive into the flash log channel.

trailing message_length bytes before forwarding to the kernel logger.

sys_ble_client_consume_read and sys_ble_client_consume_notification
dereferenced *value_length_in_out twice each: once when validating

gatt_client_consume_read_response /
gatt_client_subscriptions_consume_notification. The notification path
re-reads it a third time inside the gatt subscription code as the gate
on the actual memcpy() into the caller's buffer.

validation read and the inner read, letting the kernel write
header.value_length bytes past the buffer that was actually validated
— a classic TOCTOU into the caller's address space.

then propagate the inner function's updated count back through the
original pointer for callers that care.

re-reads tracks[i].num_notes and tracks[i].sample->num_bytes from

hazard applies to num_notes.

— but the strlen() runs first, so a malicious app could pass a kernel
pointer and have us walk kernel memory until either we find a NUL,
fault on unmapped memory, or read out into the weeds. Validation
afterwards only decides whether to abort the call; by then the read
has already happened.

fw/services/activity: snapshot session_entries and guard size overflow

sys_activity_get_sessions had the same TOCTOU + overflow shape as
get_minute_history before it was fixed: *session_entries is read once
for `sizeof(*sessions) * (*session_entries)` validation, then the
inner activity_get_sessions() re-reads it as the memcpy() count under
the activity-state mutex. A racing app thread can grow the value after
validation to make the memcpy clobber memory past the validated buffer,
and a 32-bit `requested * sizeof(*sessions)` wraps for any large
requested value — passing tiny validation while gating a much larger
write.

Apply the same fix: read *session_entries once, reject sizes that
overflow size_t, validate against the snapshot, pass a kernel-stack
copy down to the worker, and write the result back through the user
pointer after the call returns.

fw/services/activity: clamp history_len before metric validation

sys_activity_get_metric validates `history` with `history_len *
sizeof(*history)`. With history_len uint32_t and sizeof = 4, the
multiplication wraps for history_len > UINT32_MAX/4 (~1G entries) —
a tiny validated size gates a giant write because the inner
activity_get_metric() unconditionally fills history_len int32_ts with
-1 in its prologue (before later clamping to ACTIVITY_HISTORY_DAYS).
That fill happens in privileged mode, so it walks straight past the
validated buffer into kernel RAM.

The kernel never actually needs more than ACTIVITY_HISTORY_DAYS (30)
entries, so clamp history_len up front. Validation then matches what
the kernel will write and the overflow disappears too.

fw/services/analytics: bound enum key in syscalls

The analytics syscalls (set_signed / set_unsigned / set_string /
timer_start / timer_stop / add) forwarded `key` to backends that use
it as a direct, unchecked index into fixed-size kernel tables —
s_key_to_integer[], s_key_to_string[], s_string_ptrs[], s_string_lens[]
in native.c, and s_pbl_to_memfault[] in memfault.c. An app passing
key >= PBL_ANALYTICS_KEY_COUNT reads OOB kernel bytes as an int8_t
index/struct id and operates on whatever that lookup produces.

set_string is the worst: s_string_ptrs[idx] becomes a (potentially
kernel) pointer and s_string_lens[idx] becomes the strncpy length, so
the user-supplied (and validated as app-space) `value` gets written
into kernel memory at an attacker-influenced address.

dispatching to backends. Out-of-range keys are silently dropped to
match the existing behavior of unknown-but-in-range keys.

fw/syscall/ble: validate write payload as userspace

sys_ble_client_write_descriptor each accept a `(value, value_length)`
pair from the caller and hand them straight to gatt_client_op_write*,
which forwards into the BLE driver's ble_gattc_write_flat / ATT write
path. The driver reads value_length bytes starting at `value` and
transmits them to the peer device — there's no validation that
`value` aims at the caller's RAM, so an app can point it at any kernel
address and use the remote BLE central as a generic kernel-memory
exfiltration sink.

syscall boundary so the kernel only reads from the app/worker region

device, status) into the caller's output struct, where `e` is in the
app's memory and the kernel only validated `info`. But `e->info` is a
pointer the event service attached to the event when it was posted —
the app can rewrite that field in its local copy of the event before
calling us. With no check, an app can aim `e->info` at any kernel
address and read kernel memory back through `*info`. Same shape as

fw/services/accel_manager: clamp subscribe handler_task to caller's task

sys_accel_manager_data_subscribe stored the user-supplied (data_cb,
context) and `handler_task` straight into the new AccelManagerState
with no check on the task value. When accel samples arrive,
prv_call_data_callback() routes the user-supplied callback to a
dispatcher chosen by state->task:

  PebbleTask_KernelMain      → kernel-event-loop PEBBLE_CALLBACK_EVENT,
                               which invokes the callback in kernel mode
  PebbleTask_KernelBackground → system_task_add_callback() — runs callback
                               on the system task in kernel mode
  PebbleTask_NewTimers       → new_timer_add_work_callback() — runs callback
                               on the timer task in kernel mode

to any of those three pumps its own function pointer into kernel-mode
execution — full privilege escalation.

handler_task and pin it to the calling task (which must be App or
Worker). Kernel-side subscribers (the HRM manager, ecompass, etc.) are
unaffected because PRIVILEGE_WAS_ELEVATED is false for those callers.

list, copied the timer's callback + callback_data into the caller's
out-params, and (for one-shot timers) freed the timer — all without
checking that the timer's target_task matched the caller. An
unprivileged app could probe TimerIDs to find a system / kernel-side
timer and:

    KASLR-defeating leak of kernel code addresses;
  * delete it, since one-shot timers are unconditionally freed at
    the end of the syscall — denial-of-service against system work.

on evented_timer_is_current_task(). Apply the equivalent check here:
when the call entered from user mode, require timer->target_task ==
pebble_task_get_current() and silently return (0, NULL) otherwise so
the caller can't even tell whether the timer existed.

fw/drivers/mpu: hide ARMv7-M subregion math inside the backend

MpuRegion previously exposed a disabled_subregions field that callers
had to compute via tools/mpu_calc.py at build time. That field is an
ARMv7-M MPU implementation detail (rounding an arbitrary range up to a
power-of-two block plus an 8-bit subregion mask) and has no analogue on
ARMv8-M, which programs the limit register directly.

Drop the field from the public struct. Callers now pass the real
(base_address, size) pair. The ARMv7-M backend's mpu_get_register_settings
computes the block + subregion mask at runtime from these values, and
mpu_get_region decodes them back from the registers. ARMv8-M is
unchanged. The generated kernel/mpu_regions.auto.h header and the
mpu_calc.py helper that produced it both go away; memory_layout.c reads
the actual __APP_RAM__/__APP_RAM_size__/__WORKER_RAM__/__WORKER_RAM_size__
linker symbols directly, removing a source of drift between the linker
script and the auto-generated MPU sizes.

Verified on qemu_flint via gdb register inspection:
- App task running (control=0x2) sees AP=3 (priv R/W + user R/W) on
  App RAM and AP=1 (priv-only) on Worker RAM, with subregion masks
  byte-identical to what mpu_calc.py used to emit.
- Stack guard region (32B at __isr_stack_start__) programmed AP=0
  (no access).
- Menu navigation through multiple submenus exercises the App-task
  context switch path without faults.

qemu_emery still uses the ARMv8 backend and continues to boot to the
launcher (MPU still disabled at runtime via the early-return that a
later step removes).
