comm/ble: ppogatt: guard prv_send_next_packets against re-entry

prv_send_next_packets temporarily drops bt_lock around NimBLE calls.
During that window other tasks (e.g. KernelMain processing the
comm_session_send_next scheduled by comm_session_open) can re-enter the
function for the same client and observe inconsistent state — most
visibly, re-send a pending reset/ack packet that hasn't been finalized
yet.

a re-entrant call hits the guard, a send_next is re-scheduled via
comm_session so any queued data still gets flushed after the outer call

bluetooth: add reversed PPoG transport

Add reversed PPoG, so that the phone can subscribe to the watch's PPoG
service instead of the other way around.

Reasoning:
- This is simpler and will fix a class of bugs we see in the field where
  the watch either can't find the phone's ppog service, or doesn't
  realize that it needs to resubscribe on iOS because the link never
  dropped (kept alive by ANCS). Also may fix some bugs on weird Android
  devices.
- In the future it would enable us to use AccessorySetupKit on iOS
  (which is currently a pre-requisite to the new Accessory Notifications
  framework), which will not work while running a GATT server on the
  phone.

Changes:
- Add the reversed PPoG GATT service (NimBLE): notify-only data
  characteristic for outbound packets, write-without-response
  characteristic for inbound ones.
- Driver callbacks dispatch all work to KernelMain, where forward-mode
  RX (kernel_le_client GATT events) and comm session send_next jobs
  already run, keeping the whole PPoG state machine on one task. The
  NimBLE host task itself is ruled out because the state machine
  (bt_lock acquisition plus re-entrant NimBLE calls) does not fit on its
  stack. KernelBG is ruled out because its callbacks may block for
  seconds on Pebble Protocol send progress (e.g. the BT log dump blocks
  up to 4 s per line in comm_session_send_buffer_begin_write()); inbound
  ACKs would sit unprocessed behind them until the system task queue
  overflows and forces a reset (RebootReasonCode_EventQueueFull).
- Sends that fail with BTErrnoNotEnoughResources (mbuf exhaustion, e.g.
  the put_bytes inbound flood during a firmware update) are retried via
  a per-client one-shot timer after PPOGATT_SEND_RETRY_DELAY_MS (20 ms,
  about one connection event). NimBLE has no buffers-freed event to wait
  for: its NOTIFY_TX GAP event fires synchronously per send attempt with
  the attempt's own status, so a failed attempt never produces a
  follow-up event and waiting on one would stall the transport
  permanently. The timer callback bounces to KernelMain (NimBLE calls
  must not run on the timer task) and pumps prv_send_next_packets()
  directly rather than via comm_session_send_next(), because the session
  does not exist yet if a Reset Complete send fails during the
  handshake. Stalls log a warning on the first failed attempt and, on
  recovery, how many retries it took.
- The service self-registers a GAP event listener
  (ble_gap_event_listener_register) for subscribe events, the same
  pattern upstream service-grade modules (ble_eatt, ble_audio) use, so
  no central dispatcher changes are needed. Registration tolerates
  BLE_HS_EALREADY because bt_driver_start can run multiple times while
  the listener list is only reset by nimble_port_init.
- The service requires an encrypted link. The data-write characteristic
  carries WRITE_ENC and the data-notify characteristic READ_ENC, which
  the CCCD now inherits (needs the bundled mynewt-nimble fix), so both
  writing PPoG data and subscribing get an ATT insufficient-encryption
  error on an unencrypted link - triggering pairing on well-behaved
  phones. The kernel additionally refuses to start a client on an
  unencrypted connection as a backstop. This matters because, unlike
  forward PPoG (where the watch only talks to its bonded gateway), any
  central can connect to the advertising watch.
- The phone subscribes to this service if it exists, otherwise it opens
  a GATT server with the "normal" (forward) ppog service.
- The watch ignores the phone's ppog service if the phone subscribes to
  the reversed service, i.e. reversed has priority and is intended to be
  the primary connection path going forward.
- The phone is expected to send the initial ResetRequest after
  subscribing. This makes it clear that the phone initiates the
  connection and never needs to wait for the watch, which is what caused
  a lot of problems previously.

Remaining issues:
- Both iOS and Android cache the watch's GATT services and return a
  stale list to the mobile app until the device is re-paired, so the
  phone app will not see this new service initially (users are expected
  to pair in PRF, which does not have it). This is OK for now - the
  existing ppog mechanism continues to work. We should follow up by
  potentially implementing the 0x2B2A database hash characteristic,
  which NimBLE doesn't support yet (both phone OSs should trigger a full
  discovery refresh when it changes).

Testing:
- Tested on iOS and Android; works in both normal and reversed mode,
  depending on whether the app can see the new reversed service or not.
  Tried pairing in PRF -> update to FW with this service (continues to
  use normal ppog, unless the GATT cache is force-refreshed on Android,
  in which case it uses the new reversed service). Tried pairing to a
  device running this service: works using the new reversed mode.
- Firmware-update stress tested on iOS during the MOB-9394
  investigation: 16/16 consecutive update loops completed with the
  paired libpebble3 fixes (the remaining stall was an iOS bluetoothd
  GATT-pipeline issue, worked around phone-side).

bluetooth: serialize GATT client procedures with an op queue

NimBLE runs GATT client procedures concurrently and dispatches
incoming ATT responses to the first pending procedure that consumes
that response opcode (see ble_gattc_rx_read_type_elem_entries). Two
concurrent procedures consuming the same opcode get their responses
cross-delivered, corrupting both. This was observed as the GAP device
name read (read-by-UUID) racing characteristic discovery, which both
consume ATT Read By Type responses: the "device name" ended up
containing raw characteristic declaration bytes (rendered as a blank
name on the PRF getting-started screen) while discovery/PPoGATT
received the other half of the cross-delivery (meta protocol errors,
session failures, phone reconnect loops).

Add a driver-level FIFO of GATT client operations so only one
procedure ever runs at a time: an op starts when the previous op's
terminal callback fires. Ops are started from KernelBG, which makes
pushing safe from any context, including with bt_lock held (calling
NimBLE APIs under bt_lock deadlocks against the NimBLE host task, see
commit 3d5009dd0). Service discovery, the GAP device name read and
the pairing-confirmation name read in advert.c all go through the
queue now.

While at it:

- The device name read callback resolves the connection by device
  address under bt_lock instead of trusting a raw GAPLEConnection
  pointer that can go stale, and copies the name with
  ble_hs_mbuf_to_flat() so chained mbufs don't truncate it.
- Discovery start errors are reported through
  bt_driver_cb_gatt_client_discovery_complete, since the actual start
  is now asynchronous.
- Fix a discovery context leak when ble_gattc_disc_all_svcs fails.

comm/ble: fix gateway intent registration racing IRK update

After pairing completes, the driver persists our and the peer's keys
through two separate launcher-task callbacks. The first one creates
the bonding, whose DidAdd handler re-registers the kernel gateway
intent; the second one delivers the peer IRK to the connection. When
the intent was registered, prv_register_intent() looked the live
connection up by IRK only (the by-address fallback was gated on the
bonding having no IRK), so the lookup missed, the intent was
registered as not connected, and the ConnectedAndEncrypted event that
kicks off the kernel LE clients (PPoGATT, service discovery) was
never emitted. The second key store is treated as a re-pair
(DidChange), which the kernel client ignores, so pairing a different
phone got stuck after pairing completion until the phone reconnected.

The connection address is already updated to the identity address by
the time the bonding change handlers run (the identity resolved event
is delivered synchronously from the host task), so fall back to
matching by address whenever the IRK lookup misses.

services/filesystem/pfs: fall back to scan when cached header check fails

pfs_open() re-validates the start page header of fd-cache hits, and
until now failed the whole open with the raw header status (E_ERROR)
when the check did not pass, even though the copy on flash may still be
perfectly valid (e.g. a transient flash read glitch). Callers such as
settings_file_open() treat that as a hard failure, which for the GAP
bonding DB meant losing a write.

Evict the cache entry and fall back to the flash scan instead, reusing
the just-freed fd slot. This matches what already happened when the
cached page merely stopped being a start page, and makes a cached open
behave like an uncached one.

services/filesystem/pfs: unlink stale corrupt file copies during scan

A start page whose header no longer passes its CRC check but still
carries a matching file name (e.g. left behind by an interrupted
rewrite or delete) was skipped by every flash scan with a 'CRC corrupt
for page N' warning, forever: nothing ever reclaimed it, so it leaked
its pages and spammed the log on each lookup of that file.

When the scan finds a valid copy of the file, unlink the corrupt match
so it stops shadowing scans and its pages become reclaimable. If no
valid copy exists the corrupt page is left untouched, since the failed
check may be a transient read glitch and a later scan can still succeed.
The unlink walk is bounded by the per-page next_page CRC8, so a corrupt
chain cannot mark unrelated pages.

fw/drivers/imu/lis2dw12: track FIFO reads for the INT1 stall watchdog

The INT1 watchdog timed the last INT1 edge, but shake/wake-up function
interrupts share the INT1 pad (CTRL7 INT2_ON_INT1): wrist motion keeps
producing edges while the FIFO stream is dead, so a stalled stream was
never detected as long as the watch was moving. Time successful FIFO
burst reads instead, which is the signal the watchdog actually guards.

with a 1 s floor so small FIFO batches do not trip recovery on normal

a queued check is safe against sampling stopping in between.

fw/drivers/imu/lis2dw12: quiesce INT1 routing during stream recovery

The previous recovery only rewrote FIFO_CTRL and read ALL_INT_SRC.
Field logs (FIRM-2490) show it firing repeatedly without reviving the
stream: when the INT1 pad is left latched HIGH after a FIFO overrun
(known quirk, see implementation notes), rewriting FIFO_CTRL does not
release the pad, so the rising-edge EXTI never fires again.

Add a shared recovery helper, used by both the stall watchdog and the
FIFO overrun path, that disables INT1/INT2 routing first (forcing the
pad low so re-enabling produces a fresh edge), salvages queued samples
instead of discarding them, clears latched function INT sources while
quiesced (so a shake landing mid-recovery is not silently consumed),
and then re-asserts the full dynamic configuration (ODR, FIFO mode,
INT routing).

fw/drivers/imu/lis2dw12: re-check INT1 pad level after servicing

INT1 aggregates level-based (FIFO threshold) and latched (wake-up)
sources on a rising-edge EXTI, so a source asserting while the pad is
already high produces no new edge. Example: the FIFO crosses its
threshold between the sample drain and the ALL_INT_SRC read of the same
servicing pass, keeping the pad high through the wake-up clear; no edge
ever follows and the stream stays dead until the stall watchdog fires,
losing seconds of samples.

Close the race deterministically: after each servicing pass, read the
INT1 pad level back. If it is still high after FIFO progress, service
again (the pending event will produce no edge). If it is high with
nothing serviced, the pad is stuck (post-overrun latch-up quirk) and
only an INT routing reset produces edges again, so run the recovery.
The stall watchdog remains as a backstop; with this change its
recovery counter should stay at zero in normal operation.

Two constraints shape the requeue rule. WU_IA stays set while the
wake-up condition persists (LIR does not clear on source read), so
shake is dispatched only on WU assertion, tracked across passes and
reset on a fresh edge (which proves the pad went low); dispatching per
pass would flood shake events at I2C pass rate during continuous
motion. For the same reason only FIFO progress requeues the handler: a
pad held high by a persistent wake-up condition resumes producing
edges once the condition deasserts, and a FIFO threshold crossing
during the hold is covered by the stall watchdog, whose recovery
drains (rather than discards) the queued samples.

fw/services/speaker: drain audio pipeline before stopping

The service stopped the audio driver as soon as the active source had no
more samples to generate. The drivers queue up to 64 ms of audio ahead of
the DAC (double-buffered DMA/I2S pipe primed with silence plus a circular
buffer), so playback was cut off up to 64 ms early. Sounds shorter than
the pipeline depth were never heard at all: on sf32lb52, whose audio_stop
halts the DMA and cuts amplifier power immediately, a 25 ms
speaker_play_tone() produced only the amplifier pop.

Once the source is exhausted, keep feeding silence until the pipeline has
drained, then stop. Playback transitions through SpeakerStateDraining so
clients can observe it. While only padding silence remains, allow
same-priority playback to start instead of rejecting it, so rapid
re-triggers (e.g. a metronome app) are not dropped.

On nrf5/da7212 the change is behavior-neutral: its warm-pause audio_stop
keeps the I2S stream draining anyway, so the warm pause merely starts
~80 ms later. Adds a host test suite with a fake audio driver covering
the drain and preemption behavior.

fw/drivers/imu/lsm6dso: return fresh data from accel_peek while sampling

While sampling is active, accel_peek() returned the sample cached at
the last FIFO drain. The FIFO watermark is set by the most demanding
subscriber; with only the activity tracker subscribed (25 Hz x 125
samples) that sample can be up to 5 seconds old. Apps that poll
accel_service_peek() for tilt input (Gyro Maze, Mr. Runner Up, Fluid
Sim, ...) therefore saw multi-second input lag, while apps subscribing
with a small batch size were unaffected. Classic-era drivers (bmi160)
read the current output registers on every peek, which is why these
apps worked on older watches.

Read the output registers on peek instead: they update at ODR
independently of the FIFO on this part. The cached sample is now
unused, so drop it.

ci: rebase PR branches onto target branch before running

Check out the PR head SHA and rebase it onto the current tip of the
target branch before any CI job runs, following the approach used by
Zephyr. If the rebase does not apply cleanly, the job fails immediately
with an error asking the author to rebase locally.

This replaces building GitHub's ephemeral merge commit, which only
reflects the target branch at event time, so stale branches were tested
against an outdated base.

The rebase logic lives in a reusable composite action
(.github/actions/rebase) with a checkout-style 'submodules' input
(default false) to re-sync submodules after the rebase so gitlinks
match the rebased tree. Compliance diff ranges now use
origin/$GITHUB_BASE_REF instead of the event base SHA, which would
include unrelated upstream commits after the rebase.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Gerard Marull-Paretas <gerard@teslabs.com>

ci: resolve rebase action from the merge ref

Workflows checked out the PR head SHA before resolving the local
rebase action, so PR branches created before the action existed were
missing it from the workspace and every job failed at action
resolution.

Check out the default merge ref instead, which always contains the
current merged copy of the action, and let the action itself switch to
the PR head before rebasing. The head SHA is always fetchable since it
is a parent of the merge commit and the checkout is full depth. If the
PR conflicts with its base, the merge ref does not exist and checkout

fw/services/process_management: allow unaligned relocation table offsets

The SDK app relocation-data validation added in 68b30e60 rejects any
app whose image size (load_size) is not word-aligned, since the
relocation table starts right at that offset and was read as a
uint32_t array.

Legacy SDK apps routinely have non-word-aligned image sizes: the store

relocation table offset alignment" and bounces back to the launcher.

bytewise instead. All security-relevant validation is unchanged:
relocation targets must still be word-aligned, in-bounds, and past the
header, and relocated values must stay within the app image.

fw/drivers/imu/lsm6dso: retry INT1 servicing before stream recovery

The stuck-pad heuristic recovers the stream when a servicing pass takes
no action and the INT1 pad still reads high. A wake-up or FIFO threshold
source asserting between the status register reads and the pad re-check
is indistinguishable from a stuck pad, so the heuristic recovers a
healthy stream and discards the event that raced it (recovery clears
ALL_INT_SRC without dispatching).

Field logs show this clustering during sustained motion, up to 7
recoveries in 23 minutes, each one dropping a wake-up event.

Retry the servicing pass once before recovering: a racing source is
latched (wake-up) or level (FIFO threshold), so it is visible on
re-read and gets serviced normally. Only recover when a second
consecutive pass finds nothing with the pad still high, which is then a
genuinely stuck pad.

fw/put_bytes: scope BLE slowdown to the raw storage erase

pb_storage_raw_init() requested ResponseTimeMiddle with
max_period_secs=0 (added in 6d679bc73 to reduce NimbleHost stack
pressure during blocking flash operations). This had two problems:

- 0 does not mean run forever (that is MAX_PERIOD_RUN_FOREVER), it
  creates an already-expired request: the bt_conn_mgr watchdog deleted
  it ~1s later and, with no requests left, dropped the connection to
  ResponseTimeMax (45ms interval, slave latency 3).
- It shares BtConsumerPpPutBytes with the ResponseTimeMin request held
  during chunk streaming, so it cancelled the fast interval at every
  raw object boundary.

As a result, during a firmware update each object init (firmware, then
system resources) bounced the connection Min -> Middle -> Max -> Min,
and the multi-second slot erase plus its init ACK ran at up to 180ms
effective interval, adding ~5-10s per object.

Request Middle only for the duration of the erase, with a bounded
timeout as a safety net, and restore Min right after so the init ACK
goes out at the fast interval and the streaming request is never
cancelled. The NimbleHost stack overflow remains covered by the stack
size increase from 6d679bc73.

drivers/speaker: map SF32LB volume to attenuation-only DAC gain

The DAC-path volume was converted from the 0-100 UI scale as
(vol - 36) * 2 half-dB, i.e. -36..+64 dB. Any volume above 36 applied
positive digital gain, which hard-clips full-scale content: alarm tones
(volume 60, +24 dB) played as a digital-full-scale square wave, at
maximum loudness regardless of the speaker volume preference, and
overdriving the speaker well past the level the factory test validates.
Volumes above 90 exceeded the HAL's +54 dB limit, so
HAL_AUDCODEC_Config_DACPath_Volume failed without writing the gain
registers and the error was ignored, leaving the 0 dB baseline and
making the volume curve non-monotonic (90 was louder than 100).

The mapping had been dead code until 0e2afbddb started re-applying the
volume after DAC path setup (v4.20.0), which is when alarms became
loud and distorted in the field.

Map 1..100 linearly to -36..0 dB instead (0 still mutes), and log a
warning if the HAL rejects the value.

comm/ble: request connection parameter update sooner after connect

iOS creates connections with a 720ms supervision timeout and only
relaxes it once the peripheral requests new parameters. We waited the
full TGAP(conn_pause_peripheral) = 5s before sending the request, so
any RF fade during that window killed the link. Logs from a getafix
unit showed reconnect storms where most connections died of supervision
timeout (0x208) within 1-6s of connecting, i.e. before the update could
be requested, while connections that reached the 6s supervision timeout
stayed up for hours.

Shorten the initial pause to 1s. The 5s pause is a spec recommendation
("should", not "shall"), and Apple has confirmed relaxed handling of
TGAP timings (see the pre-existing note about the 30s Tgap timeout).

comm/ble: back off reconnect advertising during connection churn

When the link repeatedly drops right after connecting (e.g. supervision
timeouts in bad RF conditions), every disconnection restarted reconnect
advertising with a 30s short-interval (20ms) burst. A getafix unit
hitting a reconnect storm went through ~130 connect/disconnect cycles
in 70 minutes, each paying the full burst.

Track how often plain reconnect advertising is (re)started: after 3
starts within a 60s window, schedule only the long-interval (~1s) term.
One attempt per window still gets the short-interval burst, so
reconnection latency recovers as soon as the churn stops. BLE HRM
reconnection advertising is user-initiated and time-bounded, so it is
not backed off.

fw/services/process_management: allow unaligned relocation targets

The v4.24.0 loader hardening required every relocation target to be
word aligned. Legacy SDK apps can have pointer slots at halfword
offsets inside packed structs, e.g. 91 Dub v4.0 has seven such
relocations per platform binary and was rejected on launch with
"Invalid app relocation target[16]: 0x39da". A scan of the 400 most
popular Rebble store apps found five affected (91 Dub v4.0, Timely,
Rosewright A, Rosewright Chronograph, Directions); all of them worked
before the hardening because Cortex-M supports unaligned LDR/STR.

offsets. The bounds checks that actually prevent out of bounds writes
in a privileged context are retained. Verified in QEMU (qemu_emery):

services/notifications: fix leak and deleted-entry handling in rewrite

notification_storage_rewrite() never freed the TimelineItem buffer that

buffer per notification on each rewrite (e.g. timezone migration).

so the next header was read from payload bytes and iteration ended
early; and the loop still wrote a record for the deleted entry, using
the previous item's stale payload. Skip deleted entries entirely,
matching prv_compress(), and track the bytes written so s_write_offset
stays correct for the now-shorter file.

drivers/speaker: throttle sf32lb52 DMA refill callbacks

The AUDCODEC DMA half/full-complete ISRs enqueued a prv_audio_trans_bg
refill callback on every interrupt with no in-flight tracking. When
KernelBG is starved (e.g. an app blocking on a slow flash resource read
while holding the pfs mutexes), the system task queue fills up and the
watch hard-reboots with Event Queue Full, cutting alarm tones off a few
seconds into playback.

one refill callback is in flight, clearing it again if the enqueue

block refills on a new session.

services/ecompass: relax calibration gates for weak geomagnetic fields

The sphere-fit solver only accepts a four-point sample set when the
points are spread further apart than an absolute distance threshold:
point-to-point, point-to-line and point-to-plane all had to exceed
370 (37 uT), with a single fallback to 220 that was only armed after
two 300-sample windows in which the point-to-point gate had passed.

All samples lie on a sphere whose radius R is the local geomagnetic
field strength. In weak-field regions such as the South Atlantic
Anomaly (~22 uT, R ~= 228) those gates are unsatisfiable:
point-to-point > 370 needs ~108 degrees of orientation change, more
than the calibration UI coaches, and point-to-line > 370 is
geometrically impossible since its maximum is
R + sqrt(R^2 - (370/2)^2) < 370 for R < ~231. Because the fallback
was gated on the point-to-point pass that weak fields cannot produce,
the threshold never dropped and calibration never completed (bug
report logs show zero solutions over a 7 minute session).

Replace the strike-based fallback with deterministic progressive
relaxation: every 300-sample window that ends without a complete
point set lowers the threshold by 70, down to a floor of 90 (9 uT).
The floor keeps all three gates satisfiable at ~20 uT with realistic
<= 90 degree orientation coverage. Normal-field behavior is
preserved: the strict 370 threshold is still tried first and only
relaxes after demonstrated failure to fit, and the existing
requirement of three consecutive consistent fits within 50 counts
still rejects noisy solutions.

Also reset the threshold and the fit-consistency history in
ecomp_corr_reset() so each calibration session starts from the
strict gates instead of inheriting relaxed state.

Unit tests cover weak-field convergence (radius-228 sphere with a
hard-iron offset, 50-degree cap coverage, sensor noise: the old
gates provably never fire, the new code locks within ~80 simulated
seconds and recovers the offset within 2 counts), normal-field
regression (radius 470, locks within the first strict window), and
rejection of degenerate stationary and coplanar inputs.

services/alarms: fix user snooze delay on smart alarms

User snoozes and the smart alarm's internal sleep poll share the same
snooze timer, and its expiry always funneled back into the smart-alarm
sleep gate. Snoozing a firing smart alarm therefore turned "Snooze for
N minutes" into an open-ended 1-minute sleep-poll loop that only
re-fired the alarm once sleep exit was detected or the poll cap was hit.

snooze and bypass the sleep gate in that case, so the alarm re-fires
after exactly the configured snooze delay. The flag is cleared on every
snooze-timer teardown (dismiss, disable, delete, new alarm, clock-change
force trigger).

Add a regression test: a firing smart alarm that is user-snoozed while
the user still looks asleep (RestfulSleep, VMC 0) must put the alarm
event when the snooze timer fires instead of re-entering the sleep poll.

fw/services/activity: fire sleep summary notification once per sleep window

The "Good morning" sleep summary re-fired hours after the real morning
notification whenever the day's sleep bounds changed. Two paths re-armed
it: a pin update for an extended sleep exit cleared the notified flag,
and any shift of sleep_enter_utc was treated as a new day and reset the
whole pin state. A falsely detected evening sleep session (sedentary
awake time misclassified by the algorithm, tracked separately) was
enough to trigger either path, buzzing the user with last night's
summary in the evening or in the middle of the night.

Key the pin state to the sleep-day window (the 9pm local cutoff used by
activity_sessions_prv_get_sleep_bounds_utc, now exposed as
activity_sessions_prv_get_sleep_window_start_utc) instead of comparing
exact enter timestamps. Within one window the notification fires at
most once: pin updates no longer clear the notified flag, and only a
new window resets the state. Additionally, only notify when the sleep
exit lands at a plausible local wake-up time ([4am, 6pm)); skipping
outside that window does not consume the once-per-window notification,
so a mid-night false exit stays silent and the real morning wake-up
still notifies. The timeline pin keeps updating silently in all cases.

The persisted SleepPinState grows by a trailing window_utc field. Older
persisted blobs fail the settings read cleanly (E_RANGE zeroes the
output), and a zero window is re-seeded at init as already-notified so
the state layout change cannot re-fire a summary the user already saw;
the cost is at most one missed summary right after the update.

The U+0023 glyph header in GOTHIC_36.pbf carries top_offset_px = 6,
leaving its bottom edge 14px above the baseline, while every other size
in the family raises '#' by only 2..6px:

  GOTHIC_14       h 6  top  5  bottom 11  (+3 above baseline)
  GOTHIC_18       h 8  top  7  bottom 15  (+3)
  GOTHIC_24       h 9  top 10  bottom 19  (+5)
  GOTHIC_28       h12  top 10  bottom 22  (+6)
  GOTHIC_36       h16  top  6  bottom 22  (+14)  <- broken
  GOTHIC_36_BOLD  h16  top 14  bottom 30  (+6)

whose display maps it to GOTHIC_36: '#' hangs well above the line the
surrounding text sits on. It came in with the original font asset
import; no generated source for the legacy Gothic bitmap fonts exists
in tree, so patch the metric in place.

identical glyph height. Exactly one byte changes (offset 3637,
0x06 -> 0x0e); the bitmap data, all other glyphs, and the offset
tables are untouched. The glyph data is not shared with any other
codepoint. Verified by re-parsing the font: '#' now sits at bottom 30

fw/graphics: align substituted glyphs on the primary font baseline

render_glyph() places a glyph at cursor.origin.y + top_offset_px, but
top_offset_px is baked relative to the baseline of the font the glyph was
taken from (== that font's base resource max_height for PBF). When a glyph
is served by another font — the system emoji font, or the 14px system
fallback font — that baseline sits higher than the primary font's, so the
glyph is drawn too high. With a 36px body font a fallback glyph landed
~22px above the baseline, which is what made emoji look tiny and shifted
up in notifications at text size "Large".

Report the FontInfo that owns the resolved resource and hand the caller a
draw-time correction of MAX(0, primary base max_height - owner base
max_height). Keying it on the owning font rather than on the concrete
resource is what keeps an extension from moving: an extension belongs to
the same font and its offsets are already baked against that font's base
baseline (resource_generator_font.py passes fontgen baseline =
the nominal name_height), while the PBF header records
max_height = pixelHeight, which may be far smaller — the shipped ar_SA
pack uses pixelHeight 12/14/17/20/20 against base fonts of 14/18/24/28/36.
Measuring the resource would therefore have shoved Arabic glyphs 2..16px
too far down, and, since FontInfo.max_height is MAX(ext, base), a taller
extension would have shifted the base font's latin glyphs instead. The
adjust is consequently exactly 0 whenever the glyph came from the font we
were asked to draw with, base or extension. The clamp at 0 keeps a taller
substitute from bleeding into the previous line. For the same reason the
emoji font is now sized against the base resource height, the very
baseline its glyphs get aligned to.

The correction is applied to the glyph rect in render_glyph() before the
target and clipping rects are derived from it, so the source row maths
stays consistent; nothing is baked into the cached glyph metadata, which
is keyed by source resource and shared across primary fonts. Layout and
line heights are untouched, and horizontal advance still comes from the
substituting font as before.

fw/services/process_management: allow unaligned relocation targets

The v4.24.0 loader hardening required every relocation target to be
word aligned. Legacy SDK apps can have pointer slots at halfword
offsets inside packed structs, e.g. 91 Dub v4.0 has seven such
relocations per platform binary and was rejected on launch with
"Invalid app relocation target[16]: 0x39da". A scan of the 400 most
popular Rebble store apps found five affected (91 Dub v4.0, Timely,
Rosewright A, Rosewright Chronograph, Directions); all of them worked
before the hardening because Cortex-M supports unaligned LDR/STR.

Drop the alignment requirement and access the slot bytewise via
memcpy, mirroring the earlier fix for unaligned relocation table
offsets. The bounds checks that actually prevent out of bounds writes
in a privileged context are retained. Verified in QEMU (qemu_emery):
91 Dub v4.0 (basalt) and Rosewright A (emery) now load and render,
and a current-SDK app still loads.

fw/kernel: commit to PRF before the factory reset wipe

factory_reset() only set BOOT_BIT_FORCE_PRF and invalidated the
firmware slots after pfs_format(), which holds the PFS mutex across a
multi-minute flash erase. Any reset inside that window (task watchdog
on a task blocked on the PFS mutex, crash, power loss) rebooted the
watch straight back into normal firmware: pairing was already wiped
and the half-erased filesystem was silently reformatted on boot, so
the watch came up unpaired as if the factory reset never happened.

Set the boot bit and invalidate the slots right after the non-PFS
teardown, before starting the format, so an interrupted factory reset
lands in PRF, which is the expected outcome. A partially erased
filesystem is reformatted on first use anyway.

drivers/imu: recover stuck INT1 in shake-only mode

Both the LSM6DSO and LIS2DW12 mix latched (wake-up) and level (FIFO)
sources on a rising-edge INT1 EXTI, so a pad that latches high produces
no further edges. The existing stall watchdog recovers this, but it was
only armed while FIFO sampling was active. In shake-detection-only mode
(watch idle, no data subscribers) a latched-high pad had no recovery
path: shake events die and the pending interrupt holds the CPU out of
deep sleep until the battery drains.

Field data from an obelix device (C111131100UV) showed 12 such episodes
across v4.9.183-v4.23.0 (both drivers): drain jumps from 0.15%/hr to
3.2%/hr (~21x) with accel_shake_count pinned at zero, only clearing when
the 4% low-power runlevel coincidentally power-cycled the accelerometer.

Arm the INT1 watchdog in shake-only mode at a fixed 5s poll. When the
pad reads high, re-run the INT1 servicing pass (reading the INT source
clears the latch and releases the pad, dispatching any real shake, and
recovers directly when nothing was serviced). Count only a pad that is
still high after servicing, and escalate to a full stream recovery after
3 consecutive stuck passes. The counter resets on any genuine INT1 edge,
a low pad, or a watchdog rearm.

Also re-arm the watchdog from accel_set_sampling_interval so the FIFO
cadence cannot go stale if the ODR changes while sampling is active,
but only on an actual interval change (a re-arm resets the stall
tracking, so repeat calls must not defer it), and clamp the timer
period to at least one second.

drivers/backlight: avoid AW9364E shutdown when dimming

The AW9364E 1-wire protocol is asymmetric: extra pulses step the
current further down without a restart, but raising it requires a full
shutdown (EN low >2.5ms) followed by a fresh pulse train. The driver
previously did the shutdown unconditionally, blanking the LED for 2.6ms
on every brightness change, which made fade-out steps read as blinks.

Track the pulse count latched by the chip and only emit the delta when
dimming; reserve the shutdown/re-train sequence for turning on or
brightening. Turning off now just drives EN low instead of busy-waiting
out the shutdown time, since the turn-on path always waits it out
itself. Redundant same-level requests return early.

Run pulse trains inside a critical section: an interrupt stretching a
1us low period past 500us puts the chip in undefined territory, so the
~55us worst-case train must not be preempted.

backlight_refresh() stays a no-op on purpose; re-applying state on this
chip requires the 2.5ms shutdown, which would visibly blink the
backlight on every wake with unchanged brightness.

fw/light: pace fade-out by distinct backlight levels

The fade-out ramped intensity down in 20 fixed ticks over 500ms
regardless of what the hardware can show. On quantized backlights this
falls apart: the AW9364E has 16 current codes and getafix's 25%
backlight_on_percent cap leaves only 4 of them reachable, so most ticks
landed inside the same code. Fades dwelled for hundreds of ms at the
dimmest codes and stretched past 600ms; from the low preset the light
sat unchanged and then simply cut out.

Add backlight_get_level() so drivers expose which brightness values are
actually distinguishable, and build the fade as a ladder of only those
levels, walked at a fixed cadence normalized to a full-intensity fade
(125ms per step on getafix). Fades from dimmer settings walk fewer
rungs at the same rate and finish sooner: high is three dims then off
in ~375ms, medium ~250ms, low ~125ms.

Continuous drivers (pwm, aw2016, qemu) return the input unchanged, so
every candidate step stays distinct and those boards keep the smooth
~20-step, 25ms ramp.

ci: publish OTA payloads and symbols to eng-dash alongside Memfault

eng-dash is becoming the OTA server for Core watches, so a tagged release now
also uploads its artifacts there. Every existing Memfault step is untouched:
both services receive the same merged dual-slot .pbz until the fleet has
migrated to app versions that ask eng-dash for updates.

Each normal_<board>_<tag>.pbz and its unstripped .elf go to the OTA bucket
under ota/<tag>/ and elf/<tag>/, then a manifest with per-artifact sha256,
size and build id is POSTed to the eng-dash ingest endpoint. The app verifies
that sha256 against the bytes it downloads before flashing, so the hash is
load-bearing rather than informational.

Uploads are write-once by content: an object already holding the identical
bytes is skipped, so a job that died partway or after a failed manifest POST
can simply be re-run, while differing bytes under an existing key abort the
step. A moved or re-pushed tag would otherwise silently republish different
firmware under a version users may already have been offered.

Firmware goes to its own bucket under credentials scoped to it, so the OTA
secret cannot reach log-hash dictionaries and the log-hash secret cannot
reach firmware. Needs OTA_BUCKET_KEY_ID / OTA_BUCKET_SECRET secrets,
OTA_BUCKET_NAME / OTA_BUCKET_ENDPOINT vars, and ENGDASH_OTA_TOKEN for the
manifest POST.

fw/graphics: consult the font's other own resource when routed lookup misses

prv_font_res_for_codepoint() picks base vs extension purely from the
codepoint's Unicode class, before any glyph-presence check, and a miss
never revisited the other resource of the same font. With a language
pack loaded this breaks both ways: latin-classified codepoints
(0x2000-0x2BFF: U+2103, U+2116, U+20BD) present only in the pack's
extension render as the wildcard box, and base-only non-latin
codepoints (U+03C0, U+02C6-02DD) degrade to the 14px system fallback.

Make classification a lookup-order hint instead of a hard partition:
prv_get_glyph_in_font() tries the routed resource first and, on a miss,
retries the font's other own resource. The rescue is skipped when the
emoji font took over (owner != font_info), so emoji substitution and
baseline adjustment are unaffected. The rescue stays within the same
FontInfo, so the baseline adjust is 0 by construction. When a glyph
exists in both resources the routed one still wins. Without a loaded
extension the change is a strict no-op.

Cost: one extra offset-table load, only on lookups that missed their
routed resource, i.e. paths that already headed for the fallback font.
Side effect: an emoji-classified codepoint with no system emoji font
available can now also be rescued from the extension, which is the
desired outcome for packs carrying 0x2B00-0x2BFF glyphs.

Fixes #1709

applib/recognizer: implement single-tap recognizer

Replace the tap recognizer stub with a single-tap state machine. From a
Possible state a Touchdown records the contact point and time; a
PositionUpdate that drifts more than the movement budget in either axis
fails the gesture (a drag, not a tap); a Liftoff within the max duration
completes and reports the tap coordinate, otherwise it fails as a hold.

The reported tap coordinate is the last PositionUpdate point (falling back
to the Touchdown point when there was none), so a Liftoff at (0,0) does not
corrupt it. Duration is measured from rtc_get_ticks(), the same clock the
touch driver uses. The mid-gesture reset and wake gating stay the manager's
responsibility; prv_reset only clears the per-gesture state.

The duration (300ms) and movement (10px) budgets come from the reference
PT2 touch-nav gesture spec. Add an internal tap_recognizer_get_tap_point()
getter so the coordinate is observable, and unit tests covering completion,
the drag and hold failure paths, the movement boundary, the liftoff-at-(0,0)
case, and reset re-arming.

applib/recognizer: pan and swipe recognizers

Add continuous pan and discrete swipe recognizers on top of the recognizer
engine and manager, modeled on the tap recognizer.

Pan locks to a single axis: from Possible it Starts only when the finger
moves unambiguously along the locked axis (the dominant axis exceeds the
other by a dominance factor) AND crosses the start threshold; it Fails if
the finger instead moves unambiguously along the foreign axis, and stays
Possible while the direction is ambiguous. It exposes the total delta from
touchdown and, separately, the delta since Start (exactly zero at the
instant Started fires, so live scroll does not jump), plus the delta since
the previous event and a velocity.

Swipe carries a direction mask and stays passive until liftoff, failing
early if the path grows too crooked (minor-axis projection past half the
major once it has moved beyond the straightness minimum) or too slow. On
liftoff it completes only if the path is long enough, fast enough, has a
clear dominant axis, and its direction is in the mask.

Both measure time from rtc_get_ticks(), take component-wise deltas from
touchdown, compute velocity over the most-recent samples within a short
window (zero when the elapsed time is zero, so there is no divide-by-zero),
and ignore the liftoff coordinates (the driver's finger-up recovery reports
(0, 0), which would otherwise fabricate an up-left gesture).

Tests cover the pan start ordering and anti-jump, swipe direction/failure
paths, the zero-dt and liftoff-at-origin edge cases, and gesture
competition through the real recognizer manager (a vertical drag starts the
pan while swipe and tap fail; a fast horizontal completes the swipe). The
duration and movement budgets come from the reference PT2 touch-nav gesture
spec.

services/touch: add the touch-navigation bridge and master pref

Wire the recognizer stack into a per-task navigation bridge behind a master
preference (default off).

A per-task dispatcher routes each touch sequence: the route is resolved once
on Touchdown and latched. Walking up from the active layer, a registered
Tier-1 widget wins; otherwise the status-bar dead zone routes to the window's
sole widget or drops, and failing that the Tier-2 button bridge takes it
unless the window opted out with touch_bridge_disabled. Tier exclusion fails
the unused recognizers at routing time so a pan cannot start on the wrong
route; a gated (non-navigational) Touchdown skips routing entirely and only
ticks a counter.

The Tier-2 bridge maps swipes and taps to buttons (up/down to UP/DOWN, left to
BACK, right and tap to SELECT; pan is not bridged), guarding against the
compositor animation first so a dropped gesture is recorded, popping the
window for BACK without a handler and otherwise synthesising a click pair. No
global events are published.

The master pref is mirrored across the normal, prf and sdk shells and drives
touch_set_nav_enabled. Turning it on and off runs a strict transaction:
enable persists then subscribes the kernel slot and takes the sensor hold;
disable persists, synthesises a liftoff for a finger still down, cancels and
resets the kernel and app managers and unsubscribes, then releases the hold.
The gesture state is a per-task singleton (a kernel twin in modal_manager);
tearing a widget down cancels its gesture with no client callbacks, so a
rebuild under a live window cannot use freed state.

Counters and a ring buffer per task feed a "touch nav log" prompt command.

The recognizer set lives by value in the task state, which needs additive
static-init wrappers in tap/pan/swipe (new entry points only, no behaviour
change).

MenuLayer carries an 8-byte intrusive registry node (padding shrunk 40->32 so
the struct size is unchanged on every board, guarded by a static assert). It
registers in menu_layer_init and deregisters in menu_layer_deinit; the legacy
2.x path is not registered and falls back to the button bridge. Deinit clears
the gesture target before cancelling, so a widget torn down mid-gesture under a
live window cannot leave the gesture state pointing at freed memory; double
deinit and re-init without deinit are safe.

A pan drives the content offset live (base captured at Started, throttled),
clamped so short content and centre-focused menus cannot scroll into garbage;
the selection index is frozen during the pan (cell height depends on it) and
only changes on liftoff. Liftoff, tap and cancel all run the full
selection_will_change contract and honour every outcome: a veto keeps the old
selection and does nothing, a redirected index selects without activating, and
the requested index selects (tap activates only when the final selection is the
tapped row). This veto is the deliberate fix for the upstream tap that could
select a row the buttons cannot reach. A right swipe activates; a left swipe
emulates BACK.

The tap point arrives in screen coordinates, so it is mapped through the scroll
layer's global frame before hitting the content; without that a menu inset
below the status bar mis-hits every row by the inset height.

Hit-testing rewritten from the reference implementation, extended to run the
selection_will_change veto the reference omitted.

remove-from-window), so a bar destroyed while still on a window cannot leave a
stale rect that mis-routes later taps into up/down. The music app also drops

can be finger-scrolled and swiped without emulating buttons through the bridge.

right under it so the next-notification peek tracks the finger. A drag past the
clamped edge by the overpull threshold swaps to the adjacent notification
through the existing physical scroll path, so the swap logic is not duplicated;
a settle animation finishes the offset on liftoff. Two thresholds keep a normal
scroll-to-edge from swapping: a drag threshold before movement counts, and a
separate overpull past the edge to swap.

notification no longer closes under the finger mid-read.

Tier-1 registry; the notification window disables the system bridge so the swap
layer is the sole touch handler. A tap or right swipe selects, a left swipe
goes back. When a higher modal covers the notification the swap layer
deregisters from the registry (which, in the system-slot bridge architecture,
is what releases touch) and re-registers via its click config provider when the
notification regains focus. Deinit clears the gesture target and drains the set
so a teardown mid-gesture cannot dangle.

services/timeline: tighten round-Large body leading to fill pages

The one-line gap between round notification pages is exact-fit
arithmetic: on getafix (platform gabbro) the page is 260 - 20 (status
bar) - 16 (arrow) = 224px and the Large-theme body is Gothic 24 Bold
with a -2 line delta, so lines advance by 22px and the last line needs
24 + ceil(24/5) = 29px of room. The 10th line lands 3px short
(9*22 + 29 = 227 > 224), so every full page holds 9 lines and wastes
224 - 9*22 = 26px -- more than one line pitch, visible as a blank line
at every page seam when touch scrolling (and as bottom whitespace at
rest).

One extra pixel of negative leading fixes the fit: pitch 21 puts the
10th line at 9*21 + 29 = 238 <= 244 (screen), so pages hold 10 lines
and the seam shrinks to a 14px modulo -- in line with Medium (20px of
a 17px pitch) and ExtraLarge (16px of a 26px pitch), which already
read as acceptable. Rect keeps -2. The gap cannot be zero in general
(pages hold an integral number of lines) and -4 would regress it to
24px, so -3 is the densest fit that keeps descenders clear of the
arrow zone.

fw/drivers/vibe/aw86225: verify playback stop

The RAM waveform is configured with an infinite hardware loop
(WAVCFG9 SEQ1 loop count = 0xF), so once vibe_ctl(true) issues GO the
motor runs until a STOP sequence lands. The stop path ignored every
I2C return value and fired the forced-standby fallback blind: a stop
whose register writes all ACK but which never takes the chip to
standby leaves the motor buzzing indefinitely with nothing in the
logs (transfer-level failures would be logged by the shared i2c
layer itself), until the next unconditional vibe_ctl(false) -
typically the user dismissing the notification (vibes_cancel). This
matches the long-standing "notification vibrates endlessly until
dismissed" reports.

Make prv_aw862xx_play_go() report success, verify the chip actually
reached standby (including after the forced-standby fallback), and
log an error if the motor could not be confirmed stopped. A stop
retry is deliberately left out until this error is observed in the
field.

fw/services/process_management: allow unaligned relocation targets

The v4.24.0 loader hardening required every relocation target to be
word aligned. Legacy SDK apps can have pointer slots at halfword
offsets inside packed structs, e.g. 91 Dub v4.0 has seven such
relocations per platform binary and was rejected on launch with
"Invalid app relocation target[16]: 0x39da". A scan of the 400 most
popular Rebble store apps found five affected (91 Dub v4.0, Timely,
Rosewright A, Rosewright Chronograph, Directions); all of them worked
before the hardening because Cortex-M supports unaligned LDR/STR.

Drop the alignment requirement and access the slot bytewise via
memcpy, mirroring the earlier fix for unaligned relocation table
offsets. The bounds checks that actually prevent out of bounds writes
in a privileged context are retained. Verified in QEMU (qemu_emery):
91 Dub v4.0 (basalt) and Rosewright A (emery) now load and render,
and a current-SDK app still loads.

drivers/imu: recover stuck INT1 in shake-only mode

Both the LSM6DSO and LIS2DW12 mix latched (wake-up) and level (FIFO)
sources on a rising-edge INT1 EXTI, so a pad that latches high produces
no further edges. The existing stall watchdog recovers this, but it was
only armed while FIFO sampling was active. In shake-detection-only mode
(watch idle, no data subscribers) a latched-high pad had no recovery
path: shake events die and the pending interrupt holds the CPU out of
deep sleep until the battery drains.

Field data from an obelix device (C111131100UV) showed 12 such episodes
across v4.9.183-v4.23.0 (both drivers): drain jumps from 0.15%/hr to
3.2%/hr (~21x) with accel_shake_count pinned at zero, only clearing when
the 4% low-power runlevel coincidentally power-cycled the accelerometer.

Arm the INT1 watchdog in shake-only mode at a fixed 5s poll. When the
pad reads high, re-run the INT1 servicing pass (reading the INT source
clears the latch and releases the pad, dispatching any real shake, and
recovers directly when nothing was serviced). Count only a pad that is
still high after servicing, and escalate to a full stream recovery after
3 consecutive stuck passes. The counter resets on any genuine INT1 edge,
a low pad, or a watchdog rearm.

Also re-arm the watchdog from accel_set_sampling_interval so the FIFO
cadence cannot go stale if the ODR changes while sampling is active,
but only on an actual interval change (a re-arm resets the stall
tracking, so repeat calls must not defer it), and clamp the timer
period to at least one second.

fw/kernel: commit to PRF before the factory reset wipe

factory_reset() only set BOOT_BIT_FORCE_PRF and invalidated the
firmware slots after pfs_format(), which holds the PFS mutex across a
multi-minute flash erase. Any reset inside that window (task watchdog
on a task blocked on the PFS mutex, crash, power loss) rebooted the
watch straight back into normal firmware: pairing was already wiped
and the half-erased filesystem was silently reformatted on boot, so
the watch came up unpaired as if the factory reset never happened.

Set the boot bit and invalidate the slots right after the non-PFS
teardown, before starting the format, so an interrupted factory reset
lands in PRF, which is the expected outcome. A partially erased
filesystem is reformatted on first use anyway.

fw/services/process_management: allow unaligned relocation targets

The v4.24.0 loader hardening required every relocation target to be
word aligned. Legacy SDK apps can have pointer slots at halfword
offsets inside packed structs, e.g. 91 Dub v4.0 has seven such
relocations per platform binary and was rejected on launch with
"Invalid app relocation target[16]: 0x39da". A scan of the 400 most
popular Rebble store apps found five affected (91 Dub v4.0, Timely,
Rosewright A, Rosewright Chronograph, Directions); all of them worked
before the hardening because Cortex-M supports unaligned LDR/STR.

memcpy, mirroring the earlier fix for unaligned relocation table
offsets. The bounds checks that actually prevent out of bounds writes
in a privileged context are retained. Verified in QEMU (qemu_emery):

and a current-SDK app still loads.

drivers/imu: recover stuck INT1 in shake-only mode

Both the LSM6DSO and LIS2DW12 mix latched (wake-up) and level (FIFO)
sources on a rising-edge INT1 EXTI, so a pad that latches high produces
no further edges. The existing stall watchdog recovers this, but it was
only armed while FIFO sampling was active. In shake-detection-only mode
(watch idle, no data subscribers) a latched-high pad had no recovery
path: shake events die and the pending interrupt holds the CPU out of
deep sleep until the battery drains.

Field data from an obelix device (C111131100UV) showed 12 such episodes
across v4.9.183-v4.23.0 (both drivers): drain jumps from 0.15%/hr to
3.2%/hr (~21x) with accel_shake_count pinned at zero, only clearing when
the 4% low-power runlevel coincidentally power-cycled the accelerometer.

Arm the INT1 watchdog in shake-only mode at a fixed 5s poll. When the
pad reads high, re-run the INT1 servicing pass (reading the INT source
clears the latch and releases the pad, dispatching any real shake, and
recovers directly when nothing was serviced). Count only a pad that is
still high after servicing, and escalate to a full stream recovery after
3 consecutive stuck passes. The counter resets on any genuine INT1 edge,
a low pad, or a watchdog rearm.

Also re-arm the watchdog from accel_set_sampling_interval so the FIFO
cadence cannot go stale if the ODR changes while sampling is active,
but only on an actual interval change (a re-arm resets the stall
tracking, so repeat calls must not defer it), and clamp the timer
period to at least one second.

drivers/backlight: avoid AW9364E shutdown when dimming

The AW9364E 1-wire protocol is asymmetric: extra pulses step the
current further down without a restart, but raising it requires a full
shutdown (EN low >2.5ms) followed by a fresh pulse train. The driver
previously did the shutdown unconditionally, blanking the LED for 2.6ms
on every brightness change, which made fade-out steps read as blinks.

Track the pulse count latched by the chip and only emit the delta when
dimming; reserve the shutdown/re-train sequence for turning on or
brightening. Turning off now just drives EN low instead of busy-waiting
out the shutdown time, since the turn-on path always waits it out
itself. Redundant same-level requests return early.

Run pulse trains inside a critical section: an interrupt stretching a
1us low period past 500us puts the chip in undefined territory, so the
~55us worst-case train must not be preempted.

backlight_refresh() stays a no-op on purpose; re-applying state on this
chip requires the 2.5ms shutdown, which would visibly blink the
backlight on every wake with unchanged brightness.

fw/light: pace fade-out by distinct backlight levels

The fade-out ramped intensity down in 20 fixed ticks over 500ms
regardless of what the hardware can show. On quantized backlights this
falls apart: the AW9364E has 16 current codes and getafix's 25%
backlight_on_percent cap leaves only 4 of them reachable, so most ticks
landed inside the same code. Fades dwelled for hundreds of ms at the
dimmest codes and stretched past 600ms; from the low preset the light
sat unchanged and then simply cut out.

Add backlight_get_level() so drivers expose which brightness values are
actually distinguishable, and build the fade as a ladder of only those
levels, walked at a fixed cadence normalized to a full-intensity fade
(125ms per step on getafix). Fades from dimmer settings walk fewer
rungs at the same rate and finish sooner: high is three dims then off
in ~375ms, medium ~250ms, low ~125ms.

Continuous drivers (pwm, aw2016, qemu) return the input unchanged, so
every candidate step stays distinct and those boards keep the smooth
~20-step, 25ms ramp.

ci: publish OTA payloads and symbols to eng-dash alongside Memfault

eng-dash is becoming the OTA server for Core watches, so a tagged release now
also uploads its artifacts there. Every existing Memfault step is untouched:
both services receive the same merged dual-slot .pbz until the fleet has
migrated to app versions that ask eng-dash for updates.

Each normal_<board>_<tag>.pbz and its unstripped .elf go to the OTA bucket
under ota/<tag>/ and elf/<tag>/, then a manifest with per-artifact sha256,
size and build id is POSTed to the eng-dash ingest endpoint. The app verifies
that sha256 against the bytes it downloads before flashing, so the hash is
load-bearing rather than informational.

Uploads are write-once by content: an object already holding the identical
bytes is skipped, so a job that died partway or after a failed manifest POST
can simply be re-run, while differing bytes under an existing key abort the
step. A moved or re-pushed tag would otherwise silently republish different
firmware under a version users may already have been offered.

Firmware goes to its own bucket under credentials scoped to it, so the OTA
secret cannot reach log-hash dictionaries and the log-hash secret cannot
reach firmware. Needs OTA_BUCKET_KEY_ID / OTA_BUCKET_SECRET secrets,
OTA_BUCKET_NAME / OTA_BUCKET_ENDPOINT vars, and ENGDASH_OTA_TOKEN for the
manifest POST.

fw/graphics: consult the font's other own resource when routed lookup misses

prv_font_res_for_codepoint() picks base vs extension purely from the
codepoint's Unicode class, before any glyph-presence check, and a miss
never revisited the other resource of the same font. With a language
pack loaded this breaks both ways: latin-classified codepoints
(0x2000-0x2BFF: U+2103, U+2116, U+20BD) present only in the pack's
extension render as the wildcard box, and base-only non-latin
codepoints (U+03C0, U+02C6-02DD) degrade to the 14px system fallback.

Make classification a lookup-order hint instead of a hard partition:
prv_get_glyph_in_font() tries the routed resource first and, on a miss,
retries the font's other own resource. The rescue is skipped when the
emoji font took over (owner != font_info), so emoji substitution and
baseline adjustment are unaffected. The rescue stays within the same
FontInfo, so the baseline adjust is 0 by construction. When a glyph
exists in both resources the routed one still wins. Without a loaded
extension the change is a strict no-op.

Cost: one extra offset-table load, only on lookups that missed their
routed resource, i.e. paths that already headed for the fallback font.
Side effect: an emoji-classified codepoint with no system emoji font
available can now also be rescued from the extension, which is the
desired outcome for packs carrying 0x2B00-0x2BFF glyphs.

Fixes #1709

applib/recognizer: implement single-tap recognizer

Replace the tap recognizer stub with a single-tap state machine. From a
Possible state a Touchdown records the contact point and time; a
PositionUpdate that drifts more than the movement budget in either axis
fails the gesture (a drag, not a tap); a Liftoff within the max duration
completes and reports the tap coordinate, otherwise it fails as a hold.

The reported tap coordinate is the last PositionUpdate point (falling back
to the Touchdown point when there was none), so a Liftoff at (0,0) does not
corrupt it. Duration is measured from rtc_get_ticks(), the same clock the
touch driver uses. The mid-gesture reset and wake gating stay the manager's
responsibility; prv_reset only clears the per-gesture state.

The duration (300ms) and movement (10px) budgets come from the reference
PT2 touch-nav gesture spec. Add an internal tap_recognizer_get_tap_point()
getter so the coordinate is observable, and unit tests covering completion,
the drag and hold failure paths, the movement boundary, the liftoff-at-(0,0)
case, and reset re-arming.

Pan locks to a single axis: from Possible it Starts only when the finger
moves unambiguously along the locked axis (the dominant axis exceeds the
other by a dominance factor) AND crosses the start threshold; it Fails if
the finger instead moves unambiguously along the foreign axis, and stays
Possible while the direction is ambiguous. It exposes the total delta from
touchdown and, separately, the delta since Start (exactly zero at the
instant Started fires, so live scroll does not jump), plus the delta since
the previous event and a velocity.

Swipe carries a direction mask and stays passive until liftoff, failing
early if the path grows too crooked (minor-axis projection past half the
major once it has moved beyond the straightness minimum) or too slow. On
liftoff it completes only if the path is long enough, fast enough, has a
clear dominant axis, and its direction is in the mask.

Both measure time from rtc_get_ticks(), take component-wise deltas from
touchdown, compute velocity over the most-recent samples within a short
window (zero when the elapsed time is zero, so there is no divide-by-zero),
and ignore the liftoff coordinates (the driver's finger-up recovery reports
(0, 0), which would otherwise fabricate an up-left gesture).

Tests cover the pan start ordering and anti-jump, swipe direction/failure
paths, the zero-dt and liftoff-at-origin edge cases, and gesture
competition through the real recognizer manager (a vertical drag starts the
pan while swipe and tap fail; a fast horizontal completes the swipe). The
duration and movement budgets come from the reference PT2 touch-nav gesture
spec.

services/touch: add the touch-navigation bridge and master pref

Wire the recognizer stack into a per-task navigation bridge behind a master
preference (default off).

A per-task dispatcher routes each touch sequence: the route is resolved once
on Touchdown and latched. Walking up from the active layer, a registered
Tier-1 widget wins; otherwise the status-bar dead zone routes to the window's
sole widget or drops, and failing that the Tier-2 button bridge takes it
unless the window opted out with touch_bridge_disabled. Tier exclusion fails
the unused recognizers at routing time so a pan cannot start on the wrong
route; a gated (non-navigational) Touchdown skips routing entirely and only
ticks a counter.

The Tier-2 bridge maps swipes and taps to buttons (up/down to UP/DOWN, left to
BACK, right and tap to SELECT; pan is not bridged), guarding against the
compositor animation first so a dropped gesture is recorded, popping the
window for BACK without a handler and otherwise synthesising a click pair. No
global events are published.

The master pref is mirrored across the normal, prf and sdk shells and drives
touch_set_nav_enabled. Turning it on and off runs a strict transaction:
enable persists then subscribes the kernel slot and takes the sensor hold;
disable persists, synthesises a liftoff for a finger still down, cancels and
resets the kernel and app managers and unsubscribes, then releases the hold.
The gesture state is a per-task singleton (a kernel twin in modal_manager);
tearing a widget down cancels its gesture with no client callbacks, so a
rebuild under a live window cannot use freed state.

Counters and a ring buffer per task feed a "touch nav log" prompt command.

The recognizer set lives by value in the task state, which needs additive
static-init wrappers in tap/pan/swipe (new entry points only, no behaviour
change).

offset, and one-step tap activation, on top of the recognizer stack.

the struct size is unchanged on every board, guarded by a static assert). It
registers in menu_layer_init and deregisters in menu_layer_deinit; the legacy

the gesture target before cancelling, so a widget torn down mid-gesture under a
live window cannot leave the gesture state pointing at freed memory; double
deinit and re-init without deinit are safe.

A pan drives the content offset live (base captured at Started, throttled),
clamped so short content and centre-focused menus cannot scroll into garbage;
the selection index is frozen during the pan (cell height depends on it) and
only changes on liftoff. Liftoff, tap and cancel all run the full
selection_will_change contract and honour every outcome: a veto keeps the old
selection and does nothing, a redirected index selects without activating, and
the requested index selects (tap activates only when the final selection is the
tapped row). This veto is the deliberate fix for the upstream tap that could
select a row the buttons cannot reach. A right swipe activates; a left swipe
emulates BACK.

layer's global frame before hitting the content; without that a menu inset
below the status bar mis-hits every row by the inset height.

Hit-testing rewritten from the reference implementation, extended to run the
selection_will_change veto the reference omitted.

can be finger-scrolled and swiped without emulating buttons through the bridge.

(no animation), clamped to the scrollable range, and pulls the next layout
right under it so the next-notification peek tracks the finger. A drag past the
clamped edge by the overpull threshold swaps to the adjacent notification
through the existing physical scroll path, so the swap logic is not duplicated;
a settle animation finishes the offset on liftoff. Two thresholds keep a normal
scroll-to-edge from swapping: a drag threshold before movement counts, and a
separate overpull past the edge to swap.

notification no longer closes under the finger mid-read.

Tier-1 registry; the notification window disables the system bridge so the swap
layer is the sole touch handler. A tap or right swipe selects, a left swipe
goes back. When a higher modal covers the notification the swap layer
deregisters from the registry (which, in the system-slot bridge architecture,
is what releases touch) and re-registers via its click config provider when the
notification regains focus. Deinit clears the gesture target and drains the set
so a teardown mid-gesture cannot dangle.

services/timeline: tighten round-Large body leading to fill pages

The one-line gap between round notification pages is exact-fit
arithmetic: on getafix (platform gabbro) the page is 260 - 20 (status
bar) - 16 (arrow) = 224px and the Large-theme body is Gothic 24 Bold
with a -2 line delta, so lines advance by 22px and the last line needs
24 + ceil(24/5) = 29px of room. The 10th line lands 3px short
(9*22 + 29 = 227 > 224), so every full page holds 9 lines and wastes
224 - 9*22 = 26px -- more than one line pitch, visible as a blank line
at every page seam when touch scrolling (and as bottom whitespace at
rest).

One extra pixel of negative leading fixes the fit: pitch 21 puts the
10th line at 9*21 + 29 = 238 <= 244 (screen), so pages hold 10 lines
and the seam shrinks to a 14px modulo -- in line with Medium (20px of
a 17px pitch) and ExtraLarge (16px of a 26px pitch), which already
read as acceptable. Rect keeps -2. The gap cannot be zero in general
(pages hold an integral number of lines) and -4 would regress it to
24px, so -3 is the densest fit that keeps descenders clear of the
arrow zone.

mbedtls: enable NIST optimized reduction for P-256

Without MBEDTLS_ECP_NIST_OPTIM, every P-256 field reduction goes through
mbedtls_mpi_mod_mpi -> mbedtls_mpi_div_mpi, a heap-allocating multi-limb
division. A single point multiply performs tens of thousands of such
reductions, so the LE Secure Connections ECDH operations (lazy keygen on
first pairing, and the DHKey computation on every SC pairing) run
CPU-bound for over six seconds on the NimbleHost task.

NimbleHost runs at priority 3, above KernelBackground (priority 1).
KernelBackground's watchdog bit is only fed on its behalf while it is
idle with an empty queue, so whenever pairing coincides with queued
system-task work the 6 s task watchdog window expires and the watch
reboots: "Watchdog: Bits 0x81, Mask 0x83" with the stuck task parked in
xQueueGenericReceive. The FIRM-3726 coredump caught the keygen mid-flight
inside mbedtls_mpi_div_mpi with every other task idle.

The NIST fast reduction replaces the division with a few fixed-width
additions (and removes the per-reduction heap churn), bringing P-256
operations down to well under the watchdog window on all NimBLE boards
(asterix, obelix, getafix).

sdk: honour the platform's MAX_APP_BINARY_SIZE when injecting metadata

tools/pebble_sdk_platform.py gives emery and gabbro a MAX_APP_BINARY_SIZE of
0x20000, but inject_metadata.py carried its own module-scope
MAX_APP_BINARY_SIZE = 0x10000 and nothing ever passed the platform's value in.
Every platform was therefore held to 64 KB, and an emery or gabbro app that
went past it failed with "App image size is N ... Must be smaller than 65536
bytes" while the memory report printed alongside it correctly said 128 KB.

Thread the platform's limit through generate_bin_file ->
gen_inject_metadata_rule -> inject_metadata, defaulting to the old constant so
callers that pass nothing are unaffected. The value is read in
generate_bin_file rather than inside the rule because bld.env only holds the
platform's ConfigSet while the caller's per-platform loop is running, and the
rule does not run until later.

Raising the total exposes a second ceiling that was previously unreachable:
PebbleProcessInfo.load_size and .virtual_size are uint16_t, so neither can
exceed 65535 however large the platform's total allows. Only the relocation
table, stored past load_size, can use the space above 64 KB. Without a check
an app in that range died in pack() with a bare struct.error, so both fields
are now range-checked with a message naming the limit that was hit.

Testing:

- A 15700-entry pointer array builds on emery and gabbro to a 126932 byte
  image (load_size 64132, 15700 relocation entries, 96.8% of the 128 KB
  ceiling), installs, and reports all 15700 pointers correctly relocated at
  runtime. The same app fails on stock at 65536.
- Older platforms are unchanged: building the same project against the stock
  and patched SDK produces byte-identical app and worker binaries for aplite,
  basalt, chalk, diorite, emery, flint and gabbro, once the per-build
  resource_timestamp is masked.
- basalt, chalk, diorite and flint still reject an oversized image at exactly
  65536, and aplite still fails earlier at link time on its 24 KB APP region.

comm/ble: reset s_is_connected in gap_le_advert_init()

gap_le_advert.c keeps its connected-as-slave state in a static that no
init path clears. It is normally cleared by the disconnect handler, but
when the BT stack is torn down while a connection is up (e.g. entering
airplane mode), the module is deinitialized before any disconnect event
can be delivered -- and the handler returns early on
!s_gap_le_advert_is_initialized regardless. The stale "connected" state
then survives into the next stack start.

The consequence after leaving airplane mode: prv_cycle_timer_callback()
early-returns while "connected", so scheduled jobs neither age nor
round-robin until a real connect/disconnect cycle finally resets the
flag. Most visibly, reconnection advertising never leaves its initial
30-second 20 ms term (gap_le_slave_reconnect.c) and keeps advertising
at the fast interval indefinitely -- a battery drain that lasts for as
long as the phone stays away, i.e. exactly the case where reconnection
advertising runs the longest.

Fix: initialize s_is_connected to false in gap_le_advert_init(); a
fresh stack has no slave connection by definition.

The test suite's initialize() carried a workaround for this exact
leak-across-init (a gap_le_advert_handle_disconnect_as_slave() call to
get "a clean slate each test"); drop it, and add a regression test that
restarts the stack while connected and asserts a job scheduled on the
fresh stack still ages and completes on schedule.

applib/ui/layer: invalidate gesture latch on subtree removal

The touch recognizer manager latches the touched layer for the whole
gesture and walks its parent chain on every touch event and on every
layer_deinit. The deinit-time invalidation hook only runs while
layer->window is still set, but layer_remove_from_parent clears the
window recursively, so any remove-then-free teardown leaves the latch
dangling with no hook ever firing.

The notification window hits exactly this: swap_layer_reload_data
(re-layout when a new notification arrives) removes the old
LayoutLayers from the tree and then destroys them, while a pan gesture
latched on the old layout's layer is in flight. The notification layout
destructor also frees its base layer without layer_deinit. The next
layer_deinit of any still-attached layer then walks the freed chain and
hard-faults.

Confirmed against the FIRM-3724 coredump: HardFault on KernelMain in
layer_deinit's active-layer walk (ldr r3,[r3,#24] with r3=0x190019,
r0=&s_modal_recognizer_manager just returned by
window_get_recognizer_manager, LR=layer_deinit+14), with
manager->active_layer pointing into freed, reused heap, during a
wake-touch pan on the notification card as a second notification
triggered the re-layout.

Invalidate the latch in layer_remove_from_parent while the window is
still reachable, covering every remove-then-free pattern, and deinit
the notification layout's base layer like every other layout does.

fw/services/blob_db: don't use sync sessions after they are freed

Two paths let a BlobDBSyncSession be dereferenced after kernel_free():

prv_send_writeback fell through into the send after calling
blob_db_sync_next()/blob_db_sync_cancel() on a failed blob_db_read.
Both of those can free the session (sync_next frees it once the dirty
list drains), so the code went on to write session->state and
session->current_token into freed memory and sent a writeback built
from the freed dirty item. Return instead, and free the item buffer on
the way out.

The timeout and abandon regular timers fire on the timer task and hop
to KernelBG carrying a raw session pointer. The session can complete or
be cancelled in that window, leaving the deferred half to touch freed
memory — and, for the abandon callback, to free it a second time. Give
each session a monotonically increasing id, hand that to the timers,
and resolve it against the live session list before use. An id is never
reused, so a stale one cannot alias a new session that happens to land
on the same allocation.

Both mechanisms are consistent with the crash on the watch in
FIRM-3569, whose coredump asserted in blob_db_sync_cancel freeing a
bogus heap pointer, followed by "Found 0 apps" and an endless sync
retry loop.

The regular timer teardown race (regular_timer_remove_callback can
report failure while the callback is executing, yet the session holding
the RegularTimerInfo is freed regardless) is left alone here; it needs
deferred teardown rather than a lookup guard.

fw/services: say which setting silenced the speaker

Playback at effective volume 0 is indistinguishable from broken audio
hardware from the outside: the driver mutes the DAC, the PA still
switches around the silence, and analytics record on-time with an
average volume of 0. Three separate reports (FIRM-3417, FIRM-3731,
FIRM-3792) were triaged toward a speaker or PA fault, one of them close
to an RMA, when the cause was a persisted setting - a zero volume cap,
Sounds & Haptics mute, or Quiet Time's separate mute-speaker toggle
while DND is active.

Log which of those applies when a play starts silent, so the state is
visible in a bug report instead of requiring a factory reset to clear
blind. The flash log level defaults to INFO, so the line has to be INFO
to be captured at all. Playback starts run on every notification and
alarm, so it fires only when the set of reasons changes; an
unconditional INFO would flood the log on a muted watch and push out the
surrounding context that makes a report useful.

Tracking the reasons rather than a bare "was silent" flag also keeps a
change of cause visible, such as unmuting while the volume cap is still
zero, and clears the memo on the first audible play so a later re-mute
reports again.

While here, clamp the restored speaker volume. RESTORE_PREF writes
straight into the global and bypasses the setter that clamps it, the
same gap fixed for the ambient light threshold in FIRM-2841. An
out-of-range value can currently only make audio louder, so this is
correctness rather than a fix for the reports above.

fw/services/touch: add interaction session module

Raw touch navigation is about to be gated on deliberate interaction
rather than backlight state: the ALS keeps the backlight off in bright
ambient, so light_is_on() cannot represent "the user is interacting".
The session is a plain deadline armed by the backlight wake gesture or
a button press and extended by use. It lasts the user's backlight
timeout, sampled per arm, so arming behaves exactly as if the light
had come on even when ALS or DnD kept it dark. The idle watchface is
the only guarded surface: any other foreground UI, a focused modal, or
a lit backlight counts as active. Recovery firmware is always active
so the mfg touch test keeps its touch-follows-light behavior.

ci: rebase PR branches onto target branch before running

Check out the PR head SHA and rebase it onto the current tip of the
target branch before any CI job runs, following the approach used by
Zephyr. If the rebase does not apply cleanly, the job fails immediately
with an error asking the author to rebase locally.

This replaces building GitHub's ephemeral merge commit, which only
reflects the target branch at event time, so stale branches were tested
against an outdated base.

The rebase logic lives in a reusable composite action
(.github/actions/rebase) with a checkout-style 'submodules' input
(default false) to re-sync submodules after the rebase so gitlinks
match the rebased tree. Compliance diff ranges now use
origin/$GITHUB_BASE_REF instead of the event base SHA, which would
include unrelated upstream commits after the rebase.

ci: resolve rebase action from the merge ref

Workflows checked out the PR head SHA before resolving the local
rebase action, so PR branches created before the action existed were
missing it from the workspace and every job failed at action
resolution.

Check out the default merge ref instead, which always contains the
current merged copy of the action, and let the action itself switch to
the PR head before rebasing. The head SHA is always fetchable since it
is a parent of the merge commit and the checkout is full depth. If the
PR conflicts with its base, the merge ref does not exist and checkout
fails, which surfaces the same rebase-locally error one step earlier.
