comm/ble: back off reconnect advertising during connection churn

When the link repeatedly drops right after connecting (e.g. supervision
timeouts in bad RF conditions), every disconnection restarted reconnect
advertising with a 30s short-interval (20ms) burst. A getafix unit
hitting a reconnect storm went through ~130 connect/disconnect cycles
in 70 minutes, each paying the full burst.

Track how often plain reconnect advertising is (re)started: after 3
starts within a 60s window, schedule only the long-interval (~1s) term.
One attempt per window still gets the short-interval burst, so
reconnection latency recovers as soon as the churn stops. BLE HRM
reconnection advertising is user-initiated and time-bounded, so it is
not backed off.

The v4.24.0 loader hardening required every relocation target to be
word aligned. Legacy SDK apps can have pointer slots at halfword
offsets inside packed structs, e.g. 91 Dub v4.0 has seven such
relocations per platform binary and was rejected on launch with

popular Rebble store apps found five affected (91 Dub v4.0, Timely,

offsets. The bounds checks that actually prevent out of bounds writes
in a privileged context are retained. Verified in QEMU (qemu_emery):

fw/drivers/vibe/aw86225: verify playback stop

The RAM waveform is configured with an infinite hardware loop
(WAVCFG9 SEQ1 loop count = 0xF), so once vibe_ctl(true) issues GO the
motor runs until a STOP sequence lands. The stop path ignored every
I2C return value and fired the forced-standby fallback blind: a stop
whose register writes all ACK but which never takes the chip to
standby leaves the motor buzzing indefinitely with nothing in the
logs (transfer-level failures would be logged by the shared i2c
layer itself), until the next unconditional vibe_ctl(false) -
typically the user dismissing the notification (vibes_cancel). This
matches the long-standing "notification vibrates endlessly until
dismissed" reports.

Make prv_aw862xx_play_go() report success, verify the chip actually
reached standby (including after the forced-standby fallback), and
log an error if the motor could not be confirmed stopped. A stop
retry is deliberately left out until this error is observed in the
field.

93% of the signed 8-bit DAC range (±127). Scale it by 127/119 so the
peaks reach 0x7F/0x81, using the full available output range.

the maximum (High = unity gain), without exceeding the LRA motor's

The RAM playback gain was unity at full strength with a full-scale sine,
so the output swung rail-to-rail at VDD: ~2.6 Vrms at 4.2 V, and higher
when charging. The LRA is rated for 1.25 Vrms max, and the MFG vibration

VDD. The sample is skipped while playback is running, since the
detector requires standby.

Driving the LRA at its rated voltage leaves a 30-50 ms rise time that
makes short pulses feel weak. Play the first cycles of every playback at

then settle to the rated voltage.

for VIBE_AW86225_OVERDRIVE_CYCLES, then the same cycle scaled by

The sustain image is built at init from the single sine table.

drivers/vibe: add AW86225 CONT mode playback

Add VIBE_AW86225_CONT_PLAYBACK to drive the LRA in CONT mode instead of
looping the RAM waveform. The chip plays DRV1_LVL for DRV1_TIME half
cycles, then DRV2_LVL until stopped, tracking the resonant frequency
from back-EMF and compensating for the supply voltage in hardware, so
the software VBAT sampling is compiled out.

The datasheet gives the no-load output peak with VBAT_MODE set as
6.1 V * DRV_LVL / 128, clamped at VDD. Measured differentially across
the motor on getafix DVT2 the scale is 5.0 V: codes 31 and 63 produce
1.21 V and 2.36 V, and codes 12/18/25/37 fit the same line, so the
levels are sized from 5.0 V. CONT mode drives a square wave for
DRV_WIDTH of each half cycle, so the configured RMS voltages map to a
peak of
rms / sqrt(width / period). DRV1 is sized from the overdrive voltage
for VIBE_AW86225_OVERDRIVE_CYCLES cycles, DRV2 from the rated voltage,
both scaled by strength. Auto brake is enabled so stop is crisp.

getafix DVT2 and obelix enable it. DRV2_TIME is set to 0xFF, relied on
to mean "until stop" as in the Awinic reference driver; a vibration
longer than 255 half cycles verifies this on hardware.

drivers/vibe: play AW86225 RAM waveforms instead of CONT mode

The LRA vendor advised against CONT mode for our use and supplied RAM
waveforms for the motor. Their sustain waveform is a plain 50-sample
sine cycle at 12 kS/s, so keep one full-scale cycle in the driver and
build the RAM image at init with it scaled to the rated voltage, then
loop it with the sequencer until stop. The overdrive burst is dropped:
the LRA0825 datasheet allows at most 1.25 Vrms.

Scaling follows the Awinic reference drivers: the gain is compensated
from the VBAT sample so a full-scale sample drives the 4.2 V reference
of a full Li-ion cell, and the cycle is scaled to the rated voltage
against that reference. The chip delivers about 7 % less than that
model, so VIBE_AW86225_OUTPUT_GAIN_PERCENT carries the measured ratio
and the waveform is scaled up by its inverse. The gain is sampled
before each start. Setting GAIN_CHANGEABLE in SYSCTRL7 is required for
PLAYCFG2 writes to apply while playing, otherwise the gain is latched
at GO and strength ramps do nothing.

CONT registers are now only used by F0 detection, which sets its own
timing. Both boards set the datasheet's 1.2 Vrms and the measured 93 %
output gain; the symbols have no defaults.

Measured on obelix PVT (differential across the motor, 400 kS/s,
20 kHz low-pass, sine fit): 1.20 Vrms at strength 100, 0.73 at 60,
0.49 at 40, flat within 1.5 % from 3.3 V to 4.2 V supply. A strength
change while playing applies at the next cycle with no restart or
brake. With a neutral trim the sample clock gives exactly 240 Hz.

ci: rebase PR branches onto target branch before running

Check out the PR head SHA and rebase it onto the current tip of the
target branch before any CI job runs, following the approach used by
Zephyr. If the rebase does not apply cleanly, the job fails immediately
with an error asking the author to rebase locally.

This replaces building GitHub's ephemeral merge commit, which only
reflects the target branch at event time, so stale branches were tested
against an outdated base.

The rebase logic lives in a reusable composite action
(.github/actions/rebase) with a checkout-style 'submodules' input
(default false) to re-sync submodules after the rebase so gitlinks
match the rebased tree. Compliance diff ranges now use
origin/$GITHUB_BASE_REF instead of the event base SHA, which would
include unrelated upstream commits after the rebase.

ci: resolve rebase action from the merge ref

Workflows checked out the PR head SHA before resolving the local
rebase action, so PR branches created before the action existed were
missing it from the workspace and every job failed at action
resolution.

Check out the default merge ref instead, which always contains the
current merged copy of the action, and let the action itself switch to
the PR head before rebasing. The head SHA is always fetchable since it
is a parent of the merge commit and the checkout is full depth. If the
PR conflicts with its base, the merge ref does not exist and checkout
fails, which surfaces the same rebase-locally error one step earlier.

fw/services/process_management: allow unaligned relocation table offsets

The SDK app relocation-data validation added in 68b30e60 rejects any
app whose image size (load_size) is not word-aligned, since the
relocation table starts right at that offset and was read as a
uint32_t array.

Legacy SDK apps routinely have non-word-aligned image sizes: the store
build of Timer (c64aae42-b822-4d6d-995b-bc7c38e843f4) ships load_size
values of 17370/18110/18182 (all 2 mod 4) with 11 relocation entries,
so v4.24.0 rejects it at launch on every platform with "Invalid app
relocation table offset alignment" and bounces back to the launcher.

Drop the alignment requirement on the table start and read the entries
bytewise instead. All security-relevant validation is unchanged:
relocation targets must still be word-aligned, in-bounds, and past the
header, and relocated values must stay within the app image.

Verified on qemu_emery: the store Timer PBW is rejected at launch
before this change and launches and runs correctly after it.

fw/drivers/imu/lsm6dso: retry INT1 servicing before stream recovery

The stuck-pad heuristic recovers the stream when a servicing pass takes
no action and the INT1 pad still reads high. A wake-up or FIFO threshold
source asserting between the status register reads and the pad re-check
is indistinguishable from a stuck pad, so the heuristic recovers a
healthy stream and discards the event that raced it (recovery clears
ALL_INT_SRC without dispatching).

Field logs show this clustering during sustained motion, up to 7
recoveries in 23 minutes, each one dropping a wake-up event.

Retry the servicing pass once before recovering: a racing source is
latched (wake-up) or level (FIFO threshold), so it is visible on
re-read and gets serviced normally. Only recover when a second
consecutive pass finds nothing with the pad still high, which is then a
genuinely stuck pad.

fw/put_bytes: scope BLE slowdown to the raw storage erase

pb_storage_raw_init() requested ResponseTimeMiddle with
max_period_secs=0 (added in 6d679bc73 to reduce NimbleHost stack
pressure during blocking flash operations). This had two problems:

- 0 does not mean run forever (that is MAX_PERIOD_RUN_FOREVER), it
  creates an already-expired request: the bt_conn_mgr watchdog deleted
  it ~1s later and, with no requests left, dropped the connection to
  ResponseTimeMax (45ms interval, slave latency 3).
- It shares BtConsumerPpPutBytes with the ResponseTimeMin request held
  during chunk streaming, so it cancelled the fast interval at every
  raw object boundary.

As a result, during a firmware update each object init (firmware, then
system resources) bounced the connection Min -> Middle -> Max -> Min,
and the multi-second slot erase plus its init ACK ran at up to 180ms
effective interval, adding ~5-10s per object.

Request Middle only for the duration of the erase, with a bounded
timeout as a safety net, and restore Min right after so the init ACK
goes out at the fast interval and the streaming request is never
cancelled. The NimbleHost stack overflow remains covered by the stack
size increase from 6d679bc73.

cron: arm a one-shot timer for the next job instead of polling at 1 Hz

The cron service registered a per-second regular_timer callback that

nothing to do. Cron already knows exactly when the next job is due, so

drivers/speaker: map SF32LB volume to attenuation-only DAC gain

The DAC-path volume was converted from the 0-100 UI scale as
(vol - 36) * 2 half-dB, i.e. -36..+64 dB. Any volume above 36 applied
positive digital gain, which hard-clips full-scale content: alarm tones
(volume 60, +24 dB) played as a digital-full-scale square wave, at
maximum loudness regardless of the speaker volume preference, and
overdriving the speaker well past the level the factory test validates.
Volumes above 90 exceeded the HAL's +54 dB limit, so
HAL_AUDCODEC_Config_DACPath_Volume failed without writing the gain
registers and the error was ignored, leaving the 0 dB baseline and
making the volume curve non-monotonic (90 was louder than 100).

The mapping had been dead code until 0e2afbddb started re-applying the
volume after DAC path setup (v4.20.0), which is when alarms became
loud and distorted in the field.

Map 1..100 linearly to -36..0 dB instead (0 still mutes), and log a
warning if the HAL rejects the value.

comm/ble: request connection parameter update sooner after connect

iOS creates connections with a 720ms supervision timeout and only
relaxes it once the peripheral requests new parameters. We waited the
full TGAP(conn_pause_peripheral) = 5s before sending the request, so
any RF fade during that window killed the link. Logs from a getafix
unit showed reconnect storms where most connections died of supervision
timeout (0x208) within 1-6s of connecting, i.e. before the update could
be requested, while connections that reached the 6s supervision timeout
stayed up for hours.

Shorten the initial pause to 1s. The 5s pause is a spec recommendation
("should", not "shall"), and Apple has confirmed relaxed handling of
TGAP timings (see the pre-existing note about the 30s Tgap timeout).

Related to FIRM-3330.

Co-authored-by: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Signed-off-by: Gerard Marull-Paretas <gerard@teslabs.com>

comm/ble: back off reconnect advertising during connection churn

When the link repeatedly drops right after connecting (e.g. supervision
timeouts in bad RF conditions), every disconnection restarted reconnect
advertising with a 30s short-interval (20ms) burst. A getafix unit
hitting a reconnect storm went through ~130 connect/disconnect cycles
in 70 minutes, each paying the full burst.

Track how often plain reconnect advertising is (re)started: after 3
starts within a 60s window, schedule only the long-interval (~1s) term.
One attempt per window still gets the short-interval burst, so
reconnection latency recovers as soon as the churn stops. BLE HRM
reconnection advertising is user-initiated and time-bounded, so it is
not backed off.

Related to FIRM-3330.

services/notifications: fix leak and deleted-entry handling in rewrite

the previous item's stale payload. Skip deleted entries entirely,
matching prv_compress(), and track the bytes written so s_write_offset

drivers/speaker: throttle sf32lb52 DMA refill callbacks

The AUDCODEC DMA half/full-complete ISRs enqueued a prv_audio_trans_bg
refill callback on every interrupt with no in-flight tracking. When
KernelBG is starved (e.g. an app blocking on a slow flash resource read
while holding the pfs mutexes), the system task queue fills up and the
watch hard-reboots with Event Queue Full, cutting alarm tones off a few
seconds into playback.

one refill callback is in flight, clearing it again if the enqueue
fails. The flag is also reset in audec_start() so a stale value cannot
block refills on a new session.

services/ecompass: relax calibration gates for weak geomagnetic fields

The sphere-fit solver only accepts a four-point sample set when the
points are spread further apart than an absolute distance threshold:
point-to-point, point-to-line and point-to-plane all had to exceed
370 (37 uT), with a single fallback to 220 that was only armed after
two 300-sample windows in which the point-to-point gate had passed.

All samples lie on a sphere whose radius R is the local geomagnetic
field strength. In weak-field regions such as the South Atlantic
Anomaly (~22 uT, R ~= 228) those gates are unsatisfiable:
point-to-point > 370 needs ~108 degrees of orientation change, more
than the calibration UI coaches, and point-to-line > 370 is
geometrically impossible since its maximum is
R + sqrt(R^2 - (370/2)^2) < 370 for R < ~231. Because the fallback
was gated on the point-to-point pass that weak fields cannot produce,
the threshold never dropped and calibration never completed (bug
report logs show zero solutions over a 7 minute session).

Replace the strike-based fallback with deterministic progressive
relaxation: every 300-sample window that ends without a complete
point set lowers the threshold by 70, down to a floor of 90 (9 uT).
The floor keeps all three gates satisfiable at ~20 uT with realistic
<= 90 degree orientation coverage. Normal-field behavior is
preserved: the strict 370 threshold is still tried first and only
relaxes after demonstrated failure to fit, and the existing
requirement of three consecutive consistent fits within 50 counts
still rejects noisy solutions.

Also reset the threshold and the fit-consistency history in
ecomp_corr_reset() so each calibration session starts from the
strict gates instead of inheriting relaxed state.

Unit tests cover weak-field convergence (radius-228 sphere with a
hard-iron offset, 50-degree cap coverage, sensor noise: the old
gates provably never fire, the new code locks within ~80 simulated
seconds and recovers the offset within 2 counts), normal-field
regression (radius 470, locks within the first strict window), and
rejection of degenerate stationary and coplanar inputs.

services/alarms: fix user snooze delay on smart alarms

User snoozes and the smart alarm's internal sleep poll share the same
snooze timer, and its expiry always funneled back into the smart-alarm
sleep gate. Snoozing a firing smart alarm therefore turned "Snooze for
N minutes" into an open-ended 1-minute sleep-poll loop that only
re-fired the alarm once sleep exit was detected or the poll cap was hit.

snooze and bypass the sleep gate in that case, so the alarm re-fires
after exactly the configured snooze delay. The flag is cleared on every
snooze-timer teardown (dismiss, disable, delete, new alarm, clock-change
force trigger).

Add a regression test: a firing smart alarm that is user-snoozed while
the user still looks asleep (RestfulSleep, VMC 0) must put the alarm
event when the snooze timer fires instead of re-entering the sleep poll.

fw/services/activity: fire sleep summary notification once per sleep window

The "Good morning" sleep summary re-fired hours after the real morning
notification whenever the day's sleep bounds changed. Two paths re-armed
it: a pin update for an extended sleep exit cleared the notified flag,
and any shift of sleep_enter_utc was treated as a new day and reset the
whole pin state. A falsely detected evening sleep session (sedentary
awake time misclassified by the algorithm, tracked separately) was
enough to trigger either path, buzzing the user with last night's
summary in the evening or in the middle of the night.

Key the pin state to the sleep-day window (the 9pm local cutoff used by
activity_sessions_prv_get_sleep_bounds_utc, now exposed as
activity_sessions_prv_get_sleep_window_start_utc) instead of comparing
exact enter timestamps. Within one window the notification fires at
most once: pin updates no longer clear the notified flag, and only a
new window resets the state. Additionally, only notify when the sleep
exit lands at a plausible local wake-up time ([4am, 6pm)); skipping
outside that window does not consume the once-per-window notification,
so a mid-night false exit stays silent and the real morning wake-up
still notifies. The timeline pin keeps updating silently in all cases.

The persisted SleepPinState grows by a trailing window_utc field. Older
persisted blobs fail the settings read cleanly (E_RANGE zeroes the
output), and a zero window is re-seeded at init as already-notified so
the state layout change cannot re-fire a summary the user already saw;
the cost is at most one missed summary right after the update.

resources: fix '#' floating above the baseline in GOTHIC_36

The U+0023 glyph header in GOTHIC_36.pbf carries top_offset_px = 6,
leaving its bottom edge 14px above the baseline, while every other size
in the family raises '#' by only 2..6px:

  GOTHIC_14       h 6  top  5  bottom 11  (+3 above baseline)
  GOTHIC_18       h 8  top  7  bottom 15  (+3)
  GOTHIC_24       h 9  top 10  bottom 19  (+5)
  GOTHIC_28       h12  top 10  bottom 22  (+6)
  GOTHIC_36       h16  top  6  bottom 22  (+14)  <- broken
  GOTHIC_36_BOLD  h16  top 14  bottom 30  (+6)

The defect is visible at the largest notification text size on boards
whose display maps it to GOTHIC_36: '#' hangs well above the line the
surrounding text sits on. It came in with the original font asset
import; no generated source for the legacy Gothic bitmap fonts exists
in tree, so patch the metric in place.

Set top_offset_px to 14, matching GOTHIC_36_BOLD's '#', which has the
identical glyph height. Exactly one byte changes (offset 3637,
0x06 -> 0x0e); the bitmap data, all other glyphs, and the offset
tables are untouched. The glyph data is not shared with any other
codepoint. Verified by re-parsing the font: '#' now sits at bottom 30
(+6 above the baseline), in line with the rest of the family.

fw/graphics: align substituted glyphs on the primary font baseline

render_glyph() places a glyph at cursor.origin.y + top_offset_px, but
top_offset_px is baked relative to the baseline of the font the glyph was
taken from (== that font's base resource max_height for PBF). When a glyph
is served by another font — the system emoji font, or the 14px system
fallback font — that baseline sits higher than the primary font's, so the
glyph is drawn too high. With a 36px body font a fallback glyph landed
~22px above the baseline, which is what made emoji look tiny and shifted
up in notifications at text size "Large".

Report the FontInfo that owns the resolved resource and hand the caller a
draw-time correction of MAX(0, primary base max_height - owner base
max_height). Keying it on the owning font rather than on the concrete
resource is what keeps an extension from moving: an extension belongs to
the same font and its offsets are already baked against that font's base
baseline (resource_generator_font.py passes fontgen baseline =
the nominal name_height), while the PBF header records
max_height = pixelHeight, which may be far smaller — the shipped ar_SA
pack uses pixelHeight 12/14/17/20/20 against base fonts of 14/18/24/28/36.
Measuring the resource would therefore have shoved Arabic glyphs 2..16px
too far down, and, since FontInfo.max_height is MAX(ext, base), a taller
extension would have shifted the base font's latin glyphs instead. The
adjust is consequently exactly 0 whenever the glyph came from the font we
were asked to draw with, base or extension. The clamp at 0 keeps a taller
substitute from bleeding into the previous line. For the same reason the
emoji font is now sized against the base resource height, the very
baseline its glyphs get aligned to.

The correction is applied to the glyph rect in render_glyph() before the
target and clipping rects are derived from it, so the source row maths
stays consistent; nothing is baked into the cached glyph metadata, which
is keyed by source resource and shared across primary fonts. Layout and
line heights are untouched, and horizontal advance still comes from the
substituting font as before.

fw/services/process_management: allow unaligned relocation targets

The v4.24.0 loader hardening required every relocation target to be
word aligned. Legacy SDK apps can have pointer slots at halfword
offsets inside packed structs, e.g. 91 Dub v4.0 has seven such
relocations per platform binary and was rejected on launch with
"Invalid app relocation target[16]: 0x39da". A scan of the 400 most
popular Rebble store apps found five affected (91 Dub v4.0, Timely,
Rosewright A, Rosewright Chronograph, Directions); all of them worked
before the hardening because Cortex-M supports unaligned LDR/STR.

memcpy, mirroring the earlier fix for unaligned relocation table
offsets. The bounds checks that actually prevent out of bounds writes
in a privileged context are retained. Verified in QEMU (qemu_emery):
91 Dub v4.0 (basalt) and Rosewright A (emery) now load and render,
and a current-SDK app still loads.

drivers/imu: recover stuck INT1 in shake-only mode

Both the LSM6DSO and LIS2DW12 mix latched (wake-up) and level (FIFO)
sources on a rising-edge INT1 EXTI, so a pad that latches high produces
no further edges. The existing stall watchdog recovers this, but it was
only armed while FIFO sampling was active. In shake-detection-only mode
(watch idle, no data subscribers) a latched-high pad had no recovery
path: shake events die and the pending interrupt holds the CPU out of
deep sleep until the battery drains.

Field data from an obelix device (C111131100UV) showed 12 such episodes
across v4.9.183-v4.23.0 (both drivers): drain jumps from 0.15%/hr to
3.2%/hr (~21x) with accel_shake_count pinned at zero, only clearing when
the 4% low-power runlevel coincidentally power-cycled the accelerometer.

Arm the INT1 watchdog in shake-only mode at a fixed 5s poll. When the
pad reads high, re-run the INT1 servicing pass (reading the INT source
clears the latch and releases the pad, dispatching any real shake, and
recovers directly when nothing was serviced). Count only a pad that is
still high after servicing, and escalate to a full stream recovery after
3 consecutive stuck passes. The counter resets on any genuine INT1 edge,
a low pad, or a watchdog rearm.

Also re-arm the watchdog from accel_set_sampling_interval so the FIFO
cadence cannot go stale if the ODR changes while sampling is active,
but only on an actual interval change (a re-arm resets the stall
tracking, so repeat calls must not defer it), and clamp the timer
period to at least one second.

drivers/backlight: avoid AW9364E shutdown when dimming

The AW9364E 1-wire protocol is asymmetric: extra pulses step the
current further down without a restart, but raising it requires a full
shutdown (EN low >2.5ms) followed by a fresh pulse train. The driver
previously did the shutdown unconditionally, blanking the LED for 2.6ms
on every brightness change, which made fade-out steps read as blinks.

Track the pulse count latched by the chip and only emit the delta when
dimming; reserve the shutdown/re-train sequence for turning on or
brightening. Turning off now just drives EN low instead of busy-waiting
out the shutdown time, since the turn-on path always waits it out
itself. Redundant same-level requests return early.

Run pulse trains inside a critical section: an interrupt stretching a
1us low period past 500us puts the chip in undefined territory, so the
~55us worst-case train must not be preempted.

backlight_refresh() stays a no-op on purpose; re-applying state on this
chip requires the 2.5ms shutdown, which would visibly blink the
backlight on every wake with unchanged brightness.

fw/light: pace fade-out by distinct backlight levels

The fade-out ramped intensity down in 20 fixed ticks over 500ms
regardless of what the hardware can show. On quantized backlights this
falls apart: the AW9364E has 16 current codes and getafix's 25%
backlight_on_percent cap leaves only 4 of them reachable, so most ticks
landed inside the same code. Fades dwelled for hundreds of ms at the
dimmest codes and stretched past 600ms; from the low preset the light
sat unchanged and then simply cut out.

Add backlight_get_level() so drivers expose which brightness values are
actually distinguishable, and build the fade as a ladder of only those
levels, walked at a fixed cadence normalized to a full-intensity fade
(125ms per step on getafix). Fades from dimmer settings walk fewer
rungs at the same rate and finish sooner: high is three dims then off
in ~375ms, medium ~250ms, low ~125ms.

Continuous drivers (pwm, aw2016, qemu) return the input unchanged, so
every candidate step stays distinct and those boards keep the smooth
~20-step, 25ms ramp.

migrated to app versions that ask eng-dash for updates.

Each normal_<board>_<tag>.pbz and its unstripped .elf go to the OTA bucket
under ota/<tag>/ and elf/<tag>/, then a manifest with per-artifact sha256,
size and build id is POSTed to the eng-dash ingest endpoint. The app verifies
that sha256 against the bytes it downloads before flashing, so the hash is
load-bearing rather than informational.

Uploads are write-once by content: an object already holding the identical
bytes is skipped, so a job that died partway or after a failed manifest POST
can simply be re-run, while differing bytes under an existing key abort the
step. A moved or re-pushed tag would otherwise silently republish different
firmware under a version users may already have been offered.

Firmware goes to its own bucket under credentials scoped to it, so the OTA
secret cannot reach log-hash dictionaries and the log-hash secret cannot
reach firmware. Needs OTA_BUCKET_KEY_ID / OTA_BUCKET_SECRET secrets,
OTA_BUCKET_NAME / OTA_BUCKET_ENDPOINT vars, and ENGDASH_OTA_TOKEN for the
manifest POST.

fw/graphics: consult the font's other own resource when routed lookup misses

prv_font_res_for_codepoint() picks base vs extension purely from the
codepoint's Unicode class, before any glyph-presence check, and a miss
never revisited the other resource of the same font. With a language
pack loaded this breaks both ways: latin-classified codepoints
(0x2000-0x2BFF: U+2103, U+2116, U+20BD) present only in the pack's
extension render as the wildcard box, and base-only non-latin
codepoints (U+03C0, U+02C6-02DD) degrade to the 14px system fallback.

Make classification a lookup-order hint instead of a hard partition:
prv_get_glyph_in_font() tries the routed resource first and, on a miss,
retries the font's other own resource. The rescue is skipped when the
emoji font took over (owner != font_info), so emoji substitution and
baseline adjustment are unaffected. The rescue stays within the same
FontInfo, so the baseline adjust is 0 by construction. When a glyph
exists in both resources the routed one still wins. Without a loaded
extension the change is a strict no-op.

Cost: one extra offset-table load, only on lookups that missed their
routed resource, i.e. paths that already headed for the fallback font.
Side effect: an emoji-classified codepoint with no system emoji font
available can now also be rescued from the extension, which is the
desired outcome for packs carrying 0x2B00-0x2BFF glyphs.

applib/recognizer: implement single-tap recognizer

Replace the tap recognizer stub with a single-tap state machine. From a
Possible state a Touchdown records the contact point and time; a
PositionUpdate that drifts more than the movement budget in either axis
fails the gesture (a drag, not a tap); a Liftoff within the max duration
completes and reports the tap coordinate, otherwise it fails as a hold.

to the Touchdown point when there was none), so a Liftoff at (0,0) does not
corrupt it. Duration is measured from rtc_get_ticks(), the same clock the
touch driver uses. The mid-gesture reset and wake gating stay the manager's
responsibility; prv_reset only clears the per-gesture state.

PT2 touch-nav gesture spec. Add an internal tap_recognizer_get_tap_point()
getter so the coordinate is observable, and unit tests covering completion,
the drag and hold failure paths, the movement boundary, the liftoff-at-(0,0)
case, and reset re-arming.

applib/recognizer: pan and swipe recognizers

Add continuous pan and discrete swipe recognizers on top of the recognizer
engine and manager, modeled on the tap recognizer.

Pan locks to a single axis: from Possible it Starts only when the finger
moves unambiguously along the locked axis (the dominant axis exceeds the
other by a dominance factor) AND crosses the start threshold; it Fails if
the finger instead moves unambiguously along the foreign axis, and stays
Possible while the direction is ambiguous. It exposes the total delta from
touchdown and, separately, the delta since Start (exactly zero at the
instant Started fires, so live scroll does not jump), plus the delta since
the previous event and a velocity.

Swipe carries a direction mask and stays passive until liftoff, failing
early if the path grows too crooked (minor-axis projection past half the
major once it has moved beyond the straightness minimum) or too slow. On
liftoff it completes only if the path is long enough, fast enough, has a
clear dominant axis, and its direction is in the mask.

Both measure time from rtc_get_ticks(), take component-wise deltas from
touchdown, compute velocity over the most-recent samples within a short
window (zero when the elapsed time is zero, so there is no divide-by-zero),
and ignore the liftoff coordinates (the driver's finger-up recovery reports
(0, 0), which would otherwise fabricate an up-left gesture).

Tests cover the pan start ordering and anti-jump, swipe direction/failure
paths, the zero-dt and liftoff-at-origin edge cases, and gesture
competition through the real recognizer manager (a vertical drag starts the
pan while swipe and tap fail; a fast horizontal completes the swipe). The
duration and movement budgets come from the reference PT2 touch-nav gesture
spec.

services/touch: add the touch-navigation bridge and master pref

Wire the recognizer stack into a per-task navigation bridge behind a master
preference (default off).

A per-task dispatcher routes each touch sequence: the route is resolved once
on Touchdown and latched. Walking up from the active layer, a registered
Tier-1 widget wins; otherwise the status-bar dead zone routes to the window's
sole widget or drops, and failing that the Tier-2 button bridge takes it
unless the window opted out with touch_bridge_disabled. Tier exclusion fails
the unused recognizers at routing time so a pan cannot start on the wrong
route; a gated (non-navigational) Touchdown skips routing entirely and only
ticks a counter.

The Tier-2 bridge maps swipes and taps to buttons (up/down to UP/DOWN, left to
BACK, right and tap to SELECT; pan is not bridged), guarding against the
compositor animation first so a dropped gesture is recorded, popping the
window for BACK without a handler and otherwise synthesising a click pair. No
global events are published.

The master pref is mirrored across the normal, prf and sdk shells and drives
touch_set_nav_enabled. Turning it on and off runs a strict transaction:
enable persists then subscribes the kernel slot and takes the sensor hold;
disable persists, synthesises a liftoff for a finger still down, cancels and
resets the kernel and app managers and unsubscribes, then releases the hold.
The gesture state is a per-task singleton (a kernel twin in modal_manager);
tearing a widget down cancels its gesture with no client callbacks, so a
rebuild under a live window cannot use freed state.

Counters and a ring buffer per task feed a "touch nav log" prompt command.

The recognizer set lives by value in the task state, which needs additive
static-init wrappers in tap/pan/swipe (new entry points only, no behaviour
change).

applib/menu_layer: touch scrolling and tap activation

Make MenuLayer a Tier-1 touch widget: finger scrolling with live content
offset, and one-step tap activation, on top of the recognizer stack.

MenuLayer carries an 8-byte intrusive registry node (padding shrunk 40->32 so
the struct size is unchanged on every board, guarded by a static assert). It
registers in menu_layer_init and deregisters in menu_layer_deinit; the legacy
2.x path is not registered and falls back to the button bridge. Deinit clears
the gesture target before cancelling, so a widget torn down mid-gesture under a
live window cannot leave the gesture state pointing at freed memory; double
deinit and re-init without deinit are safe.

A pan drives the content offset live (base captured at Started, throttled),
clamped so short content and centre-focused menus cannot scroll into garbage;
the selection index is frozen during the pan (cell height depends on it) and
only changes on liftoff. Liftoff, tap and cancel all run the full
selection_will_change contract and honour every outcome: a veto keeps the old
selection and does nothing, a redirected index selects without activating, and
the requested index selects (tap activates only when the final selection is the
tapped row). This veto is the deliberate fix for the upstream tap that could
select a row the buttons cannot reach. A right swipe activates; a left swipe
emulates BACK.

The tap point arrives in screen coordinates, so it is mapped through the scroll
layer's global frame before hitting the content; without that a menu inset
below the status bar mis-hits every row by the inset height.

Hit-testing rewritten from the reference implementation, extended to run the
selection_will_change veto the reference omitted.

services/timeline: native touch for the notification swap layer

Make the notification SwapLayer a Tier-1 touch widget so a long notification
can be finger-scrolled and swiped without emulating buttons through the bridge.

swap_layer_touch_scroll_by moves the current notification 1:1 with the finger
(no animation), clamped to the scrollable range, and pulls the next layout
right under it so the next-notification peek tracks the finger. A drag past the
clamped edge by the overpull threshold swaps to the adjacent notification
through the existing physical scroll path, so the swap logic is not duplicated;
a settle animation finishes the offset on liftoff. Two thresholds keep a normal
scroll-to-edge from swapping: a drag threshold before movement counts, and a
separate overpull past the edge to swap.

notification no longer closes under the finger mid-read.

The recognizer set and gesture state are a per-task singleton registered in the
Tier-1 registry; the notification window disables the system bridge so the swap
layer is the sole touch handler. A tap or right swipe selects, a left swipe
goes back. When a higher modal covers the notification the swap layer
deregisters from the registry (which, in the system-slot bridge architecture,
is what releases touch) and re-registers via its click config provider when the
notification regains focus. Deinit clears the gesture target and drains the set
so a teardown mid-gesture cannot dangle.

applib/menu_layer: carousel touch pan for center-focused menus

A center-focused menu (the round launcher) panned like a plain list:
the focused row scrolled away from the centre with the content and
liftoff left everything wherever the finger stopped. Make it a carousel
instead: the focus stays pinned at the viewport centre, so the row
crossing the centre becomes the selection live during the pan, through
the full selection_will_change contract (veto keeps the old row
focused, a redirect focuses the redirected row). Liftoff re-tracks the
row under the centre and glides it to the exact centre; a cancelled
gesture re-centres synchronously so the handover leaves a stable state.

The mid-pan reselect walks the selection span without repositioning the
scroll -- menu_layer_set_selected_index cannot be used because
center-focused menus always snap the offset to centre the selection,
which would fight the finger on every crossing. Leaving the offset
alone is safe for focus-dependent cell heights: the newly focused row
absorbs its height reflow on its centre-facing edge, so the content
under the finger does not jump and the boundary gains natural
hysteresis.

Plain (non-center-focused) menus keep the free-scroll behaviour: pan
scrolls, tap selects, the selection never moves on a pan.

(touchEnabled): off means sensor down, events dropped at the source,
nothing touch-driven anywhere. (The duplicate Debugging > 'Touch
enable' row is removed.) A new Touch Navigation sub-pref
(touchNavMenuEnabled, default off, shown only while Touch is on)
gates the SYSTEM navigation experience: menus, notifications and the
button bridge are active only while BOTH are on, and the
enable/disable transaction (twin subscriptions, permanent sensor
hold, runtime dispatch gate) keys on that conjunction.

Third-party apps are gated differently: an app that explicitly opted
in via app_touch_navigation_enable() asked for touch itself, so its
twin follows the master Touch switch alone:

with a per-app opted_in flag set only by the opt-in syscall, while
system apps ride the conjunction through their default participation.
An app-nav-active runtime flag tracks the installed app dispatcher so
the dispatch gate and touch-driven backlight treat an opted-in app as
navigating even with system nav off (cleared via the event-service
teardown if the app dies). Pref flips RESYNC the running app's twin
instead of blindly unsubscribing, so turning only Touch Navigation
off does not cut off an opted-in app; the sensor stays powered for it
through its own touch-service subscription and the permanent hold
remains system-nav-only.

  the same per-task subscription and must not read as app subscribers.

  the backlight and the screen was off at Touchdown, so under
  gesture-based wake a screen-off tap cannot invisibly act on the UI

services/timeline: tighten round-Large body leading to fill pages

The one-line gap between round notification pages is exact-fit
arithmetic: on getafix (platform gabbro) the page is 260 - 20 (status
bar) - 16 (arrow) = 224px and the Large-theme body is Gothic 24 Bold
with a -2 line delta, so lines advance by 22px and the last line needs
24 + ceil(24/5) = 29px of room. The 10th line lands 3px short
(9*22 + 29 = 227 > 224), so every full page holds 9 lines and wastes
224 - 9*22 = 26px -- more than one line pitch, visible as a blank line
at every page seam when touch scrolling (and as bottom whitespace at
rest).

One extra pixel of negative leading fixes the fit: pitch 21 puts the
10th line at 9*21 + 29 = 238 <= 244 (screen), so pages hold 10 lines
and the seam shrinks to a 14px modulo -- in line with Medium (20px of
a 17px pitch) and ExtraLarge (16px of a 26px pitch), which already
read as acceptable. Rect keeps -2. The gap cannot be zero in general
(pages hold an integral number of lines) and -4 would regress it to
24px, so -3 is the densest fit that keeps descenders clear of the
arrow zone.

mbedtls: enable NIST optimized reduction for P-256

Without MBEDTLS_ECP_NIST_OPTIM, every P-256 field reduction goes through
mbedtls_mpi_mod_mpi -> mbedtls_mpi_div_mpi, a heap-allocating multi-limb
division. A single point multiply performs tens of thousands of such
reductions, so the LE Secure Connections ECDH operations (lazy keygen on
first pairing, and the DHKey computation on every SC pairing) run
CPU-bound for over six seconds on the NimbleHost task.

NimbleHost runs at priority 3, above KernelBackground (priority 1).
KernelBackground's watchdog bit is only fed on its behalf while it is
idle with an empty queue, so whenever pairing coincides with queued
system-task work the 6 s task watchdog window expires and the watch
reboots: "Watchdog: Bits 0x81, Mask 0x83" with the stuck task parked in
xQueueGenericReceive. The FIRM-3726 coredump caught the keygen mid-flight
inside mbedtls_mpi_div_mpi with every other task idle.

The NIST fast reduction replaces the division with a few fixed-width
additions (and removes the per-reduction heap churn), bringing P-256
operations down to well under the watchdog window on all NimBLE boards
(asterix, obelix, getafix).

comm/ble: reset s_is_connected in gap_le_advert_init()

gap_le_advert.c keeps its connected-as-slave state in a static that no
init path clears. It is normally cleared by the disconnect handler, but
when the BT stack is torn down while a connection is up (e.g. entering
airplane mode), the module is deinitialized before any disconnect event
can be delivered -- and the handler returns early on
!s_gap_le_advert_is_initialized regardless. The stale "connected" state
then survives into the next stack start.

The consequence after leaving airplane mode: prv_cycle_timer_callback()
early-returns while "connected", so scheduled jobs neither age nor
round-robin until a real connect/disconnect cycle finally resets the
flag. Most visibly, reconnection advertising never leaves its initial
30-second 20 ms term (gap_le_slave_reconnect.c) and keeps advertising
at the fast interval indefinitely -- a battery drain that lasts for as
long as the phone stays away, i.e. exactly the case where reconnection
advertising runs the longest.

Fix: initialize s_is_connected to false in gap_le_advert_init(); a
fresh stack has no slave connection by definition.

The test suite's initialize() carried a workaround for this exact
leak-across-init (a gap_le_advert_handle_disconnect_as_slave() call to
get "a clean slate each test"); drop it, and add a regression test that
restarts the stack while connected and asserts a job scheduled on the
fresh stack still ages and completes on schedule.

applib/ui/layer: invalidate gesture latch on subtree removal

The touch recognizer manager latches the touched layer for the whole
gesture and walks its parent chain on every touch event and on every
layer_deinit. The deinit-time invalidation hook only runs while
layer->window is still set, but layer_remove_from_parent clears the
window recursively, so any remove-then-free teardown leaves the latch
dangling with no hook ever firing.

The notification window hits exactly this: swap_layer_reload_data
(re-layout when a new notification arrives) removes the old
LayoutLayers from the tree and then destroys them, while a pan gesture
latched on the old layout's layer is in flight. The notification layout
destructor also frees its base layer without layer_deinit. The next
layer_deinit of any still-attached layer then walks the freed chain and
hard-faults.

Confirmed against the FIRM-3724 coredump: HardFault on KernelMain in
layer_deinit's active-layer walk (ldr r3,[r3,#24] with r3=0x190019,
r0=&s_modal_recognizer_manager just returned by
window_get_recognizer_manager, LR=layer_deinit+14), with
manager->active_layer pointing into freed, reused heap, during a
wake-touch pan on the notification card as a second notification
triggered the re-layout.

Invalidate the latch in layer_remove_from_parent while the window is
still reachable, covering every remove-then-free pattern, and deinit

fw/services/blob_db: don't use sync sessions after they are freed

Two paths let a BlobDBSyncSession be dereferenced after kernel_free():

prv_send_writeback fell through into the send after calling
blob_db_sync_next()/blob_db_sync_cancel() on a failed blob_db_read.
Both of those can free the session (sync_next frees it once the dirty
list drains), so the code went on to write session->state and
session->current_token into freed memory and sent a writeback built
from the freed dirty item. Return instead, and free the item buffer on
the way out.

The timeout and abandon regular timers fire on the timer task and hop
to KernelBG carrying a raw session pointer. The session can complete or
be cancelled in that window, leaving the deferred half to touch freed
memory — and, for the abandon callback, to free it a second time. Give
each session a monotonically increasing id, hand that to the timers,
and resolve it against the live session list before use. An id is never
reused, so a stale one cannot alias a new session that happens to land
on the same allocation.

Both mechanisms are consistent with the crash on the watch in
FIRM-3569, whose coredump asserted in blob_db_sync_cancel freeing a
bogus heap pointer, followed by "Found 0 apps" and an endless sync
retry loop.

The regular timer teardown race (regular_timer_remove_callback can
report failure while the callback is executing, yet the session holding
the RegularTimerInfo is freed regardless) is left alone here; it needs
deferred teardown rather than a lookup guard.

hardware from the outside: the driver mutes the DAC, the PA still

same gap fixed for the ambient light threshold in FIRM-2841. An

fw/board/display: use chalk packed layout for getafix legacy row infos

Getafix advertised the legacy 3.x app framebuffer as
GBitmapFormat8BitCircular but stored rows at rectangular offsets
(y * 180). Chalk apps that write to the framebuffer directly --
hardcoding chalk's well-known packed layout instead of calling
gbitmap_get_data_row_info() -- rendered garbled output (verified with
PinyWings from the store, whose terrain renderer does raw framebuffer
writes).

Regenerate g_gbitmap_legacy_3x_data_row_infos with the original chalk
(spalding) packed offsets, taken from display_spalding.c at the import
commit 3b9276848. The visibility masks were already identical, so the
legacy framebuffer is now byte-for-byte identical to real chalk
hardware: 25792 visible bytes packed back-to-back plus 76-byte guard
pads on both ends (25944 total, well within the native-sized 67600-byte
FrameBuffer).

This is safe because every system consumer of the app framebuffer
(compositor scaling/bezel/transitions, bitblt, screenshot) reads it via
gbitmap_get_data_row_info() and is layout-agnostic. The rectangular
constraint only applies to the native 260x260 table, which the JDI
display driver addresses as y * PBL_DISPLAY_WIDTH for in-place pixel
format conversion; that table is unchanged.

fw/drivers/pmic/npm1300: fix truncated battery current and temperature readings

battery_get_constants() read the two-bit ADC LSB fields as
(reg & MSK) >> POS, which is identically zero whenever POS is
non-zero. IBAT and NTC therefore discarded their two least
significant bits on every conversion and came back quantised four
times coarser than the hardware reports. VBAT was spared only
because its POS is zero.

Read them as (reg >> POS) & MSK instead. The field positions the
existing constants describe are correct: nPM1300 PS v1.1 puts
VBATRESULTLSB at GP0 bits 1:0, NTCRESULTLSB at GP0 bits 3:2 and
VBAT2RESULTLSB, which carries the IBAT result, at GP1 bits 5:4.
VBAT moves to the same form so a future change to any POS cannot
silently reintroduce this.

The fuel gauge is the visible casualty. On a Pebble Time 2 the
discharge range gives a 219 uA step, so the truncation fed
nrf_fuel_gauge battery current in 876 uA steps against an idle
draw near 1.4 mA, leaving every reading one or two counts. Over
3.4 days of logged samples all 18 distinct reconstructed counts
were multiples of four.

applib/recognizer: read nav gates and ticks through syscalls

touch_nav_dispatch() runs on the app task, which is unprivileged for
third-party apps (prv_init_from_info_common sets is_unprivileged on
every app loaded from its PebbleProcessInfo header). Its first
statement read the touch service's nav gates directly, taking the
kernel-owned mutex over kernel-owned statics, so any app that opted
into touch navigation faulted on its first touch:

  PC 0x120ffa68 -> touch_nav_enabled    services/touch/touch.c:86
  LR 0x12142e83 -> touch_nav_dispatch   recognizer/touch_nav.c:459

Add sys_touch_nav_enabled() and sys_touch_app_nav_active(), mirroring
the existing sys_touch_service_is_enabled(), and call those instead.

The recognizers had the same problem one level down: tap, pan, swipe
and the menu_layer double-tap window all called rtc_get_ticks(), which
reaches xTaskGetTickCount(). Route those nine call sites through the
existing sys_get_ticks().

Built-in system apps are privileged and never hit either path, which
is why the system UI scrolled by touch while third-party apps died.

This also affected the documented recognizer route:
window_attach_recognizer was unusable because
recognizer_manager_handle_touch_event() is only reached from
touch_nav.c:496 and :527, both downstream of the fault.

Verified on QEMU pebble-emery and on obelix hardware: tap, touch
scroll and double-tap in a third-party app that calls
app_touch_navigation_enable(true).

Fixes #1865

arrives while the transition is scheduled, with no replay. The displayed

fw/services/blob_db: canonicalize phone-sent shell-pref keys

Shell-pref backing-store keys include the trailing null:
prefs_private_read_backing looks records up with strlen + 1, and
settings-file records match on exact key length. A phone-originated
insert that sends the key without the null (key_len = strlen) therefore

the setting silently fails to apply. Notif-pref keys already normalize
the other way for the same reason.

point by pointing at the whitelist's own string, so phone writes land
at the canonical key regardless of which encoding the phone uses.

services/notifications: show images sent with notifications

The phone can now hold a photo for a timeline notification and serve it over
the imaging endpoint, the same way the music app fetches album art.

A notification carrying one gains AttributeIdImageAspectRatio, the image's
height/width in sixteenths. The card reserves a band of exactly that shape and
requests the pixels with ImagingImageTypeNotification, keyed by the item's
UUID. Taking the shape from the attribute rather than the bitmap means the
card's height is final before the transfer completes, so nothing reflows when
the image lands; a placeholder fills the band until it does, and disappears if
the phone answers NoImage.

Rendering needs no new layout node: LayoutNodeType_Constructor already injects
an arbitrary GTextNode, and graphics_text_node_create_custom is documented for
exactly this. On round the band takes a page of its own, because paging only
knows how to break text and a fixed-height band could otherwise be sliced
across a seam, and the image is sized to the largest rectangle of its aspect
that clears the bezel at that position.

Serving a second image type means a response can no longer be routed by
remembering the type of the last request: the music app and the notification
modal can both have one outstanding. The type now rides in the spare bits of
the response's flags byte. Zero is album art, which is also what a phone
predating this sends, so nothing changes for it on the wire.

The phone only attaches the attribute when the watch advertises support for
it, so older firmware never receives an id it does not know.

fw/services/touch: add a synthetic touch injection entry point

Automated input (test harnesses, console commands) needs to drive the touch
service as if a finger had produced the samples. Feeding touch_handle_update()
directly leaves three concerns with the caller that belong to the service: the
left-hand-mode mirror, whether touch is enabled at all, and what happens when a
real finger is on the screen at the same time.

touch_handle_injected_update() takes the coordinates the UI observes, plus the
phase of the gesture:

- No rotation is applied, so callers state the direction they want instead of
  pre-cancelling a mirror they would have to know about.
- A Begin arms the interaction session, the same way a button press does.
  Without it, injected contact on the idle watchface is dropped as unarmed and
  the whole gesture goes nowhere.
- Whoever puts a finger down first owns the sensor: a Begin is refused while a
  physical finger is down, and physical samples and gestures are ignored until
  the injected gesture ends. Either could otherwise corrupt the other's path
  through the service's single global finger state.

The phase is stated rather than inferred because a mid-path sample and a fresh
touchdown are both finger-down. A gesture that lost the sensor (touch reset, or
switched off and back on) would otherwise have its next sample taken as the
start of a new gesture halfway along the path, and the caller would never learn
it had been interrupted. A Move or End from a gesture that no longer owns the
sensor is refused instead.

Ownership is released wherever the finger state is forced up: touch_reset() and
touch_release_active(), which the global kill switch goes through. The injected
End that would normally clear it is itself dropped while touch is disabled, so
without that the sensor would stay owned by a gesture that can never finish,
blocking physical touch for good.

touch_injection_is_available() lets a caller report a gesture that would be
refused rather than acknowledging one that never happens.

fw/kernel: inject button presses and swipes over pebble protocol

Driving the watch UI from a connected phone previously meant a serial console,
which needs physical access. Endpoint 0xf00d accepts three commands and answers
each with a {command, status} ack, so a harness can tell an accepted command
from a rejected one:

- Button: a sequence of press/release pairs, with a hold time and an
  inter-press gap. A long press is the same command with a longer hold.
- Button set: hold exactly the given set of buttons down, as a bitmask. One bit
  held across two calls is an open-ended press; two bits are a chord; an empty
  mask releases everything. Only transitions are emitted, and a mask that swaps
  buttons releases before it presses.
- Swipe: a straight path across the middle of the screen in one of four
  directions, sized from the recognizer's own limits and injected through the
  touch service, which owns rotation and physical-touch arbitration.

Injected input is single-flight, tracked by an explicit active flag under a
mutex. The timer's scheduled state cannot stand in for either half of that:
NewTimer clears the expiry before running a callback, so a timer reports
unscheduled for as long as its callback is executing, and a request arriving in
that window would be admitted and then have its timer stolen when the running
callback rearms. The lock matters because two controllers are exposed, the
console and the endpoint, on different tasks. Held buttons and sequences are
mutually exclusive, so a sequence can never interleave with a hold and emit
transitions the UI would read as chord edges.

A swipe reports Invalid rather than Ok when it cannot become a gesture: slower
than the recognizer accepts, touch switched off, or a finger already on the
screen. If the gesture loses the sensor mid-path the service refuses the next
sample and the sequence stops, instead of leaving a half-finished path behind.

The press sequence machinery moves here from the console command that owned it,
so the console and the endpoint drive buttons through one implementation. The
counts and timeouts stay 32-bit, matching what the console has always accepted.

The endpoint is registered for PRF as well as the normal firmware: recovery is
exactly where driving the UI without physical access is most useful, and the
handler has no dependency that PRF lacks.

Nothing releases a held button but a later call, so a caller that disconnects
mid-hold leaves the watch holding it.

fw/applib/ui: tune animation pacing for gabbro's 21 Hz display

Gabbro's Sharp LS013B7DD02 panel is spec-limited to ~21 Hz full-frame
updates (BCK max 0.758 MHz, vertical period min 46.7 ms), while the
animation service schedules frames at 30 Hz. A full-frame LCDC transfer
takes ~47 ms on the wire and the framebuffer is converted in place, so
rendering cannot overlap the flush: every other animation tick lands
mid-transfer and gets coalesced into a single deferred render. Motion
advances in uneven 1-2 frame steps, which reads as choppiness compared
to obelix (whose panel refreshes at its 30 Hz spec).

Two changes, both gabbro-only:

- Introduce ANIMATION_RENDER_FRAME_INTERVAL_MS, the interval at which
  the animation service schedules frames, set to 48 ms (~21 Hz) on
  gabbro and equal to ANIMATION_TARGET_FRAME_INTERVAL_MS elsewhere.
  Sampling animations at the rate the panel can actually show them
  gives even motion steps instead of coalesced, uneven ones.

- Trim ANIMATION_TARGET_FRAME_INTERVAL_MS, the base all animation
  durations are derived from, to 28 ms. At ~21 Hz an animation shows
  fewer, larger motion steps, and design-speed durations read as
  sluggish; slightly shorter durations restore the snappy feel.

Relates to FIRM-3324.

scroll_layer: add inertial fling on touch liftoff

Project a coast target from the pan recognizer's liftoff velocity
(target = offset + v * TAU) and glide there on the shared scroll
animation with a cubic ease-out (f(t) = 1 - (1 - t)^3). The cubic
launches at slope 3, so a duration of 3000 * |d| / |v| ms (3 * TAU
unclamped) makes the animated launch velocity exactly match the finger
-- a seamless finger-to-coast handoff with pure integer math -- and its
tail brakes hard early then glides out instead of stopping dead. The
coast starts from the current (last throttled) offset so the
unthrottled liftoff residual is absorbed into the animation instead of
teleporting.

An edge-clamped target shortens the duration proportionally so the
coast keeps its launch speed instead of crawling into the clamp.
Tuning: a coast takes a deliberate flick (>= 250 px/s); velocity is
capped at 3600 px/s, bounding the hardest fling to ~864 px over at
most 720 ms. Liftoffs below the threshold settle as before, and paging
scroll layers never fling (a coast would break page alignment).

The shared animation's duration/curve/handlers are restored by the
fling's stopped handler; since that handler only fires for animations
that ran at least one frame, the pan-start takeover also restores them
explicitly via the idempotent cleanup helper.

Coast the content on a fast liftoff using the shared scroll-layer fling
helper, clamped by the menu's own offset clamp.

Plain menus coast the content only: the selection contract is unchanged
(a pan scrolls, a tap selects). Center-focused carousels coast toward
the raw projection (the widened clamp allows half a frame past the
ends) with the focus tracked live: the previously empty scroll-offset-
changed handler re-runs the centre-row tracking while a fling is

(change_ongoing_animation would kill the coast), so it is suppressed
while a fling is active. When the coast finishes, the stopped handler
re-tracks once and glides the focused row to the exact centre, which
also reconciles a mid-coast veto; a not-finished stop only clears state
since whoever unscheduled the coast owns the offset next.

The pan-start takeover now also unschedules a running scroll animation
(previously only the selection animation was cancelled), closing a
one-frame window where a settle and the first throttled pan update both
wrote the offset. Carousel coast frames are unit-tested through the
animation's actual setter (the T_STATIC internal offset setter), since
scroll_layer_set_content_offset unschedules the running animation --
something a real animation frame never does.

emits no touch events after Touchdown -- the touch service only publishes

resources: open up LECO's '5' so it can't be read as '6'

LECO's seven-segment '5' draws a partial stub in the lower-left segment --
3 of the 5 rows at size 32, 4 of 9 at size 60 -- where the '6' fills that
segment completely. That stub is the only difference between the two
glyphs: at LECO_20 they differ by 3 pixels out of 111 of ink, at LECO_32 by
8 out of 232. Users cannot tell them apart in the sleep summary, and the
same ambiguity affects steps, heart rate, the workout timer, timeline pins
and every third-party watchface that asks for a LECO font.

Every other LECO digit with no lower-left segment (3, 4, 9) draws that
region empty, so clearing the stub makes '5' consistent with its siblings
rather than inventing a new shape. It is present at 60px, so it is the
typeface's drawing rather than a rasterization artifact.

Patched with tools/font/pbf_extract.py and pbf_repack.py, which round-trip
these files byte-for-byte. The fonts are not RLE4, so glyph bitmaps are
fixed-size: clearing pixels inside an unchanged bounding box leaves every
size, offset and advance untouched. All nine files keep their exact byte
count and differ in only 2-7 bytes each, and re-extracting confirms '5' is
the sole glyph that changed in any of them.

fw/comm/ble: run conn param watchdog off the timer task

The connection parameter watchdog callback took bt_lock directly on the
NewTimers task. Timer callbacks run serially, so whenever the BT stack
held bt_lock for a while (e.g. during a reconnect storm), every other
timer in the system stalled behind it: vibe pattern steps stopped mid
segment (leaving the motor pinned on), UI timeouts slipped, and overall
event latency ballooned without ever tripping the task watchdog.

Defer the body to KernelBG instead, keeping NewTimers free of bt_lock.
The connection pointer is re-validated under bt_lock on KernelBG, same
as before, so a connection torn down between scheduling and execution
is still handled. A duplicate deferred callback (timer re-fires before
KernelBG drains) is benign: it just re-evaluates actual vs desired
params, and the attempts counter still caps retries.

Investigated from a getafix freeze where an alarm became undismissable
for ~50s during a BLE supervision-timeout storm while the watch never
crashed: KernelMain and NewTimers were repeatedly stalled on bt_lock in
sub-watchdog-threshold chunks.

fw/shell: keep the workout app pinned while a workout runs

The launcher pin for the workout app was derived from the workout event
type, with FrontendOpened/FrontendClosed falling through the switch on the
`can_expire = true` initializer. app_install_mark_prioritized() overwrites
the stored flag unconditionally, so closing the workout app while the
workout kept running downgraded the permanent pin to one expiring after
five minutes.

Pause and resume both emit PebbleWorkoutEvent_Paused, which re-set the
permanent pin -- matching the reported "pausing and resuming re-pins it,
then it unpins again later".

Derive the pin from workout_service_is_workout_ongoing() instead. This is
also correct for the Stopped event: the service posts the event before
clearing current_workout and the event drains on KernelMain afterwards, so
the existing post-workout grace period is preserved.

fw/services/alarms: don't cancel a user snooze on a clock change

alarm_handle_clock_change() force-triggers a smart alarm that is inside
its smart-snooze window, then calls prv_clear_snooze_timer(). It never
checked s_user_snoozed, so a clock change arriving during a user's 10
minute snooze destroyed that snooze and re-rang the alarm immediately.

A user snooze is an explicit deadline and must survive any clock change;
the force trigger exists only to rescue the internal sleep poll. On
SF32LB52 boards the RTC calibration cycle emits PEBBLE_SET_TIME_EVENT
every 60s, so a post-wake correction landing shortly after the alarm woke
the watch made this reachable in normal use.

Also set s_user_snoozed inside prv_snooze_alarm() before arming the
timer. It was set afterwards, leaving a window in which a snooze callback
already queued on KernelBG -- which new_timer_stop() cannot cancel --
would consume the flag and re-enter the sleep poll, replacing the
configured delay with the 60s smart poll interval.

Finally, defer the prv_alarm_operation() call on the force-trigger path
until after the settings file is closed. prv_alarm_operation() opens the
file itself, and opening it twice croaks; the path was unreachable in
tests until now.

fw/process_management: refetch an app whose cached binary has a foreign UUID

app_cache_entry_exists() is keyed on the AppInstallId alone, and install
IDs are recycled: app_db_init() recomputes the next ID as max+1 over the
surviving records on every boot, skipping tombstones. A cache entry
orphaned by an earlier uninstall therefore leaves a stale binary sitting
at an ID that a later install reuses.

prv_needs_fetch() saw the hit and never requested a fetch, and
app_install_get_md() reads PebbleProcessInfo out of the cached binary's
own header -- so the watch launched the previous app under the new app's
ID, and app_cache_app_launched() then refreshed the stale entry's
last_launch, protecting it from eviction.

Compare the metadata UUID against the app_db entry for the install ID and
drop the cache entry on a mismatch, so the launch falls through to a
normal fetch. This makes an already-poisoned watch heal on the next
launch attempt rather than needing a factory reset.

fw/apps/weather: use tm_gmtoff so DST is included in local-hour math

prv_location_local_hour() and prv_sunset_minutes() derive a wall clock
from localtime(), whose tm_gmtoff includes the DST adjustment, but then
subtract time_get_gmtoffset(), which does not. During DST both were an
hour off, giving the wrong hourly UV reading and the wrong sunrise/sunset
whenever the watch's own offset was used.

Use lt->tm_gmtoff, which is the total offset the same struct tm was built
with. Also document the tm_gmtoff contract, since the header still
described it as plain "seconds east of UTC" -- the ambiguity that had an

fw/services/hrm: stop unserved subscribers pinning the sensor on

The manager only considers a subscriber served once it receives a
Good-or-better (or OffWrist) BPM sample. A subscriber the sensor cannot
serve - poor contact, or the fresh state right after boot where every
subscriber is treated as immediately due - would hold the sensor powered
indefinitely. Telemetry from MOB-11575 shows a Pebble Time 2 running the
sensor for 42 minutes straight after an OTA reboot, then burning
~4-7 min/hour for two days against a 30-minute measurement interval.

Track how long the sensor has been continuously on. Once it exceeds a
full serve window (120 s) without producing a valid reading for a
subscriber, stamp that subscriber as served so it defers to its next
interval instead. Short-interval (live HR) subscribers become due again
immediately, so workouts and BLE HR sharing are unaffected; only
long-interval duty-cycled subscribers stop pinning the sensor. The gate
counts continuous on-time only, so subscribers that went overdue while
the sensor was forced off (charging, run level) still get served first.

drivers/vibe: scale AW86225 RAM waveform to full DAC range

The pre-loaded sinusoidal waveform peaked at ±119 (0x77/0x89), only
93% of the signed 8-bit DAC range (±127). Scale it by 127/119 so the
peaks reach 0x7F/0x81, using the full available output range.

This gives ~7% more drive amplitude at every gain setting, including
the maximum (High = unity gain), without exceeding the LRA motor's
rated maximum current (Imax 80 mA) since the peak output voltage is
clamped by VDD regardless.

fw/services/activity: release auto-activity HRM subscription on reset

The step-activity state machine takes its own HRM subscription once an
auto-detected walk or run passes three minutes. It is registered from
KernelBackground with INSTALL_ID_INVALID and expire_s = 0, so neither
hrm_manager_process_cleanup (App/Worker only) nor the expiry sweep can
reclaim it - prv_reset_step_activity_state is the only release site.

Starting a workout disables activity tracking, which calls
prv_reset_state. That deliberately skips step activities still in
progress to avoid racing the minute handler, so exactly the states
holding a subscription are the ones left alone. Tracking then stays
disabled, kalg_activities_update gates the updaters off, and the state
machine can never reach the release site. The subscription survives at a
one second interval and pins the sensor on. Charging tears the algorithm
down entirely - activity_algorithm_deinit frees the state without
unsubscribing - after which the subscriber is orphaned in the manager
until reboot, matching the reports that only a reboot restores normal
monitoring.

Release the HRM in prv_reset_state whether or not the activity is still
in progress; the next active minute re-subscribes. Add kalg_deinit so
the free path releases it too, and bound the subscription with an expiry
that each active minute re-arms, so a state machine that stops running
lapses instead of holding the sensor on.

fw/services/alarms: re-pick just once alarm days on boot

A "just once" alarm stores the day it fires on as a weekday, and is only

applib/ui: rubber-band touch overscroll with spring-back

Dragging a list past its first or last row used to stop dead at the
edge. Let a held pan pull the content a little further instead: past
the scroll bounds the excess is damped asymptotically (the content
follows at half the finger's speed at first and saturates at ~1/6 of
the frame height), and on liftoff the content glides back to the edge
in 200ms regardless of velocity. A cancelled gesture restores the edge
instantly, since a cancel is a handover that must not leave an
animation running.

The damp mapping, an unclamped offset setter, and the spring-back
animation are shared scroll_layer helpers used by both Tier-1 widgets
(bare ScrollLayer and MenuLayer). The spring-back needs its own
animation implementation: the standard one clamps the offset every
frame, which would clip the very first out-of-bounds frame to the edge
and snap instead of glide. A touchdown that catches a bare scroll
layer mid-spring-back restarts the glide so the content cannot freeze
out of bounds.

Paging scroll layers keep the hard clamp (rubber-banding would fight
page alignment), and so does content that fits the frame: nothing to
scroll, nothing to bounce. Center-focused menus rubber-band past their
widened bounds and return through their existing settle-to-center
path. Existing clamp tests are updated where the hard edge became the
damped mapping.

pan past an edge lands on the damped offset; liftoff glides back to
the edge (spring-back scheduled from the rubber-banded offset, no
snap, no coast flag); a cancelled gesture restores the edge instantly
with no animation left running; and a touchdown that catches a bare

inertial coast, and the settle-to-center glide that follows. The
pinned frame is re-derived from the offset on every change, and the
pin releases itself lazily the moment it coincides with the settled
selection's own frame (the row landed in the box), so the handoff back
to the normal selection-owned highlight is seamless. Engaging the pin
stops a running selection (bump) animation, and any button or
programmatic selection change hands the highlight straight back.

The ends get matching treatment. The carousel pan bounds tighten to
the terminal row's exact centred rest offset -- the terminal row is
the selection whenever those bounds actually clamp, so free travel
ends where a button step would rest and only the damped rubber band
goes beyond (the previous coarse half-frame widen let the row drift
half a row further first). And past the ends the pinned box glues to
the terminal row and moves together with the pull: there is no next
row to transit to, so the fixed-centre lens gives way to the row
itself, springing back with it on release. Mid-list transit is
untouched (near a terminal row the glue inequality points the other
way). The widened-clamp test follows the exact top bound.

One flag bit carved from the existing flags byte; sizeof(MenuLayer) is
unchanged.

returns as a self-contained workflow in a follow-up commit. Net effect:

fw/apps/prf: rescale obelix MFG ALS range for 99ms IT

The W1160 integration time changed from 16.83 ms to 99 ms when the
event-gated continuous sampling API landed, so raw counts for the same
light level are now ~5.9x higher. The runtime dark/k-delta thresholds

treewide: drop unused includes

Removes 1519 #include lines that nothing needs: 1264 from .c files, 255 from
headers, across 678 files.

An include goes only if the file names nothing it offers -- no macro, type,
function or object -- and if removing it leaves every object file
byte-identical in all twelve board configurations. That a file still builds
is not enough on its own: one that uses uint32_t and drops <stdint.h> still
builds, because another include drags it in, and is one reordering away from
breaking.

Deciding what an include offers needs care in both directions. Reading only a
header's own text misses forwarders -- the toolchain's stdint.h is a bare
#include_next, so it appears to declare nothing -- while following its whole
subtree makes every facade "provide" uint32_t and keeps everything. Descent
stops at the first headers that declare something of their own, passing
through forwarders and the implementation-private headers a public one
delegates to.

The object test is what a plain build cannot give. lib/os/mcu/cache_arm.c
includes cmsis_core.h, names nothing it declares and compiles without it, but
the header supplies __DCACHE_PRESENT and the file falls back to a local
#define of 0U -- dropping it compiled every cache flush and invalidate into a
bx lr stub, silently, under -Werror. 604 candidates compile cleanly and still
change generated code, nearly all of them headers feeding a macro into an #if
rather than declaring anything.

Header includes reach further, since any file reading the header can change.
gcc -H bounds that exactly: dropping #include B from A only matters where B is
opened as a direct child of A, anywhere else it was a guarded no-op. Two
effects escape per-candidate checks and surface only in a whole-tree rebuild,
which is how the pass ends -- an accepted removal invalidating a later
"already read" premise, and pairs of headers each offering the same
declaration to a third file.

Verified on asterix, getafix, obelix, the three QEMU targets and the prf
variants: every configuration builds, no object file differs, and the ELF
symbol tables are unchanged apart from log strings whose line numbers moved.
./pbl test passes.

Build time barely moves -- first-party compile CPU down 1.9%, preprocessed
text under 1% -- because a removed header is nearly always still pulled in
transitively by another. This is hygiene, not a speedup.

sdk: stop waf's minifier mangling keyword f-strings

waf runs everything it bundles into the SDK's waf through a minifier of
its own, and its token loop never separates a NAME from a following
string literal. A string that carries a prefix is an identifier character
away from the keyword before it, so `return f"..."` came out of the
bundler as `returnf"..."` and sdk_helpers failed to import at all.

Emit the separator, and match FSTRING_START as well as STRING: Python
3.12 split f-strings into their own token types, so on 3.12+ the prefix
arrives as FSTRING_START and never reached the STRING branch.

The minifier lives in vendored waf, which update-waf.sh re-downloads from
scratch, so the change is kept as a patch that script now reapplies.

It is shaped like Zephyr's west: a small core -- workspace, build
directory, PblCommand, the binary runners -- plus one module per command,
discovered by scanning pbl/commands/. Adding a command is adding a file,
and commands that should not live in the package are declared in pbl.yml,
where they are imported only when they are the one being run.

Nothing about the checkout is baked into the CLI any more:

- The workspace is wherever pbl.yml is, found by walking up from the
  current directory. It also names the build, test and language
  directories, which -b/--build-dir and PBL_BUILD_DIR override.
- The build is read back from its own byproducts, .config for the Kconfig
  symbols and CMakeCache.txt for the board, the variant and the project
  name the artifacts are named after. The pbl_env.json the build used to
  write for the CLI, and the generator that wrote it, are gone.
- The board contributes its runners and emulator decorations through its
  manifest.

Deriving the repository root from __file__ no longer works once the code
is installed, which is what the workspace lookup replaces. The binary
runners move into the package so it is self-contained.

Two options are renamed while their commands are consolidated:
--screenshot-output becomes -o/--output, and --qemu-decoration becomes
--decoration.

cmake: build the merged translation catalog

The catalog `pbl make_lang` works from was never built. src/fw set PBL_POT
with PARENT_SCOPE, which lands in src/, while pbl_link_firmware() reads it
from the top level, where it was empty -- so nothing depended on
pebbleos.pot and it stayed out of the build graph.

Depending on it directly is not enough either: a custom command's rule is
only reachable from the directory that added it, and nothing consumed
fw.pot, applib.pot, apps.pot or services.pot where they were declared, so
their rules were never emitted at all.

Give every .pot a target alongside its custom command, named after its
path so any directory can derive it, and have a merge depend on both the
input files and their targets: the target to reach the rule, the file to
keep the rebuild tracking. The firmware's catalog records its target in a
global property, the way the per-service catalogs already do, and the
firmware depends on that.

Touching a translatable string in a service now rebuilds its catalog,
services.pot and pebbleos.pot in turn. Recovery firmware builds no
catalog, as before.
