kernel: add the pbl kernel API on a FreeRTOS shim

Introduce include/pbl/kernel, a threading API owned by PebbleOS, and
kernel/, the top-level folder that implements it. The first backend,
kernel/freertos, shims the FreeRTOS fork; nothing outside kernel/ is
meant to include FreeRTOS once call sites have moved over. The API is
complete here: the migration commits that follow only touch call sites.

Objects (thread, mutex, sem, msgq, poll group) are caller-owned structs
with PBL_*_DEFINE macros. FreeRTOS V8.2.1 has no static creation, so a
DEFINE also drops a record in .pbl_kobj_init that pbl_kernel_init()
walks before anything else runs; the shim keeps the FreeRTOS control
block behind backend.handle. Blocking calls take a pbl_timeout_t and
return -errno; there are no _from_isr variants, the shim picks the path.
The mutex is recursive and records its owner and lock site. Returning
from a thread entry ends the thread.

debug.h wraps the introspection the core dump, task watchdog and
telemetry pull from FreeRTOS internals, keeping the register order the
core dump format depends on. idle.h is the contract with the per-SoC
tickless idle code, which is rewritten against it here.

The shim owns everything FreeRTOS-facing from the start. FreeRTOSConfig.h
lives in kernel/freertos, reads the tick rate, priority count and NVIC
priority levels from the kernel Kconfig symbols and decides the per-SoC
MPU region slots. The hooks that used to live in
src/fw/freertos_application.c are shim files: stack overflow and
privilege raise forward to pbl_thread_stack_overflow() and
pbl_kernel_privilege_raise_allowed(), which the firmware implements,
and the heap hooks go through libos os_malloc()/os_free(). Until the
call sites have moved, the config still pulls in the two firmware
headers the old copy did and keeps three TLS slots so the syscall code
can use the first two; the shim's back-pointer sits in the last one.

Design notes live in docs/architecture/kernel.md.

Nothing uses the API yet; the firmware still boots to the launcher on
qemu_gabbro.

kernel: move mutexes to pbl_mutex

Replace the libos PebbleMutex/PebbleRecursiveMutex handles with the
caller-owned struct pbl_mutex from the kernel API, and delete the libos
mutex implementation.

Static mutexes become PBL_MUTEX_DEFINE objects that pbl_kernel_init()
constructs before the scheduler runs, so the create-in-init calls and
the "is the mutex created yet" guards go away. Where such a guard also
stood in for "has this service been initialised", it is replaced by a
bool set at the point the mutex used to be created. Mutexes embedded in
dynamically allocated state are initialised in place and released with
pbl_mutex_deinit(), which the shim needs to free the FreeRTOS control
block.

The single pbl_mutex type is recursive, so the recursive and
non-recursive lock calls map to the same function; timeouts use
PBL_MSEC()/PBL_FOREVER and the callers check the -errno result.
pbl_mutex_lock_lr() keeps the explicit caller address bt_lock() and the
persist service pass for lock diagnostics. Ownership checks ask
FreeRTOS for the holder, so they are right for tasks not yet created
through pbl_thread_create().

The stack high-water mark reported through debug.h is now in bytes.

Tests keep their stubs_mutex.h / fake_mutex.h names with pbl_mutex
bodies; the fake registers mutexes on first use so PBL_MUTEX_DEFINE
objects work without pbl_kernel_init(). Host builds get the FreeRTOS
backend header on their include path, and the kobj registration uses a
Mach-O section name on macOS.

boot), asterix and obelix builds, and the unit test suite.

pebble_tasks keeps one thread object per PebbleTask and becomes the
registry the rest of the firmware queries: pebble_task_get_thread(),

background stacks from the linker, app and worker stacks from their
memory segments, and PBL_THREAD_STACK_DEFINE storage for the new

it stays 2 KiB.

the stack overflow hook becomes pbl_thread_stack_overflow() implemented
by pebble_tasks, and the debugger's uxTopUsedPriority moves into the
shim. The syscall code keeps its two per-thread slots in
pbl_thread.tls[] and tells threads apart by pbl_thread_id() rather
than by handle. Core dumps walk pbl_thread_foreach() with the same
register order, the task watchdog and process manager read saved
registers through pbl_thread_saved_regs(), and the run-time stats

kernel: add the native backend

kernel/native implements the pbl kernel API without FreeRTOS: a
fixed-priority preemptive scheduler with one ready list per priority
and a CLZ bitmap, round-robin within a priority on the tick,
priority-ordered wait queues, a single sorted timeout list, direct
handoff on semaphores and mutexes, single-level priority inheritance
and a tickless idle thread driven through pbl/kernel/idle.h. Objects
carry their wait queues in the per-backend state, so the public
structs are unchanged apart from the backend member becoming a
per-object type.

The Cortex-M arch keeps the saved-context layout, the SVC numbers, the
syscall-stack relocation and the per-thread MPU region switch of the
FreeRTOS port, so the syscall assembly, core dumps and fault handling
work unchanged. The two syscall hooks the port used to call are now
pbl_kernel_syscall_stack() and pbl_kernel_syscall_entered(); the shim
forwards its FreeRTOS names to them. Returning from a thread entry
ends the thread instead of faulting.

A POSIX arch runs kernel threads as pthreads that execute one at a
time under the kernel's own decisions, with a virtual clock that only
advances through delivered ticks or when everything is blocked. The
test_native_kernel suite uses it to check preemption, time slicing,
semaphores from ISR context, inheritance, queue blocking, poll groups,
suspend/resume/abort, thread exit, priority changes and the scheduler
lock.

Selected with CONFIG_KERNEL_BACKEND_NATIVE=y; the FreeRTOS shim stays
the default. The moddable glue still calls FreeRTOS, so the native
backend depends on it being disabled for now.

Verified on qemu_gabbro and qemu_flint: boot to the watchface, app
launch and exit, no asserts; the unit test suite passes.

fw/services: offer music to every phone without a media service

The music endpoint only claimed the music server when the phone said Android,
so a desktop companion got nothing: neither this endpoint, because of the
check, nor the Apple Media Service, because it does not publish one. The OS it
declares has been a first-class value for as long as the enum has had
RemoteOSX, RemoteOSLinux and RemoteOSWindows in it.

iOS is the one that has somewhere else to read from, and AMS is not gated on
the declared OS at all — it connects when its GATT service is found, and
whichever side claims music_set_connected_server last wins. So the condition
wants to be about who has an alternative rather than about Android: iOS keeps
AMS, an app that does not say what it runs on is left alone in case it is an
older iOS one, and everything else gets the endpoint.

Covered both ways: a desktop app is now asked for its state on connect, and
one that declares nothing still is not.

fw/drivers/uart/sf32lb: invalidate D-cache on the RX DMA buffer

serial_console enables RX DMA on the debug UART whenever PULSE is
active, and since the SF32LB52 D-cache was enabled the IRQ paths have
been reading rx_dma_buffer[] through stale cache lines. On obelix the
watch would answer a host frame only when the lines happened to miss,
and replayed old frames (spurious LCP Configure-Acks) whenever they
hit. Any multi-packet exchange such as "help" on the pulse console
exhausted the reliable transport's retransmits and dropped the link.

Invalidate the buffer before every read in the IDLE and DMA
half/complete handlers, flush-invalidate it before starting DMA, and
assert that the buffer is cache-line aligned and sized so the
invalidate cannot destroy neighbouring data. Size and align the
dbgserial buffer accordingly.

drivers/vibe: drive AW86225 at the LRA rated voltage

The RAM playback gain was unity at full strength with a full-scale sine,
so the output swung rail-to-rail at VDD: ~2.6 Vrms at 4.2 V, and higher
when charging. The LRA is rated for 1.25 Vrms max, and the MFG vibration
test measured ~3 Vrms at the motor.

Follow the Awinic reference driver's ram_vbat_comp: sample VDD through
the chip's own VBAT detector (DETCFG2.VBAT_GO, DET_VBAT/DET_LO, 6.1 V
full scale, clamped to 3.0-4.5 V) before each playback start, and scale
PLAYCFG2 so 100% strength equals the rated peak voltage at the sampled
VDD. The sample is skipped while playback is running, since the
detector requires standby.

The rated voltage is a new per-board Kconfig,
VIBE_AW86225_RATED_VOLTAGE_MV, set to 1250 mVrms for getafix DVT2 and
obelix. Low/Medium/High keep their 40/60/100 ratios below that cap.

drivers/vibe: overdrive AW86225 playback start

Driving the LRA at its rated voltage leaves a 30-50 ms rise time that
makes short pulses feel weak. Play the first cycles of every playback at
a higher overdrive voltage so the motor reaches steady state quickly,
then settle to the rated voltage.

The RAM sequence now chains two waveforms: the full-scale sine looped
for VIBE_AW86225_OVERDRIVE_CYCLES, then the same cycle scaled by
rated/overdrive looped until stop. Gain is global, so the ratio lives in
the sample data and full strength is sized for the overdrive voltage.
The sustain image is built at init from the single sine table.

VIBE_AW86225_OVERDRIVE_VOLTAGE_MV defaults to the rated voltage, which
disables overdrive; getafix DVT2 and obelix set 2500 mVrms, pending
confirmation against the LRA overdrive rating.

drivers/vibe: add AW86225 CONT mode playback

Add VIBE_AW86225_CONT_PLAYBACK to drive the LRA in CONT mode instead of
looping the RAM waveform. The chip plays DRV1_LVL for DRV1_TIME half
cycles, then DRV2_LVL until stopped, tracking the resonant frequency
from back-EMF and compensating for the supply voltage in hardware, so
the software VBAT sampling is compiled out.

The datasheet gives the no-load output peak with VBAT_MODE set as
6.1 V * DRV_LVL / 128, clamped at VDD. Measured differentially across
the motor on getafix DVT2 the scale is 5.0 V: codes 31 and 63 produce
1.21 V and 2.36 V, and codes 12/18/25/37 fit the same line, so the
levels are sized from 5.0 V. CONT mode drives a square wave for DRV_WIDTH of each
half cycle, so the configured RMS voltages map to a peak of
rms / sqrt(width / period). DRV1 is sized from the overdrive voltage
for VIBE_AW86225_OVERDRIVE_CYCLES cycles, DRV2 from the rated voltage,
both scaled by strength. Auto brake is enabled so stop is crisp.

getafix DVT2 and obelix enable it. DRV2_TIME is set to 0xFF, relied on
to mean "until stop" as in the Awinic reference driver; a vibration
longer than 255 half cycles verifies this on hardware.

drivers/touch/cst816: take the i2c lock around the hardware reset

cst816_hw_reset toggles the chip's reset pin with no synchronisation
against the bus: touch_sensor_set_enabled is reached synchronously from
arbitrary tasks (subscribe/unsubscribe callbacks, the backlight and
system-hold toggles) and calls the reset as its first statement, while
the system task may be mid-transfer inside prv_read_data clocking the
same chip. A chip hit by reset mid-byte stops ACKing and corrupts the
in-flight transfer.

Take s_i2c_lock inside cst816_hw_reset, the same per-transfer lock the
read/write paths use. No caller holds it already -- the only lock-takers
are prv_read_data and prv_write_data, neither of which resets -- so the
acquisition cannot self-deadlock, and the bootmode/fw-update sequences
keep their existing per-operation interleaving.

Not unit-testable: the driver has no test target (it sits on real I2C,
GPIO and EXTI), and the race is a cross-task timing window against
hardware. Validated by call-site audit and a full firmware build.

drivers/vibe: play AW86225 RAM waveforms instead of CONT mode

The LRA vendor advised against CONT mode for our use and supplied RAM
waveforms for the motor. Their sustain waveform is a plain 50-sample
sine cycle at 12 kS/s, so keep one full-scale cycle in the driver and
build the RAM image at init with it scaled to the rated voltage, then
loop it with the sequencer until stop. The overdrive burst is dropped:
the LRA0825 datasheet allows at most 1.25 Vrms.

Scaling follows the Awinic reference drivers: the gain is compensated
from the VBAT sample so a full-scale sample drives the 4.2 V reference
of a full Li-ion cell, and the cycle is scaled to the rated voltage
against that reference. The chip delivers about 7 % less than that
model, so VIBE_AW86225_OUTPUT_GAIN_PERCENT carries the measured ratio
and the waveform is scaled up by its inverse. The gain is sampled
before each start. Setting GAIN_CHANGEABLE in SYSCTRL7 is required for
PLAYCFG2 writes to apply while playing, otherwise the gain is latched
at GO and strength ramps do nothing.

CONT registers are now only used by F0 detection, which sets its own
timing. Both boards set the datasheet's 1.2 Vrms and the measured 93 %
output gain; the symbols have no defaults.

Measured on obelix PVT (differential across the motor, 400 kS/s,
20 kHz low-pass, sine fit): 1.20 Vrms at strength 100, 0.73 at 60,
0.49 at 40, flat within 1.5 % from 3.3 V to 4.2 V supply. A strength
change while playing applies at the next cycle with no restart or
brake. With a neutral trim the sample clock gives exactly 240 Hz.

fw/services/compositor: make freeze wait for in-flight display updates

compositor_freeze() only raised a flag that the KernelMain render
paths consult. It was called from the BT task by the screenshot
endpoint, which then copied the first framebuffer chunk immediately,
so a display update that had already been kicked off could still be
in flight while the screenshot read the framebuffer.

On sf32lb boards (obelix, getafix) the JDI driver converts the dirty
rows of the compositor framebuffer in-place from 2-2-2 to 3-3-2 for
the LCDC and only converts them back after the DMA completes, from a
KernelMain callback. Screenshots sampling those rows in that window
carry 3-3-2 pixels reinterpreted as GColor8: orange (0xF4) reads
back as GColorIslamicGreen (0xC8), which is the green status bar in
the report.

Turn compositor_freeze() into an asynchronous request: the freeze
takes effect on KernelMain and a callback fires there once no display
update is in progress, either straight away or from the display
update complete handler. The screenshot starts streaming from that
callback on the system task, and the ALS console command drops its
hand-rolled spin on compositor_display_update_in_progress(). Add unit
tests for both the idle and the update-in-flight cases.

kernel: keep empty MPU slots from wiping the previous region

arch_thread_regions_set() encodes an unused per-thread region slot as
RBAR=0 / RASR=0. On ARMv7-M the context switch streams the four slots
through MPU_RBAR..MPU_RASR_A3, and an RBAR write with VALID clear does
not change RNR: it updates the region RNR already points at, i.e. the
one the previous slot just programmed. For App and Worker the empty slot
3 therefore lands on region 6 and its RASR=0 disables the task stack
guard. The FreeRTOS port ORed VALID|region into every slot, which is why
v4.36 firmware still faults on the guard while v4.37+ lets an app stack
overflow walk into the kernel heap unnoticed.

Keep VALID|region on empty slots (RASR stays 0, so the region is simply
disabled). ARMv8-M selects the region through RNR and the aliases and is
unaffected.

Observed on qemu_flint: with the App thread running, region 6 read back
as RBAR=0x6 RASR=0 while the thread's saved MPU words held the guard.

fw/syscall: run syscalls on the dedicated stack on ARMv7-M too

be4d98df1 gave App/Worker syscalls their own 2 KiB privileged stack but
only on ARMv8-M, because the relocation bounded that stack with PSPLIM.
ARMv7-M apps kept running the whole privileged call chain on their 2 KiB
task stack, and asterix reboots with StackOverflow / HardFault when a
text-heavy watchface renders a glyph that misses the cache: text layout
-> text_resources -> sys_resource_load_range -> resource_storage ->
pfs_open -> FTL -> flash consumes ~1.3 KB on top of whatever the app
already used, and the overflow happens privileged, so the kernel cannot
recover and resets.

Enable the relocation everywhere. The kernel side already handles the
missing PSPLIM; on ARMv7-M the syscall stacks get a 32 B no-access MPU
region below them instead, programmed through the free fourth per-task
slot (MemoryRegion_Task4). The fault handler treats a hit in that region
like the other stack guards, so a genuine kernel-side over-budget still
reboots with StackOverflow, while an app that runs out of its own stack
now faults unprivileged and is killed.

Verified on qemu_flint with a stress app that burns N bytes of stack and
then draws text in a custom font: with the guard alone, 512 B of extra
app usage reboots the emulator (the device failure mode); with this
change the same load succeeds (app peak 1968/2016 B, syscall stack peak
608 B) and 768 B only kills the app. WeatherGraph from the app store runs
unchanged.

fw/syscall: stop scanning the task stack on every syscall return

syscall_stack_restore_target() runs on every syscall return from an
unprivileged task to recover the task SP and PSPLIM. Since f01149f52c24
("kernel: move tasks to pbl_thread") it got PSPLIM through
pbl_thread_stack_info(), which also computes the stack high-water mark by
walking the task stack from the bottom until the first word that is not
the fill pattern. Third-party apps on obelix have a 4 KiB stack that is
mostly untouched, so each syscall return scanned ~4 KB of app RAM before
the app resumed. Graphics-heavy apps issue thousands of syscalls per
frame and slowed down visibly.

Read the stack base straight off the thread instead. Measured on
obelix@pvt with an unprivileged app looping over sys_get_ticks(): 38 us
per syscall before, 3.7 us after.

Only ARMv8-M ran syscalls on the dedicated stack in v4.37.0, which is why
asterix was not affected; with the stack now enabled on ARMv7-M too this
would have hit every board.

applib/graphics: add a minimal BiDi engine

RTL rendering reverses the codepoints of each right-to-left run but never
mirrors the glyphs that call for it, so a bracket keeps facing the same
way after the reversal and "(مرحبا)" draws as ")مرحبا(". Neutral
characters are attached to whichever run happens to be open rather than
resolved against their neighbours, so the brackets around an embedded
Latin word can land in different runs and be treated inconsistently. A
combining mark is reversed away from the letter it attaches to.

Replace rtl_support.c with bidi.c, a subset of Unicode UAX 9 sized for a
single line of watch text: P2/P3 for the paragraph direction, W1 so a
mark takes the class of the character it follows, W4-W7 so a number keeps
the separators and terminators that belong to it, N1/N2 for neutrals,
I1/I2 and L2 so runs carry an embedding level and reorder by it, and L4
for mirrored glyphs. Arabic letters are AL, so a European number after
one becomes an Arabic number (W2) and terminators and signs no longer bind
to it, matching what the phone renders. Bracket pairs (N0), explicit
directional controls, isolates and embedding levels above two are out of
scope; N0 and a linear neutral resolver are tracked as a follow-up.

The weak-LTR digit and numeric separator behaviour already in
rtl_support.c is preserved, but moves from a special case inside the
reversal into the run classification: European and Arabic-Indic numbers
resolve to their own left-to-right run, which is the level UAX 9 assigns
them in either paragraph direction. Resolving neutrals also removes the
need to peel trailing spaces into their own segment, so
rtl_segment_content_end() goes away with it.

bidi_is_needed() gates the whole path on a raw byte scan covering every
block the classifier calls strong right-to-left, so the gate and the class
table agree and nothing is right-aligned while still being drawn in
logical order. Text with none of those bytes costs one comparison per byte
and keeps taking the existing left-to-right path, unchanged.

Runs carry an embedding level rather than a direction bit, because a
number following a right-to-left run sits one level deeper than the text
around it: without the level, "Total <arabic> 123" cannot be told apart
from ordinary Latin and L2 leaves the digits on the wrong side of the
Arabic. Paragraph direction is resolved from the start of the paragraph
rather than the start of the visual line, so a wrapped paragraph does not
change base direction part way down.

The run splitter in text_layout.c collapses into one bidi_next_run() call
and mirroring is applied in both the width pass and the draw pass so the
two agree. Lam-alef ligature shaping and the segment cap are untouched.

test_rtl_support.c is replaced by test_bidi.c, which keeps its digit and
separator coverage expressed as run boundaries rather than as reversal
output.

fw/comm/ble/ancs: warn the user when iOS rejects the Control Point

Several iOS users report "connected but no notifications" with the same
watch-side signature: every 15 min alive check the Control Point write
fails with ATT 0x03 (Write Not Permitted), while the Notification and
Data Source CCCD writes succeed and no notification ever arrives. The
handles are fresh (full discovery runs on every reconnect and the CP
handle changes per session), and another phone on the same iOS version
answers the same write on the same handle with the expected 0xA2. iOS is
refusing this watch, most likely because it no longer authorises it to
read notifications ("Share System Notifications" off, denied or pending
a prompt). Nothing the watch does (re-subscribe, reconnect, reboot)
recovers that, so the existing recovery loop just spins silently.

The ANCS client counts consecutive rejected alive checks and, after two,
hands off to the ANCS notifications service, which pushes a notification
telling the user how to re-enable sharing on the iPhone. The flag
persists across connections so reconnects don't repeat the warning, and
is cleared as soon as iOS answers an alive check normally.

Seen in FIRM-4277 and FIRM-4398.

fw/services/notifications: schedule Quiet Time boundaries with cron

The scheduled Quiet Time periods were driven by a new_timer armed for
the number of seconds until the next boundary. That is a wall-clock
event, so any time change (user adjustment, phone sync, DST, time
zone) invalidated the delay, and the service compensated by rebuilding
the timer from the clock change hook. It also encoded the weekday /
weekend handover as a hand-computed "days until the other schedule
starts" delay.

Register cron jobs instead: a start and an end job per enabled
schedule, masked to WDAY_WEEKDAYS / WDAY_WEEKENDS, plus a midnight job
on Monday and Saturday for the handover between the two schedules.
Cron recomputes the jobs itself when the clock changes, so the clock
change hook only re-evaluates whether we are inside a period. Being
inside a period is now computed directly from the current time rather
than inferred from which boundary the timer was armed for.

The unit test runs against the real cron service and keeps the same
next-boundary expectations, now asserted through the service's next
execute time; the private timer-id accessors are gone.

samples at each buffer edge made the waveform depend on the write partition.

one byte and left the final held samples unflushed.

On ARMv7-M platforms (asterix, flint) every app still runs on a 2 KiB
stack. Third-party apps no longer need more since 2a222a1a8 moved their
syscalls onto a dedicated privileged stack, but system apps run
privileged, so every kernel path they reach lands on that 2 KiB stack.

name needs glyphs that are not cached yet, the draw goes menu layer ->
glance -> graphics_draw_text -> text layout -> glyph load ->
resource_load_byte_range_system -> flash_read_bytes, which on qemu_flint
leaves only 256 of 2016 bytes free before the flash driver itself runs.

the watch reboots with a HardFault every time the launcher opens. With a
system watchface such as TicToc the glyphs are already cached and the
path stays shallow, which is why only custom faces are affected.

segment, so the App RAM region, and with it the ARMv7-M MPU layout, is
unchanged; system apps just lose 2 KiB of their ~64 KiB heap. On

pointing into a guard region. When the overflow happens while the core
pushes an exception frame, the fault is a stacking error (MSTKERR) and
MMFAR is not valid, so the handler took the generic path and dumped the

whose stacked LR is the return address inside fault_handler_dump(), the
"HardFault: LR 0x7c421" asterix v4.38.2 reports: a harmless app stack
overflow became a reboot, and a privileged one lost its StackOverflow
reason.

frame, so check whether the frame overlaps a guard region instead. The
check moves into fault_handling_hit_stack_guard() so the HardFault
handler can use it too.

the app stack guard and spins until an interrupt: before, the watch
rebooted with a HardFault out of fault_handler_dump(); now the fault is
reported as "Stack overflow [task: App <...>]" and only the app is

fw/hardfault_handler: report stack guard hits as StackOverflow

A thread that runs out of stack can also fault from inside an exception
handler: PendSV saves the outgoing thread's registers onto its own
stack in software, so a thread sitting just above its guard faults in
PendSV rather than in thread mode. Whenever the MemManage handler
cannot take such a fault -- today because it runs at PendSV's priority,
and in any case inside BASEPRI critical sections -- it escalates to a
HardFault, which recorded RebootReasonCode_HardFault with PendSV's
EXC_RETURN as "LR": the "HardFault: LR 0xfffffffd" asterix v4.38.2
reports next to the stacking variant.

Check the MPU fault status in the HardFault handler too and record
StackOverflow with the current task when a stack guard was hit. The
frame is only dumped when it was stacked outside the guard.

Verified on qemu_flint with a test app that points SP 40 bytes above
the app stack guard, so the exception frame fits but the context
switch's register save does not: the watch used to reboot with
"HardFault: LR 0xfffffffd" and now reboots with "StackOverflow:
Task #3".

fw/kernel/fault_handling: only recover faults taken from an unprivileged thread

The fault handlers decide whether a fault can be survived from
CONTROL.nPRIV, i.e. from whether the current thread is privileged. That
only describes the faulting code when the fault came from thread mode.
A fault raised inside an exception handler (PendSV, SVC, SysTick) that
interrupted an unprivileged app would be "recovered" by rewriting the
handler's MSP frame to return into the app landing zone, and the
MemManage/UsageFault stack overflow paths moved MSP by 1 KiB while
running on it.

This does not happen today only because the fault handlers are
configured at the same priority as those handlers, so such faults
escalate to a HardFault. Before fixing that, recover a fault only when
it was stacked on PSP by an unprivileged thread, and reboot for
anything else, including an overflow detected on MSP.

(cherry picked from commit 8eb859b4be8e3a0eab6a5ca33f3769e249298892)

fw/kernel/fault_handling: fix the fault handler priorities

enable_fault_handlers() passes PBL_IRQ_PRIO_MAX_SYSCALL (191) to CMSIS
NVIC_SetPriority(), which expects an unshifted priority and shifts it
left by 8 - __NVIC_PRIO_BITS. (191 << 5) & 0xff is 0xe0, so on every
Cortex-M4/M33 board MemManage, BusFault and UsageFault ran at 0xe0,
the same priority as SVC, PendSV and SysTick. A fault inside any of
those handlers could not be taken and escalated to a HardFault, which
hid what went wrong: a thread overflowing its stack while PendSV saved
its registers was reported as "HardFault: LR 0xfffffffd". The raw value
came from FreeRTOS's configMAX_SYSCALL_INTERRUPT_PRIORITY and was
already wrong before the native kernel.

Shift the register value down so the fault handlers land at the
intended PBL_IRQ_PRIO_MAX_SYSCALL (0xa0 with 3 priority bits) and can
preempt the kernel exceptions. Faults inside BASEPRI critical sections
still escalate, as before.

Verified on qemu_flint: SHPR1 now reads 0x00a0a0a0 (was 0x00e0e0e0);
the context-switch stack overflow test is handled by the MemManage
handler and reboots with "StackOverflow: Task #3"; the app stack
overflow test still only kills the app; normal use (launcher, system
apps, timeline, TimeStyle) shows no faults.

(cherry picked from commit 02392de2fe287662eb5b71b32e4fcc42eb211c82)

fw/kernel/events: don't assert when a queue drains early

event_queue_cleanup_and_reset() counts the events in a queue and then
takes that many without waiting, asserting that each take succeeds. The
caller is often not the queue's consumer: an exiting app resets the
from-app queue while KernelMain is still taking events from it, and
KernelMain resets an app's to-process queue while the app task may
still be reading it. When the consumer takes an event between the count
and the drain, the last take finds the queue empty and the assert
reboots the watch.

Stop draining when the queue runs empty. The consumer handles and
cleans up any event it took, and the queue is purged afterwards as

fw/drivers/sf32lb52/audio: flush D-cache on AUDCODEC DAC buffer

The audio codec reads the playback buffer via DMA, but the CPU fills it
from cached HPSYS SRAM in two places: the initial memset() during init
and the memset()/circular_buffer_copy() pair in the half/complete IRQ
that refills whichever half DMA just finished. Without a cache flush,
the DAC can replay whatever was in RAM before those writes -- noise on
the first transfer and intermittent clicks on underrun.

Flush each half after the CPU fills it, and flush the whole buffer once
before HAL_AUDCODEC_Transmit_DMA kicks off so the codec starts on real
silence. To make flushing each half safe in isolation, over-allocate by
one cache line so haudcodec->buf lands on a line boundary; bufSize and
CFG_AUDIO_PLAYBACK_PIPE_SIZE are already multiples of the line size.

drivers/speaker: disable SF32LB DAC gain ramp to fix fade-in

HAL_AUDCODEC_Config_TChanel enables the DAC output gain ramp (RAMP_EN)

text_resources: pre-load glyph bitmaps during layout to prevent stack overflow

During text rendering, walk_line() calls get_horiz_advance() immediately
before render_glyph() for each character. Previously, get_horiz_advance()
only loaded glyph metadata (need_bitmap=false), so render_glyph() had to
load the bitmap from flash via a deep call chain (pfs_read -> flash_read
-> qspi_flash_read_blocking). On the app task's tight 2 KB stack, this
38+ frame deep chain overflows when rendering non-Latin text (e.g.
Cyrillic) through action menus.

By passing need_bitmap=true in get_horiz_advance(), the bitmap is loaded
into glyph_buffer during the advance call. The immediately following
render_glyph() then finds it cached, avoiding the deep flash I/O path
entirely.

third_party/memfault: add coredump reconstruction from PebbleOS flash coredump

On SF32LB52, HAL_PMU_Reboot() power-cycles the SoC so RAM does not
survive across reboots, and calling Memfault SDK functions from
NMI/ISR context is not possible (mutexes, flash reads). Instead of
capturing the coredump during the crash, reconstruct it after reboot
from the PebbleOS flash-based coredump.

The reconstruction reads the PebbleOS coredump from SPI flash, extracts
crash registers, FreeRTOS kernel state (task lists, pxCurrentTCB), per-
thread TCBs, and stack memory from pxTopOfStack for each thread. This
data is serialized into a Memfault-format coredump in dynamically
allocated RAM storage, which is freed after the chunk collector has
read all data.

New files:
- memfault_pebble_coredump.c/h: Core reconstruction logic. Parses the
  PebbleOS coredump chunks, builds CachedMemory regions for thread
  stacks and TCBs, and calls memfault_coredump_save(). Uses the
  memfault_exported flag to avoid re-exporting the same coredump.
- memfault_platform_coredump_storage.c: Dynamically allocated RAM-backed
  coredump storage with platform hooks (read/write/erase/clear).

Modified files:
- memfault_platform_port.c: Call reconstruction at boot, remove old
  crash-time coredump region collection code that could not work from
  NMI context.

bluetooth-fw/nimble: fix infinite loop in NimBLE store delete

When deleting a bonding via ble_store_util_delete_peer(),
NimBLE's ble_store_util_delete_all() loops calling our
store_delete callback until it returns BLE_HS_ENOENT.

prv_nimble_store_delete_sec() returned 0 (success) but relied on
a side-effect chain to remove the entry from the in-memory list:
bt_persistent_storage_delete_ble_pairing_by_addr() would call
prv_remove_ble_bonding_from_bt_driver(), which reads the identity
from SPRF, then calls bt_driver_handle_host_removed_bonding() to
remove the in-memory entry.

On the first iteration, this worked and also erased SPRF. On
subsequent iterations, SPRF was already erased, so
shared_prf_storage_get_ble_pairing_data() returned false,
prv_remove_ble_bonding_from_bt_driver() returned early without
removing the in-memory entry, and the callback returned 0 again,
creating an infinite loop that starved all lower-priority tasks
and triggered the task watchdog.

This was triggered in PRF by a repeat pairing scenario (pair
phone A, pair phone B, then phone A reconnects after removing
its pairing).

Fix by removing the entry directly from the in-memory list in
prv_nimble_store_delete_sec() before calling into persistent
storage. bt_driver_handle_host_removed_bonding() already handles
the entry being absent (null check), so no double-free risk.

Fixes FIRM-1522

analyze_coredump: handle GDB errors without aborting script

GDB --batch mode aborts the entire sourced command file on the first
error. When analyzing corrupted coredumps, commands like
'thread apply all info frame' can fail with inaccessible memory,
which silently prevents all subsequent commands (pbl heap, pbl
lockstats, pbl metadata) from ever running.

Wrap each GDB command in a python try/except so errors are printed
but execution continues. Also add a backtrace limit to prevent
infinite frame chasing on corrupted stacks, and a 5 minute timeout
as a safety net.

ble: add PPoGATT handshake timing and disconnect reason logging

Add instrumentation to diagnose FIRM-1305, where the phone gets stuck
in a Negotiating loop because the PPoGATT handshake fails repeatedly.

Key additions:
- Log HCI disconnect reason in NimBLE GAP event handler (at INFO level
  so it reaches flash logs)
- Track PPoGATT client creation time and log elapsed milliseconds at
  each handshake phase: meta read, data subscribe, session open, and
  client deletion
- Log GATT service discovery completion time relative to connection
- Add rtc stub to test_ppogatt for the new timing code

All diagnostic messages use PBL_LOG_INFO or PBL_LOG_ERR to ensure they
appear in flash logs (flash log level defaults to INFO).

fw/comm/ppogatt: reset disconnect counter on destroy

The global s_disconnect_counter was not reset when ppogatt_destroy() was
called during a BLE disconnection. This meant the counter persisted
across BLE connections, and after enough disconnect cycles (triggered by
supervision timeouts during RF interference), the PPoGATT client would
enter a permanent "stalled" state with no automatic recovery path,
requiring the user to manually toggle Bluetooth.

Reset the counter in ppogatt_destroy(), since tearing down all clients
means we are starting from a clean slate and each new BLE connection
should get a full set of recovery attempts.

fw/apps/system/music: fix divide-by-zero in track progress

Guard against track_length being zero before computing the progress
percentage. A TOCTOU race exists between music_get_pos() (which copies
track_length into local app data) and music_is_progress_reporting_supported()
(which re-reads track_length from the music service). If track_length
transitions from 0 to non-zero between those two calls, the else branch
is taken with a local track_length of 0, causing an integer divide-by-zero
UsageFault that crashes the system.

fw/services/common/accel_manager: implement accel_manager_enable

accel_manager_enable() was a no-op stub, meaning the accelerometer
was never disabled when the runlevel dropped to BareMinimum (e.g.
during factory reset). This caused an event storm as the driver kept
firing sample, shake, and double-tap callbacks into queues that were
being torn down.

Implement accel_manager_enable() to:
- On disable: stop sampling (set num_samples to 0), power down the
  ODR (set sampling_interval to 0), disable shake and double-tap
  detection.
- On enable: reconfigure the driver and re-enable shake and
  double-tap detection if there are active subscribers.

Early-return guards are also added in the driver callbacks as a
safety net against any race between disable and in-flight callbacks.

third_party/nimble: fix H4 stream desync on transport OOM

When hci_h4_sm_rx returns -1 (OOM), the transport was breaking out of
the processing loop, dropping unprocessed bytes still in the read
buffer. Since ipc_queue_read is destructive, those bytes are
permanently lost, causing the H4 state machine to desync. Eventually
the parser interprets a data byte as a packet type, leading to asserts
like the one at hci_h4.c:122 (CMD packet received from controller).

Instead of dropping bytes, yield with vTaskDelay(1) and retry, giving
other tasks a chance to free buffers. This turns a transient OOM into a
brief stall rather than a fatal desync.

fw/services/common/battery: fix false critical shutdown after charger removal

The s_low_on_first_run flag in battery_monitor was a one-way latch (||=)
that could get permanently stuck. If the first battery event after boot had
is_charging=false (e.g. charge complete) and a transiently low fuel gauge
reading, the flag latched true and never cleared. Any subsequent unplug,
even at 100%, triggered critical mode and immediate shutdown.

Fix by:
- Only setting s_low_on_first_run when booting unplugged with a low battery
  (the intended use case for quick shutdown of a dead watch).
- Clearing the flag when battery recovers above the low power threshold.

Fixes FIRM-1511

fw/logging: emit Memfault compact log entries from PBL_LOG

Add PBL_MFLT_LOG_SAVE macro that calls MEMFAULT_COMPACT_LOG_SAVE with
the PebbleOS log level mapped to Memfault levels. Integrate it into
PBL_LOG_COLOR_D so every async log call emits both a PebbleOS hashed
log entry (for serial/flash) and a compact log entry (for crash dumps).

The sync variant (PBL_LOG_COLOR_D_SYNC) is intentionally left unchanged
since it runs from ISR/constrained contexts where Memfault's recursive
mutex is not safe.

Use __has_include to guard the Memfault header for translation units
that don't have the Memfault include path (e.g. FreeRTOS). Suppress
-Wpointer-arith around the SDK macro expansion since Memfault's

fw/drivers/vibe: fix vibration strength having no effect on AW86225

vibe_set_strength() only wrote to CONTCFG7 (phase 2 amplitude), while
phase 1 amplitude in CONTCFG6[6:0] was left at the chip's power-on
default. Since vibe_ctl() sets both phase durations to max, the motor
spent all its time in phase 1 at a fixed amplitude, making the strength
setting imperceptible.

Fix by:
- Writing the scaled amplitude to both CONTCFG6[6:0] and CONTCFG7
- Initializing CONTCFG6 with full-scale drv1_lvl during vibe_init()
- Applying a blended linear/quadratic curve for wider perceptual spread
- Scaling drive durations (CONTCFG8/CONTCFG9) with strength

Fixes FIRM-1023

tests/fakes/fake_spi_flash: cover obelix filesystem without huge alloc

Tests historically pass (0, 0x1000000) to fake_spi_flash_init — sized
for snowy's flash layout, where the filesystem region sits inside the
first 16 MB of flash. On platforms whose filesystem region lives at a
higher absolute address (obelix's filesystem starts at 0x12AB0000),
every flash_read_bytes call from PFS trips the
start_addr <= s_state.offset + s_state.length assertion.

A naive expansion of length to FLASH_REGION_FILESYSTEM_END would
allocate ~319 MB per test on obelix (0x13F40000 - 0), which blows
DUMA's protect-free heap and manifests as test_put_bytes_obelix
failing on CI around install_message_while_not_idle.

Translate offset 0 to FLASH_REGION_BASE_ADDRESS on platforms with a
non-zero base, then expand length to FLASH_REGION_FILESYSTEM_END.
The obelix window now spans 0x12000000 → 0x13F40000 (~32 MB) instead
of 0 → 0x13F40000 (~319 MB). Snowy and silk are unaffected (their
base is 0, so they already cover their filesystem region).

Guarded with #ifdef so the shared_prf_storage_v3 tests, which
substitute their own minimal flash_region.h, continue to compile.

buffer from 128 ms to 320 ms. Every voice session then aborted at
pdm.c:97 ("Failed to allocate circular buffer storage") before any
audio was captured.

Both buffers are fixed-size, exist once per device, and are only used
while the mic is running. Move them to .bss, drop the alloc/free
helpers, and remove the now-dead NULL guards. This also takes ~21 KB of
pressure off the kernel heap for everything else.

Fixes FIRM-1662

fw/services/normal: instrument storage mutex and settings compaction

Add temporary timing instrumentation to help diagnose multi-second
KernelMain UI stalls reported in FIRM-1649. Two known triggers (a
QuickView event arriving from the phone, saving an Alarm) both reduce
to "something wrote a settings/BlobDB file while a flash-heavy
operation was running", and the suspected root cause is
settings_file_compact() running under TimelineItemStorage->mutex while
ftl_erase_sector_blocking() ties up the flash bus for several seconds.
flash_erase_sector_blocking() feeds the task watchdog internally, which
explains why the user sees a recoverable freeze rather than a reboot.

This patch wires up two pieces of telemetry to confirm or kill the
hypothesis:

- timeline_item_storage.c: wrap every mutex_lock/unlock pair with
  prv_storage_lock/prv_storage_unlock helpers that measure both the
  wait-for-lock time and the hold time, and PBL_LOG_WARNING when
  either crosses 100 ms. The log line includes __func__ and the
  storage name so we know which operation stalled and on which
  database (pin_db, reminder_db, ...).

- settings_file.c: log entry and exit of settings_file_rewrite_filtered
  with elapsed ms and final status. This covers both the auto-trigger
  via settings_file_compact() from settings_file_set() and the
  explicit rewrite path used by timeline_item_storage_flush().

If the hypothesis is right we expect to see triples like:

  FIRM-1649: settings_file_rewrite_filtered start file=pin_db
  FIRM-1649: settings_file_rewrite_filtered end file=pin_db
  elapsed=4823ms status=0
  FIRM-1649: timeline_item_storage_read waited 4810ms for pin_db mutex

To revert once we land the real fix:
git grep FIRM-1649 src/fw/services/normal

Refs FIRM-1649

fw/comm/ble/ppogatt: fix infinite disconnect/reconnect loop

ppogatt_destroy() was unconditionally resetting s_disconnect_counter on
every BLE disconnect. This meant the stall protection (which should kick
in after PPOGATT_DISCONNECT_COUNT_MAX consecutive failed resets) never
triggered, causing an infinite disconnect/reconnect loop when the phone
doesn't respond to ResetRequest.

Only reset the counter when the disconnect was external (e.g. RF
interference, phone out of range). When we initiated the disconnect
ourselves due to max resets (disconnect_requested), preserve the counter
so the stall state can be reached after repeated failures.

This partially reverts 5b55ae808 ("fw/comm/ppogatt: reset disconnect
counter on destroy"), which fixed the opposite problem (FIRM-1419:
premature stalling after legitimate disconnects). The new approach
handles both cases by checking disconnect_requested to distinguish
self-initiated from external disconnects.

third_party: scope per-library cflags to their targets

Several third_party wscripts modified the shared bld.env.CFLAGS via
append_unique to add library-specific warning suppressions. Because
bld.env is global and targets capture it at definition time, those
flags leaked into every subsequently-defined target (hal_sifli,
fw drivers, nimble, ...). This hid the fact that some of those
downstream targets had genuine sign-compare/type-limits/unused-*
warnings, and flagged them only on boards where the upstream leak
path wasn't taken (e.g. getafix_dvt, which doesn't build gh3x2x and
so did not inherit -Wno-sign-compare from nonfree).

Move each suppression to the cflags= keyword of the specific target
that needs it:

- qr_code_generator: -Wno-type-limits on qrcodegen.c
- nonfree/gh3x2x: -Wno-sign-compare on the gh3x2x objects
- hal_sifli: existing -Wno-unused-* plus -Wno-sign-compare and
  -Wno-type-limits on the hal_sifli stlib

With the prior commits cleaning up the warnings in our own code
that were previously masked by the leak, both obelix_dvt and
getafix_dvt now build cleanly without relying on flag leakage.

fw/shell/normal/prefs: enable stationary mode by default

Stationary mode is the mechanism that drops the system to
RunLevel_Stationary after 30 minutes of no motion (when not on
charger), which in turn disables the HRM, backlight, BT, and vibes
until the user touches the watch or an alarm fires. With the
release default set to false on every non-Spalding platform, this
safety net was effectively dormant in the field: users would have
to find Settings > Display > Stationary Mode to opt in, so on an
Obelix left off-wrist at night the HRM kept firing its green LEDs
every 10 minutes.

Flip the default to on so every platform matches what Spalding and
debug builds already do. Users who previously opted out retain
their saved preference, since the load loop only overwrites the
default when a value is persisted.

Fixes FIRM-1523

fw/kernel: fix task_cpu_app_pct overflow when apps come and go

The App and Worker task slots are dynamic: tasks are created on launch
and destroyed on exit, so their FreeRTOS ulRunTimeCounter does not
persist across an app restart. Diffing the current counter against a
stale previous value underflowed uint32 and pushed the reported
percentage to ~4 billion cycles per delta_total, surfacing as spikes
around 116k on the task_cpu_app_pct chart.

Capture each dying task's final ulRunTimeCounter into a per-slot
sticky accumulator from pebble_task_unregister(), and report cumulative
slot cycles (sticky + currently-alive counter) in the heartbeat. This
keeps cycles attributed to the App/Worker slots even when several apps
launch and exit within a single (~1 hour) heartbeat period.

The unregister clears the task handle before crediting the cycles, and
the collector snapshots sticky cycles before walking the live task
list. Together these orderings ensure cycles consumed by a task that
dies mid-collection are never double-counted; in the worst case they
are reported one heartbeat late.

fw/services/settings: add growable settings files

settings_file_open pre-allocates the PFS file at ~120% of
max_used_space, so a large per-app cap forces every persist file to
claim that much flash up front, even when most apps only use a few
hundred bytes. To make raising the cap cheap, decouple the enforcement
cap from the physical allocation.

Add an alloc_used_space field to SettingsFile that tracks the physical
allocation budget separately from max_used_space. A new
settings_file_open_growable() API sets alloc_used_space to a small
initial value. When a write needs more physical space but fits within
the enforcement cap, the file is automatically grown via rewrite with
doubling allocation (e.g. 4K -> 8K -> 16K -> ... up to max_used_space).

To prevent grown files from holding flash hostage indefinitely after
the data is no longer needed, settings_file_compact picks the smallest
doubling step that leaves ~2x headroom over live data and lowers
alloc_used_space toward the floor before rewriting. The new
min_alloc_used_space field tracks the per-file floor (the
initial_alloc_size requested at open) so files never shrink below the
caller's stated minimum. Existing callers of settings_file_open() are
unchanged: alloc_used_space and min_alloc_used_space both equal
max_used_space, preserving the old pre-allocation behavior with no
shrink.

The persist service now uses settings_file_open_growable() with a
4 KiB initial allocation (~5 KiB physical), close to the existing
6 KiB cap.

fw/services/settings: speed up file rewrite, pause watchdog

settings_file_rewrite_filtered runs under a held mutex while issuing
flash erases and writes that, on a 1 MiB persist file, can take many
seconds. Once the per-app cap was raised the rewrite started tripping
the 5-second task watchdog and triggering App Throttling. FIRM-1649
flagged this; it didn't matter at the old 6 KiB cap.

Three changes:

- Pause the task watchdog for the duration of the rewrite (60 s
  budget, comfortably covers a worst-case 1 MiB rewrite). Same pattern
  already used during boot in main.c.
- Add settings_raw_iter_read_key_val / write_key_val helpers that
  read or write the key and value as a single contiguous PFS call.
  Drops per-record I/O from 6 PFS round-trips (separate header, key,
  val) to 4, which on a file with thousands of records saves a few
  hundred ms of seek/read state-machine overhead.
- Allocate one reusable buffer outside the rewrite loop instead of
  two kernel_malloc/kernel_free pairs per record.

Flash erase and program time still dominate, so this doesn't make
small rewrites feel different, but the watchdog pause keeps big
rewrites from triggering throttle/recovery storms in the logs.

fw/services/notifications: only persist migrated vibe scores at boot

alerts_preferences_init() unconditionally rewrote all three vibe score
keys to the settings file on every boot. With settings sync now using
settings_file timestamps for conflict resolution, that fresh-timestamp
rewrite let the watch win every conflict against the phone and made the
phone's INSERT_WITH_TIMESTAMP for the user's chosen value look stale.
The watch's writeback then got DATA_STALE from the phone, sync.c marked
the item synced anyway with no retry, and the user's setting could no
longer propagate.

Capture each vibe score after RESTORE_PREF and only re-persist a key
when migration or validation actually changed its value. Steady-state
boots no longer touch the file, so on-disk timestamps reflect real user
intent rather than the most recent boot.

fw/services/blob_db: canonicalise notif-pref key length

The phone-side BlobDB protocol writes notif-pref keys with a trailing
null terminator (key_len = strlen+1), while alerts_preferences locally
uses strlen() (no null) for both reads and writes. settings_file matches
records on exact key_len, so a phone-pushed value landed in a record
that alerts_preferences_init's RESTORE_PREF could not find on the next
boot, leaving the in-memory state at the platform default
(VibeScoreId_NudgeNudge on obelix). The user-visible symptom was the
notification vibe pattern resetting to "Nudge Nudge" after every reboot.

Strip a trailing null at every settings_blob_db notif-pref entry point
so on-disk records converge on the canonical strlen() length, and probe
both lengths in RESTORE_PREF so legacy records written before this
change still resolve.

fw/services/compositor: render request for App-to-App transition

When `compositor_transition()` reached the "App to App" else branch
(also taken when a Modal-to-App transition was cancelled mid-animation
and a new transition kicked off while no modal exists), it set the
state to `AppTransitionPending` without calling
`prv_send_app_render_request()`. This left the compositor waiting on a
`PEBBLE_RENDER_READY_EVENT` that the app never sent, freezing the
display until an external event triggered another transition.

This was reproducible by dismissing a notification and immediately
receiving and dismissing a second one, leaving the screen frozen
until a third notification arrived.

Mirror the Modal-to-App branch and request an app render before
moving to `AppTransitionPending`.

Fixes FIRM-1713.

third_party/nimble/transport/hci_sf32lb52: wake LCPU before power off

lcpu_power_off() touches LPSYS_AON registers via
HAL_RCC_Reset_and_Halt_LCPU(), which only succeed while the HP->LP wake
request is held. lcpu_power_on() finishes by cancelling that request,
so a subsequent ble_transport_ll_deinit() call faults with a precise
bus fault at LPSYS_AON_BASE (0x40040000) once the LP system has slept.

Hold the wake request across the deinit and drop it after, mirroring
what lcpu_power_on() does on the way in.

bluetooth: refresh advertising state on host resync

Add a bt_driver_handle_host_resynced() callback that the BT driver
invokes each time the NimBLE host (re)synchronizes with the controller.
gap_le_advert handles it by clearing the cached ad-data pointer (the
controller forgot it across the reset) and re-running the current job,
so advertising comes back up on its own after a host reset.

Without this, anything that triggers ble_hs_sched_reset() while
advertising leaves the watch silent: the disconnect propagates up
before the host has resynced, so the upper layer's set-data and
adv-enable calls fail with BLE_HS_ENOTSYNCED / BLE_HS_ENOADDR and
nothing retries them once sync completes.

applib/graphics: measure Arabic words using shaped widths

word_init() and the renderer's segment-collection pass measured
each Arabic letter using its basic codepoint (U+0621-U+064A), but
the renderer shapes letters to their contextual presentation forms
(initial/medial/final/isolated) before drawing. Isolated forms are
typically wider than the connected forms that actually render, so
the layout over-estimated word widths and wrapped them to the next
line even when they fit, and the segment-collection pass dropped
trailing letters once its (unshaped) running width hit the line's
(shaped) budget, leaving a visible gap at the line edge.

Extract the per-letter shaping decision from arabic_shape_text()
into arabic_shape_codepoint(prev, curr, next) and use it for width
measurement in both places so layout, segment collection, and the
draw pass agree on every glyph's advance. Non-Arabic codepoints
short-circuit and pass through unchanged, so other scripts are
unaffected.

services/speaker: anti-alias square wave with PolyBLEP

Naive square-wave generation produced clean output only at
frequencies whose half-period was an integer number of output
samples, i.e. f = 8000/n at our 16 kHz output rate. For every
other frequency, including essentially all MIDI notes, the
half-cycles drifted in length and the unbandlimited harmonics
aliased into the audible band, producing the harsh distortion
users reported.

Apply PolyBLEP at the rising and falling edges of the square wave
to suppress aliasing without changing the fundamental. Sine,
triangle, and sawtooth are unchanged; only the square branch picks
up the correction.

Verified at 16 kHz output: zero-crossings now match the requested
fundamental exactly for 100, 261.6 (C4), 440 (A4), 1000, 2000 and
4000 Hz. The amplitude tapers near Nyquist as the band-limited
square converges to a sine, which is the expected behavior.

Fixes SDK-99 / #1215

bluetooth-fw/nimble: roll back host state on failed start

When bt_driver_start() fails after ble_hs_sched_start() has already run
(host_started semaphore timeout, or ble_hs_util_ensure_addr failure),
NimBLE has already transitioned ble_hs_enabled_state to ON. Returning
false to the caller leaves a state mismatch: bluetooth_ctl believes the
stack is stopped (s_comm_is_running = false), but NimBLE thinks the
host is on. The next bt_driver_start() call schedules another start,
ble_hs_start() returns BLE_HS_EALREADY, and the bare assert(rc == 0)
in ble_hs_event_start_stage2 reboots the watch.

Fix it from both ends:

- Add an idempotency guard at the top of bt_driver_start(): if the
  host is already enabled, treat the call as a successful no-op so
  the bluetooth_ctl state machine can converge.
- On the failure paths inside bt_driver_start(), call ble_hs_stop()
  and wait for it to drive the state back to OFF before returning.

Fixes FIRM-1837.

The DA7212 is the I2S master here, so dropping SYSTEM_ACTIVE=0 yanks

its STOP task — anomaly 194's resource-release workaround assumes some
clocking is still in flight, so EasyDMA gets left in a stale state.

to: mute → I2S stop+uninit → codec power-down.

fw/drivers/nrf5/audio: keep codec + I2S warm across pause

Spamming play/pause distorted audio on Asterix as a sweeping phaser
that only a hard power cycle would clear. Each audio_stop power-cycled
the DA7212; over many cycles, residual DC bias from mid-ramp DAC
shutdowns latched onto the LINE-out coupling cap and drove the speaker
amp into self-oscillation, beating against new audio.

Stop power-cycling on every pause. audio_stop now just clears
is_running / trans_cb — the codec stays SYSTEM_ACTIVE=1 with its DAI
master running, the nRF I2S keeps clocking, and the ISR's
prv_fill_i2s_buffer auto-zero-fills as soon as the circular buffer
drains, so the codec sees uninterrupted clocks and a continuous (silent)
data stream throughout a spam sequence. Within
AUDIO_IDLE_SHUTDOWN_MS, audio_start just flips is_running back on and
the next refill lands real audio — no PLL re-lock, no I2S re-init, zero
transitions on the analog domain. A new_timer fires the real shutdown
only after the device has actually been idle.

Add a PebbleMutex around the cold/warm/active transitions so
audio_start, audio_stop, and prv_idle_shutdown can't race across
threads.

Fixes FIRM-1742

fw/comm/ble/ancs: bound notification queue and fail-soft on OOM

Users with many chatty ANCS apps (e.g. Tapo, Apple Home, Nanit,
Outlook, Mail, Slack, Twitter, Flipboard) hit a watch reboot whenever
the post-reconnect notification storm drove the kernel heap to
exhaustion. prv_notif_queue_push_attr_request used kernel_malloc_check
for a 20-byte allocation; a single failure called PBL_CROAK_OOM and
took the system down — losing BlobDB sync state and forcing the user
back through pairing.

Cap the pending-attribute queue at 16 entries, bounding worst-case
heap exposure to ~320 B regardless of how many UIDs the iPhone pushes
in a burst. Action ops aren't capped — they're user-initiated and
rare.

Switch both push paths to kernel_malloc and drop the request with a
WRN if the allocation fails. Missing one ANCS get-attributes round
trip is recoverable (iOS will resend on the next state change); a
reboot is not.

flake.nix: pin make SHELL to /bin/sh on Darwin

Moddable's build/makefiles/mac/tools.mk generates launcher scripts for
mcconfig, mcrun, etc. via `echo '#!/bin/bash\n...'` and relies on the
shell's `echo` builtin expanding `\n` into a real newline. macOS
/bin/sh (bash 3.2, XSI-compliant in POSIX mode) does this; Nix's bash
5.x — which `make` finds first as `sh` via PATH inside the devshell —
does not. The result is a single-line script with a malformed shebang,
so `mcconfig` fails to launch and `./waf configure` aborts with
"Failed to build Moddable tools".

runs recipes under the expected shell regardless of PATH ordering.

fw/drivers/mic/sf32lb52: switch to mono capture

Obelix and Getafix were configured for stereo PDM capture even though
Speex compresses to mono and there is no current consumer of the second
channel (it is reserved for future environmental noise cancellation but
unused today). The PDM circular buffer was hard-coded for two channels
and asked the kernel heap for a 20 KB contiguous block on every voice
session, which frequently fails once the heap fragments.

Drop the hard-coded PDM_CH_COUNT macro and size the circular buffer
from MicDevice.channels at allocation time, so the board file controls
the footprint. Flip both Obelix and Getafix to mono, halving the
contiguous block we ask the heap for (10 KB requested / 4 KB floor).

fw/services/voice: keep Speex encoder alive across sessions

voice_speex_init() allocated the Speex encoder state, frame buffer, and
encoded buffer on every dictation session; voice_cancel_dictation()
armed a 100 ms timer to call voice_speex_deinit() on every cancellation.
When the phone fires a retry storm (e.g. sessions 14 through 25 within
a second on the same connection) the watch runs that alloc/free cycle a
dozen times in quick succession, which is the textbook way to fragment
a coalescing heap. Once fragmented, even the fallback 4 KB PDM circular
allocation can fail.

Stop tearing the encoder down between sessions. voice_speex_init()
already short-circuits when initialized, so the first dictation pays
the alloc cost and every subsequent session reuses the buffers.

This also removes the delayed-cleanup machinery whose only reason for
existing was to dodge a race between cancel and the audio endpoint
shutdown -- with no cleanup happening the race vanishes. The three
divergent branches in voice_cancel_dictation collapse to a single
inline teardown.

Cost: the Speex state (~6 KB after the mono switch) and its frame /
encoded buffers stay resident in the kernel heap once voice has been
used at least once. Boot footprint is unchanged.

Fixes FIRM-1862
Fixes FIRM-1843

The kernel heap analytics reported only memory_pct_max (peak usage),
which hides fragmentation: an allocation can fail because no single

third_party/memfault: fingerprint crashes on the real call site

The reconstructed Memfault coredump's PC came from the PebbleOS coredump's
running/ISR thread, which is unconditionally set to NMI_Handler in
core_dump.c. That made every assert/OOM/watchdog/EventQueueFull issue group
under titles like "Assert at NMI_Handler" or "Out Of Memory at __DSB" /
"... at core_dump_reset" depending on how far Memfault's symbolicator
unwound past the handler frame.

The kernel already stashes the real crash-site address in RebootReason
before pending the NMI (the LR captured via __builtin_return_address, or
the specialized fields for OOM/watchdog/EventQueueFull). Use that to
override s_core_regs.pc so Memfault fingerprints on the function that
actually faulted instead of the crash handler.

The deeper stack trace still won't unwind cleanly through NMI_Handler
since SP points into ISR context — that's a separate problem.

normal-FW pairing) and could not connect until they manually forgot

one replaces the old. Also prune at boot in case the DB was already in
a multi-bonding state (legacy data, or a PRF pairing layered on top of
an existing one): keep the most recently modified BLE bonding (by the
settings file last_modified timestamp) and delete the rest.

the delete out into an internal helper that does not touch shared PRF
storage; the existing public delete keeps its current behavior of
erasing it.

match the qemu/stub driver behavior (no-op when the bonding was never
registered) instead of asserting, since the new prune path issues
removes for entries the driver may never have been told about.

bluetooth-fw/nimble: track driver state to prevent stage2 assert

ble_hs_event_start_stage2 asserts if ble_hs_enabled_state isn't OFF when
it runs. The existing ble_hs_is_enabled() guard at the top of
bt_driver_start only catches the ON case, so a leaked STOPPING state
(error-path ble_hs_stop whose s_host_stopped wait times out before the
vendor's completion callback fires) slips past the guard and trips the
stage2 assert on the next start attempt, rebooting the watch.

Track our own driver state (Stopped / Starting / Started / Stopping) and
gate bt_driver_start on it:

- On entry, if state is Stopping, retry the s_host_stopped wait so a
  late vendor completion (the vendor's own 2 s timeout always fires
  ble_hs_stop_done eventually) can transition us back to Stopped before
  we schedule a new start.
- On a successful start, advance to Started; on the err: path, mark
  Stopping before invoking ble_hs_stop and roll back to Stopped only
  once the stop completion is observed (or vendor reports EALREADY).
- Drain stale host_started / host_stopped signals before each wait so a
  semaphore left over from a prior cycle can't satisfy this cycle's
  wait.
- bt_driver_stop mirrors the same transitions; keeps the existing
  PBL_ASSERT on stop timeout.

If the retry wait still times out, probe the vendor with
ble_hs_stop(NULL, NULL, NULL) to recover from a lost completion signal:

- BLE_HS_EALREADY -> vendor state is OFF; the completion signal was
  lost, but it's safe to mark Stopped and proceed with the start.
- 0 -> vendor is still STOPPING; refuse, as before.

The probe is side-effect-free in OFF (no work done) and STOPPING (no
listener registered since we pass NULL). It would otherwise initiate
a stop from ON, which can't happen on this path: we only enter
Stopping by calling ble_hs_stop ourselves, and the only vendor
transition out of STOPPING is to OFF.

Writes to s_driver_state happen only on the lifecycle thread (callers
serialize via bluetooth_ctl's state mutex); the stop completion callback
still only signals the semaphore.

Refs FIRM-1837.

not-worn signal, but its accel-only off-wrist heuristic takes 30+

sys_send_pebble_event_to_kernel forwarded any PebbleEvent posted by an
app/worker straight onto the kernel queue without inspecting its type.

kernel main loop call into app-supplied code with full kernel rights.

from app memory but only asserted the struct itself was in userspace.
The embedded ListNode prev/next pointers were trusted, so an app could
craft a handler whose list_node.{prev,next} aimed at kernel memory and
call unsubscribe to make list_remove() run

user-supplied list head also let list_find traverse from app memory
into kernel memory.

RAM before list_remove runs, and re-derive the list head in-kernel
from the authoritative per-process state instead of trusting the

Every syscall in this file (data_unsubscribe, set_sampling_rate,
set_sample_buffer, get_num_samples, consume_samples) took an
AccelManagerState* straight from the app. The kernel then read and
wrote fields on it (timestamp_ms, raw_buffer, num_samples, list_node)
without checking the pointer was one we had handed out. An app could
fabricate a struct that overlaid a target kernel address and use
get_num_samples in particular as an arbitrary 8-byte read/write
primitive on kernel memory:

  get_num_samples(&fake, (uint64_t *)addr);

really is one we allocated, and reject the call via syscall_failed()
otherwise. Also validate the timestamp_ms out-parameter is in the
caller's userspace.

    far past the validated buffer.

    can change *num_records after we validated it but before the
    callback reads it — classic TOCTOU.

fw/drivers/mpu: hide ARMv7-M subregion math inside the backend

MpuRegion previously exposed a disabled_subregions field that callers
had to compute via tools/mpu_calc.py at build time. That field is an
ARMv7-M MPU implementation detail (rounding an arbitrary range up to a
power-of-two block plus an 8-bit subregion mask) and has no analogue on
ARMv8-M, which programs the limit register directly.

Drop the field from the public struct. Callers now pass the real
(base_address, size) pair. The ARMv7-M backend's mpu_get_register_settings
computes the block + subregion mask at runtime from these values, and
mpu_get_region decodes them back from the registers. ARMv8-M is
unchanged. The generated kernel/mpu_regions.auto.h header and the
mpu_calc.py helper that produced it both go away; memory_layout.c reads
the actual __APP_RAM__/__APP_RAM_size__/__WORKER_RAM__/__WORKER_RAM_size__
linker symbols directly, removing a source of drift between the linker
script and the auto-generated MPU sizes.

- App task running (control=0x2) sees AP=3 (priv R/W + user R/W) on
  App RAM and AP=1 (priv-only) on Worker RAM, with subregion masks
  byte-identical to what mpu_calc.py used to emit.
- Stack guard region (32B at __isr_stack_start__) programmed AP=0
  (no access).
- Menu navigation through multiple submenus exercises the App-task
  context switch path without faults.

launcher (MPU still disabled at runtime via the early-return that a
later step removes).

fw/drivers/mpu: replace bool-quad permissions with symbolic enum

MpuRegion previously carried four bool fields (priv_read, priv_write,
user_read, user_write) and the backends matched all four against a
table to find the AP encoding. The mapping is small and well-known
(6 useful combinations), so the table-lookup-per-region was overkill
-- and worse, the bool quad pretended that arbitrary combinations
were expressible. Two of them aren't on ARMv8-M, and the backend
silently aliased them to the wrong-but-closest encoding.

Replace the four bools with an MpuPermissions enum (NoAccess, PrivRW,
PrivRW_UserRO, PrivRW_UserRW, PrivRO, PrivRO_UserRO) and drop the
PermissionMapping struct. The enum doc in drivers/mpu.h calls out
which values are degraded on ARMv8-M (NoAccess -> PrivRO; PrivRW_UserRO
-> PrivRW_UserRW) so callers can't be surprised. The forward lookup
becomes a direct O(1) array index; the reverse lookup (for
mpu_get_region) is a small switch.

mpu_init_region_from_region() now asserts that its source is a PrivRW
region (the App/Worker RAM case) and toggles between PrivRW and
PrivRW_UserRW based on allow_user_access -- the previous code wrote
into user_read/user_write directly with no check that the source
permissions made sense.

memory_layout_dump_mpu_regions_to_dbgserial() prints the symbolic
name now ("PrivRW_UserRO") instead of "Priv: RW User: R " -- easier
to scan in fault output.

Verified on qemu_flint and qemu_emery: identical AP values written
to the MPU, test_mpu_violation still triggers MemManage with CFSR=0x82
MMFAR=__WORKER_RAM__.

fw/kernel/pebble_tasks: drop redundant MPU stack guard on ARMv8-M

The Cortex-M33 has hardware stack-pointer-limit registers (PSPLIM /
MSPLIM) that raise UsageFault on any push below the limit. The
FreeRTOS CM33 port we use already sets PSPLIM per task in
portSetupTCB() to the bottom of the task's stack, so thread stack
overflows are caught directly in hardware -- no MPU region required.

The per-task MPU stack-guard region was redundant on ARMv8-M and not
even particularly effective: ARMv8-M's two-bit AP field can't encode
"no access", so the slot was programmed with AP=2 (priv-RO) as the
closest approximation. That catches an unprivileged write to the
guard but lets a privileged kernel task read or write into it -- the
opposite of what a stack-overflow detector should do.

Skip programming the per-task stack-guard region on ARMv8-M and let
PSPLIM do the job. Frees one of the four per-task MPU slots (slot 6
on QEMU CM33, slot 10 on SF32LB52) -- now disabled when the App task
runs.

ARMv7-M behavior is unchanged: the MPU AP=0 ("no access") encoding
is precise there and PSPLIM doesn't exist, so the per-task MPU
stack-guard region remains the canonical mechanism. ISR-stack
overflow is independently caught by MSPLIM (set elsewhere) plus the
static MemoryRegion_IsrStackGuard region, which still gets programmed
on every board.

Verified on qemu_emery: App task runs with slot 6 disabled, PSPLIM
points to __APP_RAM__+__stack_guard_size__ (0x20048020), MSPLIM
points to __isr_stack_start__ (0x200130e0), and test_mpu_violation
still triggers MemManage on the Worker RAM write. qemu_flint App
task still has slot 6 active (AP=0, 32 B at __APP_RAM__).

fw/drivers/mpu: plumb an executable bit through MpuRegion

MpuRegion's existing fields described address range, cache policy and
access permissions, but not whether the region is executable. The
backends silently programmed XN=0 (execute allowed) for every region,
which is fine on every board the firmware ships on today (the only
executable RAM is App / Worker / Flash regions that we want
executable anyway), but it's the wrong default once we start carving
new firmware-managed regions out of SRAM that should be data-only.

Add `bool executable:1` to MpuRegion, defaulting to false (XN=1).
Wire it through both backends: ARMv7-M sets RASR.XN (bit 28),
ARMv8-M sets RBAR.XN (bit 0). Region initializers in memory_layout.c
opt in for the three executable regions:

  - s_microflash_region (firmware text in flash)
  - s_app_region        (App process .text relocated into App RAM)
  - s_worker_region     (Worker process .text relocated into Worker RAM)

Everything else (RO BSS, stack guards) stays XN=1, which is a small
defense-in-depth improvement: code injection into kernel BSS or a
stack-guard region can't be executed even from privileged context.

memory_layout_dump_mpu_regions_to_dbgserial() grows an "X"/"-" column
in the fault dump.

No behavior change on QEMU boards (the existing regions that needed
to be executable opt in; nothing else relied on RAM being globally
executable, since the vendor's wide RAM region with XN=0 only exists
on SF32LB52). Verified on qemu_flint: launcher renders, App task
runs the unprivileged test_mpu_violation app, Worker-RAM write still
faults (CFSR=0x82, MMFAR=__WORKER_RAM__). qemu_emery and obelix_dvt
build clean.

fw/drivers/mic/sf32lb52: invalidate D-cache on PDM DMA buffer

The PDM peripheral writes captured samples straight into pRxBuffPtr via
DMA, bypassing the CPU's D-cache. The half/complete callbacks then read
that buffer from cached HPSYS SRAM, so they can pick up pre-DMA bytes
that are still sitting in cache instead of the freshly captured audio.

Invalidate the relevant half before the CPU touches it. To make that
safe (invalidation discards dirty lines), over-allocate by one cache
line so pRxBuffPtr lands on a line boundary; the half-buffer stride is
already a multiple of the line size, so the two halves don't share any
lines and neither shares lines with neighboring allocations.

fw/drivers/sf32lb52/audio: flush D-cache on AUDCODEC DAC buffer

The audio codec reads the playback buffer via DMA, but the CPU fills it
from cached HPSYS SRAM in two places: the initial memset() during init
and the memset()/circular_buffer_copy() pair in the half/complete IRQ
that refills whichever half DMA just finished. Without a cache flush,
the DAC can replay whatever was in RAM before those writes -- noise on
the first transfer and intermittent clicks on underrun.

Flush each half after the CPU fills it, and flush the whole buffer once
before HAL_AUDCODEC_Transmit_DMA kicks off so the codec starts on real
silence. To make flushing each half safe in isolation, over-allocate by
one cache line so haudcodec->buf lands on a line boundary; bufSize and
CFG_AUDIO_PLAYBACK_PIPE_SIZE are already multiples of the line size.

fw/drivers/mpu/armv8m: shift MAIR indices on SF32LB52

On SF32LB52 the SiFli vendor code (system_bf0_ap.c) programs its own
MPU regions during SystemInit() and burns MAIR indices 0..2 (code,
ram-non-cacheable, device) for those regions. Pebble's MpuCachePolicy
values previously mapped directly to MAIR indices 0..3, which means
turning on mpu_enable() would silently overwrite SiFli's attributes
and mislabel its regions.

Route Pebble's cache policies through mair_index(), which adds a
MAIR_INDEX_BASE offset of 4 on SF32LB52 (0 elsewhere), so Pebble owns
indices 4..7 while SiFli keeps 0..2 untouched. Reverse the offset in
mpu_get_region() so cache_policy round-trips through MpuCachePolicy.

Also stop clobbering MPU_CTRL when the MPU is already enabled --
ARM_MPU_Enable() writes the whole register, which on SF32LB52 would
drop SiFli's HFNMIENA bit. OR in PRIVDEFENA instead when MPU is live.

fw/drivers/mpu: fix ARMv8-M MAIR indices and task RBAR

Two latent bugs surfaced once per-task MPU regions were turned on for
SF32LB52, both causing UsageFault UNALIGNED when an app first touched
its own RAM:

1. SF32LB52 kept five reserved entries in MpuCachePolicy to avoid
   colliding with vendor MAIR slots. The ARMv8-M backend also shifted
   policies by MAIR_INDEX_BASE, so Pebble regions used attribute indices
   9..12. CMSIS correctly treats those as invalid, leaving Pebble's
   MAIR slots at reset value 0 = Device-nGnRnE. Remove the reserved
   enum entries and let mair_index() be the single place that maps
   symbolic cache policies onto MAIR slots 4..7 on SF32LB52.

2. xRegion[].ulRegionBaseAddress was the raw base on ARMv8-M. The
   FreeRTOS CM33 port copies that field straight into MPU_RBAR, which
   on ARMv8-M carries the SH/AP/XN bits in addition to the base
   address. Pebble's mpu_set_task_configurable_regions() was storing
   `mpu_region->base_address` there, so the AppRAM region landed with
   AP=00 (priv-RW only). ARMv7-M's RBAR does not carry AP, so the raw
   base is wanted there. Pick base_reg vs raw base based on
   MPU_TYPE_ARMV8M, and initialize disabled slots to a known zero base.

fw/drivers/display/sf32lb: crash on LCDC silent loss

A class of field-reported "frozen screen, buttons still react" issues
(FIRM-1740 family) traces to the SiFli HAL's ICB-overflow path
(bf0_hal_lcdc.c HAL_LCDC_IRQHandler) setting HAL_LCDC_ERROR_OVERFLOW
without invoking XferCpltCallback or XferErrorCallback, so the firmware
silently loses the completion. s_updating stays true, the compositor
quiesces, and the user sees a frozen screen that never recovers and
never crashes (so we never get a Memfault coredump either).

Add a 500ms detection timer in the compositor update path. If the EOF
callback hasn't fired by the timeout, snapshot the LCDC peripheral
register file into a BSS buffer (Sifli needs these for HAL-side
analysis; the PebbleOS coredump captures all of HPSYS SRAM but not
MMIO) and PBL_CROAK. The user sees a reboot instead of a freeze, and
we ship a coredump to Sifli for root-cause analysis.

The race between EOF firing and the timer expiring (terminate event
sitting on the KernelMain queue past the timeout) is handled by a
volatile s_eof_observed flag set from the IRQ; the timer handler
aborts the crash if EOF was observed, keeping false-positive crashes
out of the picture.

A debug-only prompt command `display drop_complete`
(!RELEASE && (OBELIX || GETAFIX)) arms a one-shot drop of the next
EOF callback for end-to-end verification on hardware.

Builds on the work in #1189; supersedes it with the simpler crash
approach (per review feedback). Drops the recovery + telemetry layer
since coredumps capture richer state than CDRs and Memfault classifies
crashes naturally without a separate heartbeat metric.

fw/drivers/qemu: reset callback_pending on drain entry

prv_uart_irq_handler() sets s_qemu_state.callback_pending = true when
queueing a drain callback into KernelMain via event_put_isr(), but
nothing ever clears it again. After the first callback fires:

  1. Subsequent ISR-side triggers (footer sighting, ISR buffer full,
     recv error) all hit the !callback_pending guard and silently drop
     the request to schedule another drain.
  2. The ISR keeps appending bytes to s_qemu_state.isr_buffer.
  3. Once the buffer fills, the ISR disables the UART RX interrupt and
     waits for prv_process_receive_buffer() to drain — but no callback
     will ever be scheduled to do that, because callback_pending is
     stuck true.

The whole protocol stack wedges mid-transfer. Symptom: pebble install
runs cleanly for ~8 cycles against a freshly-booted emulator, then
PutBytes hangs partway through resources transfer with the firmware
silent. With the qemu_emery board this is reproducible by looping
`pebble install --qemu localhost:12344` against `./waf qemu`.

Reset the flag at the entry of prv_process_receive_buffer() so any
subsequent ISR trigger queues a fresh callback. Drain semantics are
unchanged — the function still loops until the assembly buffer has no
complete message — but new bytes that arrive after this drain finishes
will now make it past the guard.
